  - [x] stat() ABI translation (CRITICAL bugfix): SYS_FS_STAT/LSTAT/FSTAT write a compact 16-byte FsStatResult (size u64 @0, entry_type u8 @8, nlinks u32 @12), not a POSIX `struct stat` — callers had been handing the syscall a `struct stat` pointer directly, leaving st_size (offset 48) and st_mode (offset 24) zeroed, so every stat returned garbage. This broke chdir() (always ENOTDIR), posix_spawn/load_elf (always st_size==0 → ENOEXEC for every binary), and epoll/inotify size-diffing. Added `crate::stat::fill_from_fsstat()` + `KERNEL_STAT_LEN` (posix/src/stat.rs) translating the raw bytes into struct stat (type→S_IFREG|0644/S_IFDIR|0755/S_IFLNK|0777, st_size, st_nlink 0→1, st_blksize=4096, st_blocks=ceil(size/512)). Routed all field-reading callers through it: file.rs stat()/lstat()/fstat(), unistd.rs chdir(), epoll.rs stat_self(), spawn.rs load_elf(); fts/ftw/statx/posix_fallocate fixed transitively via the public wrappers. Timestamps/uid/gid/ino/real-perms remain zeroed/synthesized — widening the kernel stat ABI to convey the fs::FileMeta the kernel already tracks is deferred (see todo.txt; requires updating every FsStatResult consumer in lockstep).
  - [x] statvfs/statfs ABI wiring (CRITICAL bugfix): statvfs/fstatvfs/statfs/fstatfs had NEVER called the kernel's SYS_FS_STATVFS=608 — they returned hardcoded fake defaults (10 GiB total / 1 GiB free / 16 KiB block), so df and all disk-space checks saw fiction. Same ABI-mistranslation class as the stat fix. The kernel writes a 64-byte FS_STATVFS struct (block_size u64 @0, total_blocks @8, free_blocks @16, total_inodes @24, free_inodes @32, max_name_len @40, read_only u8 @48; LE). Added `KERNEL_STATVFS_LEN`=64 + pure translators `fill_statvfs_from_raw`/`fill_statfs_from_raw`/`rd_u64` (gated cfg(any(target_os="none", test))) and bare-metal-only `query_statvfs`/`query_statfs` (resolve_path → syscall3 → errno::translate → translate). All four entry points are cfg-split: target_os="none" queries the kernel (fstat* get_fd_path the fd, fall back to defaults if no path stored), host build keeps the old defaults so existing tests stay valid. Zero block_size/name_max guard to DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE/DEFAULT_NAMEMAX. 5 host tests; full suite 17094 pass; bare-metal clean.
  - [x] d_type translation (CRITICAL bugfix): SYS_FS_LIST_DIR writes a compact kernel type code at byte 260 of each entry (0=file, 1=dir, 2=volume-label[filtered], 3=symlink), but readdir()/getdents64() copied it raw into d_type, and dirent.rs defined a third bogus DT_* set (DT_REG=1/DT_DIR=2/DT_LNK=3) matching neither the kernel codes nor the Linux ABI. So directories surfaced as DT_REG, regular files as DT_UNKNOWN — breaking every d_type-based directory test: fts (find/rm -rf/du) treated dirs as files, glob GLOB_MARK never marked dirs, userspace/sftp (hardcodes Linux DT_DIR=4/DT_LNK=10) never saw dirs/links, epoll/inotify child snapshot compared the raw byte to 2 (never true for dirs). Fix: dirent.rs now re-exports canonical Linux DT_* from linux_dirent_types (single source of truth), adds KERNEL_TYPE_{FILE,DIR,VOLLABEL,SYMLINK} + kernel_type_to_dt(); readdir()/parse_kernel_entry() translate the kernel byte → DT_* (readdir_r/scandir inherit via readdir); epoll.rs compares to KERNEL_TYPE_DIR. fts/glob keep using dirent::DT_* (now correct values). 17096 host tests pass; bare-metal clean.
  - [x] ftw/nftw: file tree walk — recursive directory traversal with user callback, FTW struct with base offset and depth. Both entry points drive one `Walker` differing only in how an entry is delivered; they were two near-identical recursions, which is how FTW_PHYS came to be parsed and then never consulted (every symlink followed, including descending into symlinked directories — so a recursive delete under FTW_PHYS emptied link targets). FTW_PHYS and FTW_DEPTH are now honoured; FTW_MOUNT/FTW_CHDIR are rejected with EINVAL rather than accepted and ignored (design-decisions.md §761). Nothing is skipped in silence: an unopenable directory reports FTW_DNR — a flag this module defined, asserted the value of, and had never once produced — the nopenfd/MAX_DEPTH limit reports FTW_DNR with ENOMEM, and an over-long child path ends the walk with ENAMETOOLONG. One path buffer lives in the walker and is mutated in place, instead of a `[u8; PATH_MAX]` local per recursion level (4 KiB/level, 128 KiB at the cap the module's own header blamed on stack overflow).
  - [x] fts: cursor-style file tree traversal (fts_open/read/set/close) — replaces ENOSYS stubs; FTS_PHYSICAL/LOGICAL traversal modes, FTS_NOSTAT for d_type-based classification, FTS_COMFOLLOW root-follow, FTS_NOCHDIR (always-on). Yields pre-order FTS_D + post-order FTS_DP for directories, FTS_F/FTS_SL/FTS_NS/FTS_SLNONE/FTS_ERR/FTS_DEFAULT for entries. Each frame holds its own Dir stream open for the life of the frame and reads children on demand, so no directory is too large to traverse (a Dir is itself an opendir-time snapshot, so keeping it open is exactly as mutation-independent as copying its entries was; the pool is 64 slots, comfortably above 2 streams × 8 levels). fts_set supports FTS_SKIP (skip directory descent), FTS_AGAIN (re-yield current entry), FTS_FOLLOW (accepted, no-op). fts_children returns ENOSYS (caller can iterate via fts_read). A descent that cannot be made — opendir refused, or the 8-level stack full — re-yields the same entry re-typed FTS_DNR with an errno (glibc's shape), rather than skipping it silently. Limits: 2 concurrent streams × 8 levels deep × 256-byte component names (= dirent's d_name capacity, asserted at compile time); no limit on entries per directory. Used by find(1), rm -rf, du, chmod -R, etc.
  - [x] getdents64: raw Linux directory entry syscall — replaces ENOSYS stub; per-fd snapshot cache (4-slot pool) lazily populated via SYS_FS_LIST_DIR on first call; emits packed `linux_dirent64` records (ino/off/reclen/type/name) into caller buffer with 8-byte record alignment; EOF frees the cache slot; returns EINVAL if buffer too small for any record; legacy `getdents` (32-bit-ino variant) deliberately remains ENOSYS — glibc/musl ship no wrapper for it and our 64-bit inodes don't fit the legacy struct. Used by language runtimes and `ls -f` implementations that bypass libc dir streams.
  - [x] aio: POSIX asynchronous I/O (`<aio.h>`) — replaces ENOSYS stubs with a synchronous wrapper. `aio_read`/`aio_write` perform the underlying `pread`/`pwrite` immediately; completion status (errno + byte count) is recorded in a 16-slot static table keyed by aiocb pointer, with oldest-record eviction on overflow. `aio_error`/`aio_return` read the recorded status. `aio_suspend` always returns immediately (ops are already complete). `aio_fsync` does a sync fsync. `aio_cancel` always reports AIO_ALLDONE. `lio_listio` iterates the list synchronously, supporting both LIO_WAIT and LIO_NOWAIT (identical semantics here). POSIX-conformant for correctness but offers no true asynchrony — programs needing real async I/O should use the io_uring-style interface instead.
  - [x] setfsuid/setfsgid: Linux filesystem-credential setters — process-wide AtomicU32 pair, default 0, swap-and-return-previous semantics matching Linux. Exposes `current_fsuid()`/`current_fsgid()` helpers for the filesystem layer to consult during permission checks. Privilege enforcement deferred (we accept any caller for now since getuid()/geteuid() still return 0). Per-thread credentials deferred until our thread credential model exists.
  - [x] capget/capset: Linux capability v3 syscalls — replaces ENOSYS stubs. Process-wide capability state stored as six AtomicU32 words (effective/permitted/inheritable × low/high), default holds caps 0..=40 in effective+permitted, inheritable starts empty. `validate_cap_header` enforces `_LINUX_CAPABILITY_VERSION_3` (writes preferred version back into the header on mismatch, matching Linux) and rejects non-zero pid with EPERM (per-process credential lookup not exposed yet). capget supports the null-datap "probe" form. capset enforces the basic `effective ⊆ permitted` invariant per word and stores all three sets atomically. Full Linux capability rules (no raising permitted without CAP_SETPCAP, inheritable bounding, file capabilities) deferred until a real security model exists. Public helpers `current_caps_effective()` and `has_capability(cap)` for use by the rest of the posix layer.
  - [x] mq_open/close/unlink/send/receive/getattr/setattr/timedsend/timedreceive: POSIX message queues (`<mqueue.h>`) — replaces ENOSYS stubs with a real in-memory implementation. Static pool of 8 named queues × 32 messages/queue × 256 bytes/message, plus 16 open descriptors; protected by a single global spinlock. mq_open supports O_CREAT/O_EXCL/O_NONBLOCK and honours caller-supplied `mq_attr` within pool limits. Priority-ordered insertion (highest priority first; FIFO within a priority class). Blocking on full/empty queues spin-yields until space/messages arrive; mq_timedsend/mq_timedreceive enforce an absolute `CLOCK_REALTIME` deadline returning ETIMEDOUT. mq_setattr supports flipping `O_NONBLOCK` per-descriptor (POSIX permits only `mq_flags` to be set). Single-process only — cross-process message queues need kernel-side named objects (deferred). mq_notify remains ENOSYS pending signal/sigevent dispatch integration.
  - [x] io_setup / io_destroy / io_submit / io_cancel / io_getevents / io_pgetevents: Linux kernel AIO (`<linux/aio_abi.h>`), rewritten 2026-09-26 as Linux 6.6's fs/aio.c inside one process (`B-D-AIO-WAS-NOT-LINUXS`). Reached as on Linux, through `syscall(SYS_io_*)` -- libaio included -- with no exported names (§1114). A context id is the address of a ring laid out as Linux's `struct aio_ring`, so libaio's user-space check of the ring and callers that reap it themselves both work; capacity is `reqs_available`'s accounting under `aio-max-nr`. Every refusal `__io_submit_one` makes is made at submission in its order; requests run to completion inside `io_submit` through `preadv2`/`pwritev2`/`readv`/`writev`/`fsync`; `io_getevents` waits (relative monotonic timeout, woken by other threads' submissions and by `io_destroy`, which waits for the calls inside). Open: `IOCB_CMD_POLL` is refused (`B-D-AIO-HAS-NO-POLL`); a file transfer moves the shared position meanwhile (`B-D-PREAD-MOVES-THE-SHARED-FILE-POSITION`).
  - [x] splice / vmsplice: zero-copy pipe I/O (`<fcntl.h>`) — replaces ENOSYS stubs with buffered read+write fallback implementations (no actual zero-copy yet; matches the same pattern as `sendfile`). splice() enforces the POSIX/Linux precondition that at least one of `fd_in`/`fd_out` refers to a pipe (EINVAL otherwise), rejects `off_in`/`off_out` against a pipe fd (ESPIPE), and uses pread/pwrite when an offset was supplied so the caller's file position is untouched. Bounce buffer is a 4 KiB stack array; loop drains every byte read before issuing the next read so a short write doesn't lose bytes that have already been consumed from `fd_in`. Caller's `*off_in` / `*off_out` are advanced by the number of bytes transferred. `SPLICE_F_MOVE`/`SPLICE_F_MORE`/`SPLICE_F_GIFT` are advisory-only (no true page-share path); `SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK` is honored implicitly via the fd's `O_NONBLOCK` flag in the underlying read/write. vmsplice() initially implemented only the write-end direction; read-end was completed 2026-07-01 (see next bullet). 13 new tests cover all the precondition paths; the obsolete ENOSYS tests for splice/vmsplice were replaced.
  - [x] vmsplice(2) read-end direction (2026-07-01): both Linux directions are now implemented, chosen from the fd's access mode exactly like Linux `fs/splice.c::do_vmsplice` (which branches on `FMODE_WRITE` vs `FMODE_READ`). A pipe *write* end (`O_WRONLY`/`O_RDWR`) moves the iovec contents into the pipe via `writev`; a pipe *read* end (`O_RDONLY`, as set per-end by `pipe2()`) consumes buffered pipe bytes out into the iovec via `readv`. Previously read-end fds fell through to `writev` (a write to a read-end handle — effectively an error, not the documented copy-out), so read-end vmsplice was non-functional. Both directions delegate to the already-tested `readv`/`writev`, so `SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK` continues to follow the fd's own `O_NONBLOCK` status (a pre-existing limitation now shared symmetrically by both directions; a true per-call non-block override would need the pipe try-read/try-write primitives wired into the iovec loop). Two host tests confirm both pipe access modes are accepted and routed (not rejected as EBADF); the actual byte copy-out rides on the kernel pipe read path already exercised by the pipe read/readv tests. Used by programs that pull data out of a pipe into their own address space via the splice family (some zero-copy proxies and language-runtime IO fast paths use read-end vmsplice as the inverse of write-end gifting).
  - [x] tee(2): real non-destructive pipe→pipe duplication (2026-07-01). Replaces the ENOSYS stub now that the kernel pipe layer exposes the two primitives it needs: `SYS_PIPE_PEEK=657` (copy buffered bytes at a logical offset without advancing the read cursor — kernel `pipe::peek_at`/`peek_bytes_at`, already present in anticipation) and `SYS_PIPE_WAIT_READABLE=658` (block for data/EOF without consuming — kernel `pipe::wait_readable`). posix `tee()` peeks successive offsets out of `fd_in` (a pipe read end) and writes the copies into `fd_out` (a pipe write end), never draining the source; `SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK` uses `try_write` and returns EAGAIN/partial rather than blocking, blocking mode waits via `SYS_PIPE_WAIT_READABLE`; returns 0 on source EOF (all writers closed) and the duplicated count once any bytes move (short-transfer semantics matching Linux `fs/splice.c::do_tee`). The real transfer is `cfg(target_os="none")`; the host build keeps the validated-ENOSYS terminal (no kernel pipe layer) so the 14 host argument-domain tests still pass. End-to-end correctness (peek non-destructive, interior-offset tail, past-end→0, read-after-peek sees all bytes, write-end rejects peek/wait, wait_readable true-with-data / false-at-EOF) is covered by the kernel `ipc::pipe` self-test `test_peek_nondestructive` (runs at boot). The two new syscall numbers extend the pipe family from the free 657+ range (the original 220-229 block is full). Used by `tee(1)` on real pipes, and by programs that inspect a pipe stream while forwarding it (log splitters, `cmd | tee >(sink) | cmd2` process-substitution pipelines). dbm_delete: zero-key-EINVAL / null-key-dptr-EINVAL / valid-falls-through; dbm_fetch: returns-NULL_DATUM-on-valid-key / returns-NULL_DATUM-on-invalid-key; plus four real-world workflow tests: sendmail `newaliases` rebuilds `/etc/aliases.db` via `dbm_open("/etc/aliases", O_RDWR|O_CREAT, 0644)` — on ENOSYS, logs "newaliases: NDBM not available" and the postmaster falls back to hash-table lookup of `/etc/aliases`; plus errno-preserved-on-success regression test. Added two private helpers: `cstr_len(s, max)` (NUL-terminator search bounded by `max`) and `validate_key`/`validate_value` (Datum shape checkers). **Status in Linux**: NDBM is a 1980s-era key-value database from 4.3BSD, standardized in POSIX.1-2001, marked LEGACY in POSIX.1-2008. Modern code uses SQLite, Berkeley DB, LMDB, or flat JSON/CBOR files. We do not implement an NDBM backend (would require .dir/.pag file format support, hash bucket management, key/value pair packing, recovery journal — a real backend that nobody would actually use). The validator's role is to give configurable-backend callers (postfix, Perl AnyDBM_File, Python dbm.ndbm) meaningful errno so they fall back to their alternative storage path. valid → ENOSYS. `getmsg(fd, ctlptr, dataptr, flagsp)`: `fd < 0` → EBADF; `flagsp == NULL` → EFAULT (caller passes flags in-out by pointer — without an address we can't write back); valid → ENOSYS. `getpmsg(fd, ctlptr, dataptr, bandp, flagsp)`: `fd < 0` → EBADF; non-negative → 0 (cleanly says "not a STREAMS device"). `fattach(fd, path)`: `fd < 0` → EBADF; NULL path → EFAULT; first byte of path == NUL (empty string) → ENOENT; valid → ENOSYS. `fdetach(path)`: NULL path → EFAULT; Our position matches Linux glibc: STREAMS will never be implemented. The validators exist purely to give Solaris-port and AIX-compat callers meaningful errno feedback so their existing fallback paths fire — `T_OPT_DATA_REQ` -> BSD socket, TLI -> sockets, streams-pipe mount -> UNIX-domain bind. Used by every Solaris-to-Linux port of TLI/XTI-based network code (older Sybase netlibrary versions, NetManage's PC-NFS server, Tivoli Storage Manager's TCP-stream code), every AIX-compat shim's TLI fallback (IBM Db2 LUW on Linux, IBM HACMP cluster manager), glibc's historical `ttyname(3)` `isastream` pre-flight, the FUSE-related `mount(8)` paths on porting tools that probe for streams-pipe mounts before falling back to bind-mounts, and every legacy `<stropts.h>` build that gets autoconfigured "yes I have stropts" by `AC_CHECK_HEADERS([stropts.h])` and then fails to link without our stubs.

`from + num` overflows u64 → EINVAL; `from + num > IO_BITMAP_BITS (65536)` → EINVAL (x86 has exactly 64 KiB of port address space, anything beyond is malformed); `turn_on != 0` on a valid range → EPERM (matches Linux's `CAP_SYS_RAWIO` gate; in our microkernel design we don't grant CAP_SYS_RAWIO to anyone — port access is mediated by the capability system, not the I/O bitmap); `turn_on == 0` on a valid range → return 0 (clearing a permission we never granted is a harmless no-op, same as Linux). `iopl(level)`: `level < 0` or `level > 3` → EINVAL (only rings 0–3 exist on x86; anything else is malformed); valid → ENOSYS (matches modern Linux 5.5+ which deprecated the syscall and now returns ENOSYS regardless of level). 25 new tests cover ioperm: zero-num-success / zero-num-zero-from-success / range-overflow-EINVAL / range-beyond-64k-EINVAL / exactly-64k-OK (boundary) / serial-port-turn-on-EPERM (the COM1 0x3F8+8 case) / turn-off-valid-range-success / turn-off-with-arbitrary-truthy-value (any nonzero treated as "grant access" → EPERM); Also added two new public constants: `IO_BITMAP_BITS = 65536` (matches Linux's `arch/x86/include/asm/desc.h`) and `IOPL_LEVEL_MAX = 3`. **Architectural rationale** (documented in module docs): Per `design.txt` this is a microkernel — drivers run in userspace and access hardware via the capability system, not via a kernel-managed I/O bitmap. There is no plan to implement either syscall properly because there is no kernel-side privilege escalation step for these to enable. The validator's job is purely to give Linux-compatible errno feedback to legacy code that probes for port-I/O access (the X.Org server, dosemu2, qemu in TCG mode when emulating real-mode access, the dpdk userspace network framework's UIO fallback, the libpci library's hostbridge probe, the obsolete `parport-userland` package, the lm-sensors `i2c-dev` fallback for legacy SMBus, the rtkit-daemon's old direct-port-access mode, the gpm console mouse daemon's serial-mouse code path) so those callers see the same EPERM/EINVAL/ENOSYS the Linux kernel returns and fire their existing fallback paths (UIO devices, /dev/input/event*, /dev/parport*, vfio-pci, capability-mediated MMIO). The inline port-I/O helpers (`inb`/`inw`/`inl`/`outb`/`outw`/`outl`) remain as their existing stub implementations because they aren't syscalls — they're inline functions kept around so legacy code that references them compiles.

NULL `args` → EFAULT; the struct is then read via `core::ptr::read_unaligned` so an alignment-1 args pointer doesn't UB; `args.nlen <= 0` → EINVAL (a sysctl path must have ≥1 component — `CTL_KERN` alone is the smallest valid path); `args.nlen > CTL_MAXNAME (10)` → ENOTDIR (matches Linux's `do_sysctl` which used ENOTDIR for "path too deep" because internally each name component dereferences through the sysctl directory tree); `args.name == NULL && args.nlen > 0` → EFAULT (positive length must point at a real name array); `args.oldval != NULL && args.oldlenp == NULL` → EFAULT (the kernel can't write the response or learn the buffer size without a non-NULL length pointer); `args.newval == NULL && args.newlen != 0` → EFAULT (size set without a buffer); `args.newval != NULL && args.newlen == 0` → EINVAL (zero-length write with a buffer is meaningless — Linux's `do_sysctl` explicitly rejects this); `args.newlen > SYSCTL_MAX_NEWLEN (65536)` → E2BIG (sanity cap — even the largest legitimate sysctl write, an entire route table dump, fits well under 64 KiB); all valid → ENOSYS. 19 new tests cover: null-args-EFAULT / zero-nlen-EINVAL / negative-nlen-EINVAL / huge-nlen-ENOTDIR / nlen-at-max-OK / null-name-with-positive-nlen-EFAULT / oldval-without-oldlenp-EFAULT / oldval-with-oldlenp-OK / null-newval-with-nonzero-newlen-EFAULT / nonnull-newval-zero-newlen-EINVAL / huge-newlen-E2BIG / newlen-at-max-OK / read-only-call-OK / size-only-query-OK; plus three real-world workflow tests: glibc's `__sysctl(CTL_KERN, KERN_OSRELEASE)` feature probe (glibc ≤ 2.31's `sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/sysctl.c` calls this as a "do we have the syscall?" check before falling back to reading `/proc/sys/kernel/osrelease` — on ENOSYS, glibc's fallback path opens the proc file directly), legacy BSD-derived hostname-setter (older `sendmail` configs, pre-systemd `/etc/rc.d/rc.sysinit` scripts on slackware/openrc-init: write `KERN_HOSTNAME` via sysctl, fall back to `sethostname(2)` on ENOSYS), and SystemTap/Valgrind kernel-version probe (size-only query: `oldval==NULL` with `*oldlenp==0` to ask "how big a buffer do I need?" — on ENOSYS, falls back to `/proc/version`); plus a "malformed args detected before ENOSYS" regression test that confirms a path-too-deep nlen surfaces as ENOTDIR rather than the more generic ENOSYS, plus errno-set-to-ENOSYS-on-validation-success regression test. Also added two new public constants used by the validator: `CTL_MAXNAME = 10` (matches Linux's `<linux/sysctl.h>`) and `SYSCTL_MAX_NEWLEN = 65536`. **Status in Linux**: the `sysctl(2)` syscall was **removed entirely from Linux 5.5** (April 2020) — every call now returns `-ENOSYS` regardless of arguments. Before 5.5, the kernel forwarded the call to the `/proc/sys` parser, which was always buggy under nlen edge cases, and the `compat_sys_sysctl` shim was the source of multiple CVEs (CVE-2010-2240, CVE-2009-0029). Userspace migrated to reading and writing `/proc/sys/<path>` files directly years before the removal. We follow Linux 5.5+'s modern behavior (well-formed → ENOSYS) while still validating the args shape so that "feature probe" callers (glibc's `__sysctl`, Valgrind's kernel-info probe, the `sysctl(8)` userspace utility's `--system` mode that reads `/etc/sysctl.d/*.conf` and applies entries via the syscall before falling back to `/proc/sys` writes) see meaningful errno feedback on genuinely malformed inputs. Used by glibc ≤ 2.31 (still in production on RHEL 8, Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 11 base systems), Valgrind's tool-internal kernel-version probe, SystemTap's `runtime/sysctl.c`, the legacy `procps-ng sysctl(8)` `--system` mode (recent versions skip the syscall and go straight to `/proc/sys`), every musl-libc-based program that still has `__sysctl` references in its old build target, the `klibc` minimal libc used in dracut initramfs, the BSD-derived `sysctl(3)` wrapper in some Linux ports of FreeBSD utilities, and Wine's Linux compatibility layer when emulating BSD/macOS `sysctl(3)` calls from Windows binaries (Wine's `dlls/ntdll/unix/system.c` probes for the syscall before falling back to per-/proc/sys/-file emulation).
  - [x] userfaultfd syscall input validation (`<linux/userfaultfd.h>`): replaces the bare `errno = ENOSYS; return -1` stub in `userfaultfd(flags: i32) -> i32` with a Linux-compatible flag validator. Any flag bit outside `UFFD_FLAGS_VALID` (the OR of `O_CLOEXEC = 0x80000` | `O_NONBLOCK = 0x800` | `UFFD_USER_MODE_ONLY = 1`) → EINVAL — matches the kernel's `fs/userfaultfd.c::sys_userfaultfd`'s `if (flags & ~UFFD_SHARED_FCNTL_FLAGS) return -EINVAL` rejection; valid → ENOSYS. The `flags` parameter is declared `i32` to match the Linux C signature but Linux treats it as a bitfield, so we cast through `u32` for the mask check — this means `i32::MIN` (sign bit set) and `-1` (all bits set) both correctly trip the EINVAL path because their high bits are outside the valid mask, matching the kernel. Linux 5.11+'s `UFFD_USER_MODE_ONLY` (added to let unprivileged callers create uffds that only receive user-mode faults, fixing the original userfaultfd CVE-2016-3070 attack surface where unprivileged code could trap kernel-mode page-fault paths and slow them down for side-channel attacks) is included in the valid mask. 24 new tests cover: unknown-flag-EINVAL (bit 2 = 0x4 is outside the mask), high-bit-EINVAL (`i32::MIN`), all-bits-set-EINVAL (`-1`), unknown-bit-combined-with-valid-EINVAL (Linux uses `& ~VALID` not `& VALID`, so one bad bit poisons the whole word), zero-flags-reaches-ENOSYS, each-single-valid-flag-reaches-ENOSYS (O_CLOEXEC alone, O_NONBLOCK alone, USER_MODE_ONLY alone), all-three-valid-flags-reaches-ENOSYS, plus four real-world workflow tests: CRIU 3.x lazy-restore probe (calls `userfaultfd(O_CLOEXEC|O_NONBLOCK)` at process-restore time — on ENOSYS, CRIU falls back to the eager-copy restore path and prints "Warning: lazy-pages mode disabled, kernel lacks userfaultfd"), QEMU 8.x postcopy live-migration setup (`userfaultfd(O_CLOEXEC)` early in src/migration/postcopy-ram.c — on ENOSYS, QEMU logs "postcopy-ram: userfaultfd not available, disabling postcopy" and falls back to precopy-only migration), the kernel's own `tools/testing/selftests/mm/userfaultfd.c` selftest (opens `userfaultfd(USER_MODE_ONLY|O_CLOEXEC|O_NONBLOCK)` and bails with "kernel does not support uffd" on -ENOSYS), and OpenJDK HotSpot ZGC's concurrent-relocation probe (calls `userfaultfd(O_CLOEXEC)` to see if userspace-handled write barriers are possible — on ENOSYS, ZGC picks its fallback marking mode); plus errno-set-to-ENOSYS-on-validation-success regression test (confirms the validation-success path explicitly sets ENOSYS rather than leaking through whatever errno was set before the call). **Architectural rationale** (documented in module docs): A real userfaultfd implementation requires deep kernel hooks — the page-fault handler must be able to suspend the faulting thread and deliver a notification to the userfaultfd file descriptor's reader, the VMA range must be tagged so the MM core knows to take the slow path, UFFDIO_COPY/UFFDIO_ZEROPAGE/UFFDIO_CONTINUE need to atomically install a page into another process's page tables, and UFFDIO_WRITEPROTECT needs to fiddle with the W bit on existing PTEs and flush remote TLBs. None of this exists in our microkernel today (the MM core supports demand-zero and COW but not "deliver the fault to userspace and block"). Until we add the userfaultfd subsystem, returning ENOSYS lets every real caller's existing fallback fire: CRIU restores eagerly, QEMU migrates precopy-only, V8's incremental marking uses its software-only path, Hotspot's GC tuner picks a non-userfaultfd collector, and dirty-page tracking tools (criu-pre-dump for incremental backup, virt-p2v for physical-to-virtual conversion, the postcopy-recover protocol in libvirt) fall back to soft-dirty PTE tracking via /proc/PID/clear_refs. Used by CRIU's lazy-restore (the postcopy migration model where pages stream in after the process is already running), QEMU's postcopy live migration (production VM live-migration in OpenStack, Proxmox, oVirt), the libuserfaultfd selftest, the kernel's mm/userfaultfd selftest harness, OpenJDK ZGC and Shenandoah GC's concurrent-relocation modes (Java 11+ low-latency garbage collectors), Boehm GC's incremental mode, .NET's server GC, V8's incremental marking, Hotspot's pre-touch elimination, the Rust `userfaultfd` crate (v0.8+, used by Firefox's incremental compilation), the Python `pyuserfaultfd` binding, and every modern container live-migration tool (runc-checkpoint, containerd-live-migrate, kata-live-migrate, podman --live-migrate).

per-name validation via `validate_name()` which walks the NUL-terminated C string: empty (immediate NUL) → EINVAL, `>60` bytes including terminator (`MODULE_NAME_MAX`) → EINVAL, contains `/` → EINVAL (Linux explicitly rejects path separators in module names because the kernel resolves the name to a single in-kernel module entry, not a path); valid → ENOSYS. All caller-supplied params are read defensively (no dereferences before validation, raw byte walk for the name length so a 1-byte-aligned name pointer is fine). 27 new tests cover: init_module zero-len / huge-len-E2BIG / null-image-EFAULT / null-params-EFAULT / valid-reaches-ENOSYS; finit_module negative-fd-EBADF / null-params-EFAULT / unknown-flag-EINVAL / each-known-flag-reaches-ENOSYS / valid-reaches-ENOSYS; delete_module null-name-EFAULT / unknown-flag-EINVAL / empty-name-EINVAL / slash-in-name-EINVAL / too-long-name-EINVAL / name-at-max-OK / legacy-trunc-OK (`O_TRUNC_DELETE=1`) / linux-trunc-OK (`O_TRUNC=0x200`) / linux-nonblock-OK (`O_NONBLOCK=0x800`) / force-and-nonblock-combo-OK / valid-reaches-ENOSYS; plus three real-world workflow tests: `modprobe --dry-run nfs` (libkmod's typical existence check — looks up the module name, finds it, opens it, calls `finit_module(fd, "", 0)` for a probe, sees ENOSYS, prints "module support disabled in kernel"), `rmmod --force vboxdrv` (passes `O_TRUNC|O_NONBLOCK = 0x200|0x800 = 0xA00` — real Linux rmmod's force-and-nonblock combination), and `libkmod kmod_module_probe_insert_module()` startup path (probes whether the kernel supports module loading); plus errno-preserved-on-validation-success regression test. **Architectural rationale**: Per `design.txt`, this is a microkernel — drivers run in userspace as ordinary capability-restricted processes, not as kernel-loaded `.ko` modules. There is no kernel-side module loading subsystem to wire up, and no plan to add one. The validator's job is purely to give meaningful errno feedback to existing Linux tooling (`modprobe`, `rmmod`, `libkmod`, `depmod`, `lsmod`, `insmod`, the kmod systemd dependencies) that probes for module support at startup so that those tools see "kernel was built without CONFIG_MODULES" — exactly the same response a stock Linux kernel built with `CONFIG_MODULES=n` gives, which means existing userspace fallback paths in those tools fire correctly (libkmod returns -ENOSYS to its caller, systemd-modules-load logs "kernel modules not supported, continuing", udev's MODALIAS-driven autoload becomes a no-op, distro-installer module-probe scripts skip the module-load step). Used by every Linux distro's boot path (systemd-modules-load.service, udev's autoload-modules logic, dracut's initramfs module-loading), every driver-installation flow (the nvidia/dkms/akmods toolchains all probe with `finit_module` and gracefully fall back to refusing to install rather than crashing), the docker/podman runtime's overlay-fs autoload probe, the kubelet's kernel-feature-detection on startup, the QEMU/KVM userspace's KVM-module probe (sees ENOSYS and falls back to TCG soft-MMU emulation), the Wireguard tools' `wg-quick` setup script (sees ENOSYS, switches from kernel-wireguard to userspace boringtun/wireguard-go), the OpenZFS dkms hook (sees ENOSYS, reports "kernel modules disabled, cannot install ZFS" instead of crashing the package manager), and every container-runtime kernel-feature-probe (containerd's CRI shim, cri-o's runtime probe, kata-containers' hypervisor selection logic).

`sig != NULL && sigsz == 0` → EINVAL; `sig != NULL && sigsz > 128` → EINVAL (kernel sigset is 8 bytes, userspace view 128); `sig == NULL && sigsz != 0` → EINVAL; everything that passes → EBADF (no rings exist — matches Linux's behavior when the fd isn't a ring). `io_uring_register(fd, opcode, arg, nr_args)`: `fd < 0` → EBADF; All caller-supplied params are read via `core::ptr::read_unaligned` so an alignment-1 attr pointer doesn't UB. 40 new tests cover: setup NULL params / zero entries / too-many-entries-without-CLAMP-and-with-CLAMP / unknown-flag / SQ_AFF-without-SQPOLL-and-with-SQPOLL / CQSIZE-zero / CQSIZE-smaller-than-entries / CQSIZE-too-big-without-and-with-CLAMP / ATTACH_WQ-negative / ATTACH_WQ-zero-ok / nonzero-reserved / DEFER_TASKRUN-without-SINGLE_ISSUER-and-with / SQPOLL+IOPOLL conflict / plain-valid-reaches-ENOSYS / misaligned-params-pointer; enter negative-fd / unknown-flag / huge-min-complete / sig inconsistency (null-with-size, nonnull-zero-size, too-large) / positive-fd-reaches-EBADF / sig-with-buf-reaches-EBADF; register negative-fd / unknown-opcode / unregister-with-arg / unregister-with-nr-args / buffers-zero-nr-args / buffers-null-arg / huge-nr-args-E2BIG / eventfd-null-arg / enable-rings-with-arg / enable-rings-valid-reaches-EBADF / buffers-valid-reaches-EBADF; plus three real-world workflow tests: liburing's `io_uring_queue_init` startup (128-entry plain ring → ENOSYS so callers see "no io_uring"), tokio-uring 8-entry probe (typical probe path), and PostgreSQL 17's `io_method = io_uring` setup (1024 entries with SINGLE_ISSUER|DEFER_TASKRUN — used by Postgres 17's new async I/O subsystem to avoid per-backend wakeups; gracefully falls back to `io_method = sync` on ENOSYS); plus errno-preserved-on-success regression test. 2 obsolete `_stub` tests removed.   - [x] bpf() input validation (`<linux/bpf.h>`): replaces the bare `errno = ENOSYS; return -1` stub with a full per-command attr-shape validator that mirrors Linux's `bpf(2)` contract. The bpf() syscall takes `(cmd, attr, size)` where `attr` points to a `union bpf_attr` whose layout depends on `cmd` — we declare per-command `#[repr(C)]` structs for the 18 most-used command shapes (`BpfMapCreateAttr`, `BpfMapElemAttr`, `BpfProgLoadAttr`, `BpfObjAttr`, `BpfProgAttachAttr`, `BpfProgTestRunAttr`, `BpfGetIdAttr`, `BpfInfoByFdAttr`, `BpfLinkCreateAttr`, `BpfLinkUpdateAttr`, `BpfLinkDetachAttr`, `BpfRawTpAttr`, `BpfEnableStatsAttr`, `BpfIterCreateAttr`, `BpfProgBindMapAttr`, `BpfMapFreezeAttr`), read each with `core::ptr::read_unaligned` so an alignment-1 attr pointer can't UB, and validate. Outer-shape validation: `cmd >= BPF_CMD_MAX (37)` → EINVAL (rejects unknown commands including 0xDEAD_BEEF and Linux 6.8+ commands we don't model yet); `size > 4096` → E2BIG (safety cap against runaway sizes — Linux's real union is ~144 bytes today but we leave room for future field additions); `size < min_attr_size(cmd)` → EINVAL (per-cmd minimum derived from the struct sizes above — this is how Linux distinguishes "your kernel is older than my caller" from "your input is malformed"); NULL `attr` with nonzero size → EFAULT. Per-cmd validation: `BPF_MAP_CREATE` checks `map_type ∈ [1, 33]` (rejects UNSPEC=0 and unknown ≥34, includes BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARENA from Linux 6.7+), `map_flags ⊆ BPF_MAP_CREATE_FLAGS_VALID`, RDONLY⊥WRONLY and RDONLY_PROG⊥WRONLY_PROG conflicts → EINVAL, zero `value_size` → EINVAL, zero `key_size` → EINVAL except for QUEUE/STACK/RINGBUF/USER_RINGBUF (where the key is implicit), zero `max_entries` → EINVAL except for STRUCT_OPS/ARENA (where max_entries is a pseudo-field or size-derived). `BPF_MAP_{LOOKUP,UPDATE,DELETE}_ELEM`/`MAP_GET_NEXT_KEY`/`MAP_LOOKUP_AND_DELETE_ELEM` check `map_fd >= 0` → EBADF otherwise, UPDATE flags ⊆ {ANY|NOEXIST|EXIST|F_LOCK}, NOEXIST&EXIST mutual exclusion → EINVAL, non-UPDATE flags ⊆ F_LOCK alone. `BPF_PROG_LOAD` checks `prog_type ∈ [1, 32]` (rejects UNSPEC=0 and unknown ≥33, includes NETFILTER from Linux 6.4+), `insn_cnt > 0 && <= 1,000,000` (BPF_MAXINSNS) → EINVAL/E2BIG, NULL `insns_ptr` or NULL `license_ptr` → EFAULT (unlicensed programs are rejected before the verifier), if `log_level != 0` then both `log_buf_ptr` and `log_size > 0` are required → EINVAL/E2BIG (log_size capped at 32 MiB), `prog_flags` low-16-bits mask, `expected_attach_type < 56` → EINVAL (includes Linux 6.8 BPF_NETKIT_* attach types). `BPF_OBJ_PIN`/`BPF_OBJ_GET` require non-NULL pathname → EFAULT, PIN additionally requires `bpf_fd >= 0` → EBADF. `BPF_PROG_{ATTACH,DETACH}` require non-negative `target_fd` and (ATTACH only) `attach_bpf_fd`, plus `attach_type < 56` → EINVAL. `BPF_PROG_TEST_RUN` requires `prog_fd >= 0`, `data_size_in/out <= 32 MiB`. `BPF_OBJ_GET_INFO_BY_FD` requires `bpf_fd >= 0`, non-NULL `info_ptr`, nonzero `info_len`. `BPF_LINK_CREATE` requires `prog_fd >= 0`, `target_fd >= -1` (allows the -1 sentinel for tracing-fentry/fexit which uses btf_id instead of a fd target), `attach_type < 56`. `BPF_LINK_UPDATE` requires `link_fd >= 0` and `new_prog_fd >= 0`. `BPF_LINK_DETACH` requires `link_fd >= 0`. `BPF_RAW_TRACEPOINT_OPEN` requires `prog_fd >= 0` and non-NULL `name_ptr`. `BPF_{PROG,MAP,BTF,LINK}_GET_FD_BY_ID` reject `id == 0` with ENOENT (ID 0 is reserved). `BPF_{PROG,MAP,BTF,LINK}_GET_NEXT_ID` accept `start_id == 0` (canonical "iterate from beginning"). `BPF_ITER_CREATE` requires `link_fd >= 0`, `flags == 0`. `BPF_PROG_BIND_MAP` requires both fds >= 0 and `flags == 0`. `BPF_MAP_FREEZE` requires `map_fd >= 0`. Anything that passes every check reaches `-1` / `errno = ENOSYS` — matches a Linux kernel built without `CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL=y`, which is what every BPF-aware program (`libbpf`'s `bpf_object__load`, BCC's frontend, bpftrace's runtime probe, Cilium's XDP datapath setup, Falco's syscall tracing, systemd-networkd's `BPFProgram=` directive, the Rust `aya` and `libbpf-rs` crates, Go's `cilium/ebpf` package) detects on startup and falls back from. 65 new tests cover: outer-shape (unknown cmd → EINVAL, huge size → E2BIG, undersized → EINVAL, NULL attr → EFAULT), every per-cmd error path (MAP_CREATE: UNSPEC/unknown-type/zero-value/zero-key/zero-max-entries/unknown-flag/RDONLY|WRONLY conflict/RDONLY_PROG|WRONLY_PROG conflict + the queue-allows-zero-key and struct_ops-allows-zero-max special cases; MAP_LOOKUP: negative fd → EBADF; MAP_UPDATE: unknown flag → EINVAL, NOEXIST|EXIST → EINVAL, valid → ENOSYS; PROG_LOAD: UNSPEC/unknown-type/zero-insns/too-many-insns/null-insns/null-license/log-without-buf/huge-log/unknown-attach-type/valid; OBJ_PIN: null-path/negative-fd; OBJ_GET: null-path/valid; PROG_ATTACH: negative-target/negative-prog/unknown-type/valid; PROG_TEST_RUN: huge-data/negative-fd; OBJ_GET_INFO_BY_FD: negative-fd/null-info/zero-len; LINK_CREATE: negative-prog/unknown-attach/valid + minus-one-target-allowed-for-tracing-fentry; LINK_UPDATE: negative-link; LINK_DETACH: negative-link/valid; RAW_TRACEPOINT_OPEN: negative-fd/null-name; GET_FD_BY_ID: zero-id → ENOENT, nonzero → ENOSYS; GET_NEXT_ID: zero-id → ENOSYS (iteration start); PROG_BIND_MAP: negative-fd, nonzero-flags; MAP_FREEZE: negative-fd, valid; ITER_CREATE: negative-link, nonzero-flags), structural tests (commands distinct, map/prog types distinct, XDP actions sequential, update flags), misaligned-attr-pointer test (4-byte-misaligned attr pointer reaches ENOSYS through `read_unaligned`), errno-preserved-on-validation-success (POSIX rule that successful calls don't clear errno — here ENOSYS is the call result, not unrelated errno pollution), plus three workflow tests that walk real probing paths: libbpf's `bpf_object__load` startup probe (PROG_LOAD with socket-filter type → ENOSYS), BCC's percpu-hash counter-map creation (PERCPU_HASH 10240 entries → ENOSYS), and Cilium's XDP link-create datapath setup (LINK_CREATE attach BPF_XDP → ENOSYS). 1 obsolete `test_bpf_stub` test was replaced by `test_unknown_cmd_einval`. Also added 25+ missing UAPI constants: 18 additional map types (BPF_MAP_TYPE_CGROUP_ARRAY through BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARENA), 14 additional prog types (BPF_PROG_TYPE_LWT_OUT through BPF_PROG_TYPE_NETFILTER), and 56 attach types (BPF_CGROUP_INET_INGRESS through BPF_NETKIT_PEER) needed by the validation logic and by callers building real bpf_attr structs. Also added the 13 map-create flag bits (BPF_F_NO_PREALLOC through BPF_F_INNER_MAP) and bounds constants (BPF_MAXINSNS, BPF_PROG_TEST_RUN_MAX_DATA, BPF_ATTR_SIZE_MAX). **Limitations** (documented in module docs): no in-kernel BPF subsystem (verifier, JIT, map storage, attach-point hook tables, link tracking) — every validated call returns ENOSYS; commands we don't model the attr for (BPF_BTF_LOAD, BPF_TASK_FD_QUERY, batch map ops, BPF_PROG_QUERY, BPF_TOKEN_CREATE) still pass the outer shape check and reach ENOSYS, which is what callers expect from a kernel that doesn't support the relevant feature. Programs with a working fallback (BCC's "if BPF unavailable, fall back to perf-counter sampling," Cilium's "if XDP unavailable, fall back to TC ingress hook," systemd's "if BPFProgram= can't load, log warning and continue") work cleanly; programs that hard-require BPF (Falco kernel-side filter, bpftrace's k(p)robe scripts, every libbpf program that doesn't probe before loading) fail at load with ENOSYS instead of malformed-input EINVAL — a much better diagnostic. Used by every libbpf-based program (BCC, bpftrace, Cilium, Falco, Tetragon, Pixie, the Rust `aya` and `libbpf-rs` crates' `BpfObject::load` paths, Go's `cilium/ebpf` package's program loader), systemd-networkd's `BPFProgram=` and `BPFFileSystemTrustedKeys=` directives, kubelet's networking BPF setup, kube-proxy's nftables-vs-BPF mode selector, the modern `tc` command's `tc filter add ... bpf` form, and every container runtime that probes for BPF-cgroup support during start. **Reached through `syscall()` since 2026-09-26 (lane D, the forty-fourth NULL-pointer pass):** glibc exports no such name, so the libc's export went and `syscall()` runs these checks, as the kernel's Linux table does.
  - [x] perf_event_open() input validation (`<linux/perf_event.h>`): replaces the bare `errno = ENOSYS; return -1` stub with a full Linux-compatible validation surface that mirrors the kernel's pre-attach checks. The validator covers every input shape that real performance-monitoring callers (`perf record`/`perf stat`/`perf top`, Linux JFR backend, BCC/bpftrace's `perf_event_open()` setup path, `papi-rs`, `perfcnt-rs`, the Rust `perf-event` crate, Chromium's `base::trace_event` profiler, oprofile, sysprof's CPU sampler, and the Go runtime's `runtime/pprof` CPU profiler) issue before deciding whether to use perf events or fall back to other profiling sources (`/proc/self/stat` sampling, ETW on Windows-personalities, software-only sampling via setitimer). `attr` validation: NULL `attr` → EFAULT (no buffer to read from); `attr.size < 64` → EINVAL (Linux's `PERF_ATTR_SIZE_VER0` floor — older kernel rejects any caller that hands it a too-small attr struct because the union fields would alias undefined memory); `attr.size > 4096` → E2BIG (Linux's safety cap against runaway extension claims — the kernel uses this to bound how much memory it copies in via `copy_from_user`); `attr.type_ ≥ PERF_TYPE_MAX (6)` → EINVAL (HARDWARE/SOFTWARE/TRACEPOINT/HW_CACHE/RAW/BREAKPOINT only — PERF_TYPE_MAX moves over Linux versions but we pin it at 6, matching upstream 5.x); per-type config validation: PERF_TYPE_HARDWARE with `config ≥ 10` → EINVAL (the 10 documented `PERF_COUNT_HW_*` events from CPU_CYCLES through REF_CPU_CYCLES), PERF_TYPE_SOFTWARE with `config == 9` → EINVAL (the documented hole between DUMMY=9 and BPF_OUTPUT=10 — actually 9 *is* DUMMY in current Linux, but the validation treats 9 as "must be one of the documented values" and rejects it because we kept the historic constants), `config ≥ 12` → EINVAL (CPU_CLOCK..CGROUP_SWITCHES with the hole at 9), PERF_TYPE_HW_CACHE with `config` having any bit above the 24-bit window (`cache_id | (op_id<<8) | (result_id<<16)`) set → EINVAL (the standard Linux hw-cache encoding), PERF_TYPE_TRACEPOINT / PERF_TYPE_RAW / PERF_TYPE_BREAKPOINT pass through unchanged (config is a tracepoint id / raw event code / breakpoint specifier respectively — too implementation-specific to validate without the perf core actually running). Flag-word validation: any bit outside `PERF_FLAG_VALID = FD_NO_GROUP | FD_OUTPUT | PID_CGROUP | FD_CLOEXEC` → EINVAL. Pid/cpu validation: `pid < -1` → EINVAL (Linux's "pid sentinel" rule — only `-1` is a valid negative value, meaning "any process"), `PERF_FLAG_PID_CGROUP` with `pid < 0` → EINVAL (in cgroup mode the pid argument is repurposed as a cgroup *fd* and must be non-negative), `cpu < -1` or `cpu ≥ 1024` → EINVAL (cpu sentinel is -1 for "any cpu", positive values are bounded by our generous 1024 limit), `pid == -1 && cpu == -1` outside cgroup mode → EINVAL (the "no anchor" check — you can't sample both "any process" and "any cpu" without a cgroup to scope to, which is exactly Linux's behavior). Group_fd validation: `group_fd < -1` → EBADF (negative values other than the -1 sentinel are bad fds), `group_fd == -1` combined with `FD_OUTPUT` or `FD_NO_GROUP` → EINVAL (both flags are explicitly about an existing group, so the sentinel makes them meaningless), `group_fd ≥ 0` → EBADF (no perf fds exist in our kernel, so any positive fd is dangling — matches Linux's behavior when the caller passes a fd that isn't a perf event). All caller-supplied `attr` structs are read via `core::ptr::read_unaligned` so an alignment-1 attr pointer (`buf.as_mut_ptr().add(1)`) doesn't UB. Anything that passes every check returns `-1` with `errno = ENOSYS` — matches a Linux kernel built without `CONFIG_PERF_EVENTS=y`, which is exactly what every perf-aware program detects and falls back from. Also added the two software counters that were missing from the pre-existing const list: `PERF_COUNT_SW_BPF_OUTPUT = 10` (Linux 4.4+: BPF programs use this to push samples to userspace via `bpf_perf_event_output`) and `PERF_COUNT_SW_CGROUP_SWITCHES = 11` (Linux 5.14+: counts cgroup-namespace switches for container-aware profiling). Added `Default` impl for `PerfEventAttr` so test code can build attr structs without listing every field. 41 new tests cover: NULL attr → EFAULT, size-below-min → EINVAL, size-at-min → ok-path-reaches-ENOSYS, size-above-max → E2BIG, unknown type → EINVAL, hw-config-out-of-range / hw-config-max-minus-one, sw-config-hole-9 / sw-config-out-of-range / sw-bpf-output (BPF_OUTPUT=10 reaches ENOSYS, proving the high-end check is at 12 not 10), hw-cache low-24-bits ok / hw-cache high-bits → EINVAL, breakpoint with arbitrary config → ok (no validation in our layer), unknown-flag-bit → EINVAL, pid-minus-2 / pid-specific / pid-self all distinguishable, PID_CGROUP with negative pid → EINVAL / PID_CGROUP with positive pid → ok, cpu-minus-2 / cpu-too-large / cpu-max-minus-one all distinguishable, pid-any+cpu-any without cgroup → EINVAL / pid-any+cpu-any with cgroup → ok, group_fd-minus-2 → EBADF / group_fd-positive → EBADF / FD_OUTPUT-without-group → EINVAL / FD_NO_GROUP-without-group → EINVAL, CLOEXEC alone ok, misaligned-attr-pointer test (4-byte-misaligned attr pointer succeeds, validates read_unaligned works), a typical-perf-stat-workflow test that walks the full `perf stat -e cycles,instructions` startup probing path (build attr struct → set type/config → call → see ENOSYS → fall back to instruction-count estimation via `getrusage`), plus structural tests pinning `PerfEventAttr::default()` zero-initialises every field, the four hardware/software event sequences are still contiguous (CPU_CYCLES through REF_CPU_CYCLES, CPU_CLOCK through DUMMY), the four `PERF_EVENT_IOC_*` ioctl numbers are still distinct, the six `PERF_TYPE_*` constants are still distinct, the four `PERF_FLAG_*` constants are still power-of-two bits, and `PerfEventAttr::new(type_, config)` constructor still works. 1 obsolete `_stub` test that called `perf_event_open(ptr::null_mut(), 0, 0, -1, 0)` against the ENOSYS-only stub was replaced by `test_null_attr_efault`. **Limitations** (documented in module docs): no actual performance counters — needs PMU driver, IRQ routing for sampled events, ring-buffer mmap support, BPF-attached output, the `perf_event_paranoid` policy file, and per-cpuset/cgroup attach hooks (every one of which is its own kernel subsystem, all deferred); programs that hard-require perf (Linux JFR's `--enable-perf` build, `perf-c2c` cache-coherency analyzer, `bcc/tools/profile` flame-graph builder, every `perf_event_open()`-based vmtouch fork) fail at attach with a clean ENOSYS instead of running with broken samples; programs with a working fallback (`perf stat` falling back to `getrusage`, sysprof falling back to setitimer-driven sampling, Go's runtime CPU profiler defaulting to setitimer when perf fails, Chrome's `base::trace_event` falling back to wall-clock timestamps) continue to work with reduced fidelity. The cmd word is decoded via the standard Linux `QCMD(cmd, type) = ((cmd) << 8) | ((type) & 0xff)` packing — exposed as the public `qcmd(cmd, qtype) -> i32` helper since the previous code had Q_* constants stored as the pre-shifted value, which made `Q_GETQUOTA | USRQUOTA` look like "compose a cmd word" but actually produced garbage because the subcommand and qtype overlapped in the same byte. New constants are the raw subcommand numbers (`Q_SYNC = 0x800001`, `Q_QUOTAON = 0x800002`, ... `Q_SETQUOTA = 0x800008`) and the user composes them via `qcmd(Q_GETQUOTA, USRQUOTA)`. Same architectural pattern as the System V semaphores and message queues phases: a static pool of segments (4 segments × 64 KiB per segment) backed in BSS, a single AtomicBool spinlock serialising metadata, and generation-tagged shmid encoding `(generation << 16) | (slot + 1)` so stale identifiers after `IPC_RMID` cleanly resolve to EINVAL instead of silently aliasing the next allocation. The backing buffers are wrapped in `UnsafeCell<[u8; SEGMENT_SIZE + SHMLBA]>` with `#[repr(C, align(8192))]` (Windows COFF section alignment caps below `SHMLBA = 16384`, so we keep the maximum supported static alignment and add `SHMLBA - 1` slack bytes, then `segment_ptr()` rounds the raw address up to the next `SHMLBA` multiple). Result: every pointer returned by `shmat` is properly 16 KiB-page-aligned (matching `SHMLBA`), satisfying the precondition that classic Sys V consumers depend on for direct page-table mapping equivalents. shmget: validates `size > SEGMENT_SIZE → EINVAL`; `IPC_PRIVATE` always allocates fresh regardless of flags (matches Linux); non-private keys look up by key (skipping segments already marked-for-rmid, so a future `shmget` for the same key gets a brand-new slot) then optionally allocate per `IPC_CREAT`/`IPC_EXCL`; lookup of an existing segment with `size > current_size → EINVAL` (Linux semantics — a smaller-than-existing request is fine); collision with `IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL → EEXIST`; missing key without IPC_CREAT → ENOENT; pool exhaustion → ENOSPC; `size == 0` on create → EINVAL. shmat: validates shmid (decode + slot in-use + generation match) → EINVAL on failure; refuses to attach to a segment marked-for-rmid → EIDRM (Linux semantics — existing attaches stay valid but new attaches must fail so the segment can actually drain); increments `nattch` and returns the page-aligned backing pointer (caller-supplied `shmaddr` and `SHM_RND` are ignored — we don't have userspace page tables for callers to choose addresses in; `SHM_RDONLY` is accepted but unenforced because we lack per-mapping permission machinery). shmdt: pointer-based slot lookup via `slot_for_ptr()` (compares against each slot's aligned base address) → EINVAL if the pointer isn't one of ours; decrements `nattch`; if `nattch == 0` AND the slot is marked-for-rmid, frees the slot and bumps the generation counter, completing the deferred-free lifecycle. shmctl: IPC_RMID flips `marked_for_rmid` (does *not* immediately free — Linux semantics for active segments); if `nattch == 0` at that moment, frees immediately; either way the segment can no longer be looked up by key, so `shmget(same_key, IPC_CREAT)` always creates a brand-new slot afterwards. IPC_STAT populates `ShmidDs` with `shm_segsz` (requested size, not pool size), `shm_perm_mode`, `shm_nattch`; time fields and pid fields stay 0 (no per-segment clocks or pids tracked yet). IPC_SET applies `shm_perm_mode` from the caller's struct. SHM_LOCK / SHM_UNLOCK are accepted as no-ops (our memory is never swapped). Unknown cmd → EINVAL. NULL buf on IPC_STAT/IPC_SET → EFAULT. Backing buffers are zeroed via `core::ptr::write_bytes` on slot reuse so a recycled segment doesn't leak the previous tenant's data. 32 new tests cover: every error path (EINVAL/ENOENT/EEXIST/ENOSPC/EIDRM/EFAULT), shmid encode/decode roundtrip, decode rejects zero and negative shmids, IPC_PRIVATE fresh-each-time, EEXIST on `IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL`, pool exhaustion, attach returns SHMLBA-aligned pointer, attach/detach refcount visible via IPC_STAT, write to one attached pointer is visible on the next attach (data sharing is real, not per-call buffer), RMID with no attaches frees immediately, RMID with active attaches defers free and a follow-up shmget creates a new slot, attach after RMID returns EIDRM, detach of unknown pointer / unattached slot / NULL pointer → EINVAL, IPC_STAT layout, IPC_SET updates mode, IPC_STAT/IPC_SET NULL-buf EFAULT, SHM_LOCK/SHM_UNLOCK no-op, full classic workflow (shmget → shmat → write → shmdt → IPC_RMID). 4 obsolete ENOSYS tests removed. **Limitations** (documented in module docs): single-process only — the table lives in this address space, so a second process wouldn't see segments created by the first (cross-process visibility needs kernel-side namespacing, deferred); caller-supplied `shmaddr` is ignored (we don't expose a virtual-address chooser); `SHM_RDONLY` accepted but unenforced; `SHM_REMAP` accepted but unused; `shm_atime`/`shm_dtime`/`shm_ctime`/`shm_cpid`/`shm_lpid` stay 0; SHMMAX is fixed at the per-segment pool size (64 KiB) — programs requesting bigger get EINVAL (raising SHMMAX would mean either a larger static pool or a real backing allocator, both deferred until kernel mm is mature enough to back arbitrary-size shared regions).   - [x] System V message queues (`<sys/msg.h>`): real in-memory implementation of `msgget` / `msgsnd` / `msgrcv` / `msgctl`, replacing the four ENOSYS stubs. Same architectural pattern as the System V semaphores phase: static pool of 8 queues × 32 messages per queue × 256 bytes per message body, single AtomicBool spinlock, generation-tagged msqid encoding that invalidates stale identifiers after `IPC_RMID`. msgget: IPC_PRIVATE always allocates fresh; non-private keys look up first then optionally allocate per `IPC_CREAT`/`IPC_EXCL`; pool exhaustion → ENOSPC; missing key without IPC_CREAT → ENOENT; collision with IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL → EEXIST. msgsnd: validates the `mtype` prefix (the first 8 bytes of `msgbuf`) is strictly positive — Linux semantics, programs use `mtype == 0` as a wildcard marker on `msgrcv` so non-positive types on the wire are nonsensical and Linux returns EINVAL; rejects `msgsz > MAX_MSG_TEXT` (EINVAL) and NULL `msgp` (EFAULT); rejects stale/unknown msqid (EINVAL); respects per-queue `msg_qbytes` quota so a runaway producer can't burn the whole queue. With `IPC_NOWAIT`, a full queue (either out of message slots or out of byte quota) returns EAGAIN; without it, the call spin-yields the lock between retries. msgrcv: implements all three POSIX selection modes — `msgtyp == 0` returns the oldest message regardless of type, `msgtyp > 0` returns the oldest message of that exact type, `msgtyp < 0` returns the lowest-typed message with `1 ≤ mtype ≤ |msgtyp|` (ties broken by FIFO order). `MSG_EXCEPT` flag inverts the positive-msgtyp match (return first message whose type is *not* the given one). Oversized messages return E2BIG and stay on the queue by default; `MSG_NOERROR` truncates to `msgsz` and dequeues. Empty queue or no-matching-type with `IPC_NOWAIT` returns ENOMSG (the Linux contract — POSIX is silent on the precise errno but glibc / musl both ship code that checks `errno == ENOMSG`). NULL `msgp` → EFAULT. msgctl: IPC_RMID bumps the slot generation counter so stale msqids become EINVAL; IPC_STAT walks the message ring to populate `msg_qnum` / `msg_cbytes` along with `msg_perm_mode` and `msg_qbytes` (time fields stay 0 — no per-queue clock tracking yet); IPC_SET applies `msg_perm_mode` and `msg_qbytes`, clamping `msg_qbytes` to the static pool capacity so callers can't push the queue past the backing store. NULL buf on IPC_STAT/IPC_SET → EFAULT. Unknown cmd → EINVAL. 33 new tests cover: every error path (EINVAL/ENOENT/EEXIST/ENOSPC/EAGAIN/ENOMSG/E2BIG/EFAULT), msqid encode/decode roundtrip, IPC_PRIVATE fresh-each-time, FIFO ordering across multiple types, positive-type exact match, negative-type lowest-type selection, MSG_EXCEPT inversion, MSG_NOERROR truncation, byte-quota enforcement via IPC_SET, IPC_STAT field population (qnum/cbytes/qbytes/mode), IPC_SET clamping to pool max, RMID frees slot and invalidates old id, full classic workflow (msgget → msgsnd → msgrcv by type → IPC_RMID). 14 obsolete ENOSYS tests removed. **Limitations**: single-process only; permission bits stored but unenforced; `IPC_STAT` time fields (`msg_stime`/`msg_rtime`/`msg_ctime`) stay 0; `MSG_COPY` (peek by queue index without dequeue) is accepted but treated as a normal receive that does dequeue — full MSG_COPY would need an absolute-index accessor (deferred). Used by classic Sys V IPC consumers — Oracle background processes, Sybase ASE inter-process notifications, Postfix's master ↔ worker handoff, dbmail's authentication daemon, `ipcs`/`ipcrm` userspace tools (now usable for inspection/cleanup), the `lockfile-progs` package, and most C/C++ tutorial code targeting "real" Unix IPC.
  - [x] System V semaphores (`<sys/sem.h>`): real in-memory implementation of `semget` / `semop` / `semtimedop` / `semctl` plus the four-arg `semctl_setval` / `semctl_setall` / `semctl_getall` helpers (POSIX `semctl` is C-variadic with a `union semun` payload — Rust can't safely emit variadics on stable, so the variadic forms are split into named helpers; a tiny C shim can re-fuse them for full POSIX surface). Replaces the four ENOSYS stubs that were blocking real legacy software (PostgreSQL refuses to start with `IpcSemaphoreCreate: semget failed (No such file or directory)`, Oracle, Sybase, classic UNIX shell mutexes). Static pool of 16 semaphore sets × 32 semaphores per set, protected by a single AtomicBool spinlock; tests serialize via a separate `std::sync::Mutex` because cargo runs them in parallel. Semid encoding packs (slot_index+1) in the low 16 bits and a 15-bit generation counter (bumped on `IPC_RMID`) in the next 15 bits, so any stale semid returned to userspace after the slot is reused or removed cleanly resolves to EINVAL instead of silently aliasing a different set. semget: `IPC_PRIVATE` always allocates fresh, non-private keys look up first then optionally allocate per `IPC_CREAT`/`IPC_EXCL`; pool exhaustion → ENOSPC; nsems out of `1..=MAX_SEMS_PER_SET` → EINVAL; lookup of an existing set with `nsems > current_nsems` → EINVAL (matching Linux). semop: blocking by default — drops the lock and spin-yields between retries so other threads can release the semaphore; `IPC_NOWAIT` in any sembuf's `sem_flg` turns blocking into an immediate EAGAIN. Multi-op batches are **atomic and rollback-safe**: ops are applied to a scratch copy of the values array and only committed if every op succeeded, so a 2-op batch where the second op would block leaves the first op's effect undone — matches kernel semantics that real software relies on for deadlock-free composite acquisition. `sem_op > 0` (release) caps at `SEMVMX = 32767`, overflow → ERANGE; `sem_op == 0` (wait-for-zero) blocks while the value is nonzero; `sem_op < 0` (acquire) blocks while `value + delta < 0`. Bad sem_num → EFBIG. Bad semid → EINVAL. Null sops → EFAULT. nsops == 0 or > 32 → E2BIG. semtimedop: same blocking loop but uses `clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)` to enforce the absolute deadline; expired deadline → EAGAIN (POSIX requires EAGAIN here, not ETIMEDOUT — semop unifies "would block" with "timed out"); NULL timeout is "wait forever" (same as semop); malformed timespec (negative or `tv_nsec >= 1e9`) → EINVAL. semctl: IPC_RMID frees the slot and bumps the generation counter to invalidate stale semids; GETVAL returns current value; GETPID / GETNCNT / GETZCNT return 0 (no per-process wait tracking — would need a futex-style waiter table); IPC_STAT/IPC_SET/SEM_INFO etc. return EINVAL pending the union-semun bridge. semctl_setval validates `0..=SEMVMX` (ERANGE otherwise). semctl_setall validates all values *before* writing any (atomic batch: ERANGE on any bad value leaves the set unchanged). 31 new tests cover: every error path (EINVAL/ENOENT/EEXIST/ENOSPC/E2BIG/EFBIG/ERANGE/EFAULT/EAGAIN), encode/decode roundtrip, IPC_PRIVATE always-fresh semantics, EEXIST on `IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL` against existing, pool exhaustion, RMID frees slot and invalidates old semid, semop atomic rollback on partial-block, SEMVMX overflow detection, semtimedop past-deadline / immediate-success / NULL-timeout / bad-timespec paths, semctl_setall atomic rollback on bad value, classic-mutex workflow (semget → setval(1) → P → V → RMID). 17 pre-existing ENOSYS tests removed since the functions no longer return ENOSYS. **Limitations** (documented in module docs): single-process only (table lives in this address space), `SEM_UNDO` accepted but ignored (no per-process undo tracking — programs relying on rollback after crash don't get it), permission bits stored but unenforced (getuid() returns 0 in our world), IPC_STAT/IPC_SET deferred, semvariadic forms exposed as named helpers (semctl_setval/setall/getall) rather than C variadic. Bails on the first invalid pointer, NULL return address, or after 256 frames (catches corrupt-loop cases). Caps at the caller-supplied `size`. Non-x86_64 builds and any future no-FP build return 0 (correct fallback). `backtrace_symbols(addrs, n)` allocates one `malloc` block of `n × sizeof(*mut u8) + n × 19` bytes — first half is the pointer array, second half is 19-byte slots (`"0x" + 16 hex chars + NUL`); each pointer in the array points into the strings area, so a single `free()` releases everything (matches glibc's documented contract). Without an in-process symbol table the best we can do is format hex; programs that need names should post-process with `addr2line` against the on-disk binary (or link in a future symbol-table reader). `backtrace_symbols_fd(addrs, n, fd)` formats inline on the stack (no malloc — safe in signal handlers) and `write()`s one `"0x...\n"` line per address; best-effort, ignores short writes. Critical detail: `posix_fadvise` returns the error directly (positive value), it does **not** set errno and return -1; added a test (`test_posix_fadvise_does_not_set_errno`) pinning that behavior because it's a frequent source of caller bugs. `fadvise64` delegates to `posix_fadvise` so both wrappers stay in sync. 6 new tests cover: bad-fd EBADF, bad-advice EINVAL, negative-len EINVAL, errno-untouched on failure, pipe-fd ESPIPE, fadvise64 delegation. Reads `crate::mm::frame::stats()`; total clamps to ≥ 1, free is reported raw. Because our kernel page size *is* 16 KiB (= one frame), frame counts equal POSIX page counts so no scaling is needed. posix `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES | _SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` and the glibc aliases `get_phys_pages()` / `get_avphys_pages()` now report real memory instead of hardcoded 8192/4096 page constants. Host test build retains the hardcoded values via cfg(not(target_os = "none")). Used by language runtimes (Java -Xmx auto-sizing, Go's `runtime.MemStats`, Python's `psutil`, Node's `os.totalmem`), top/htop/free, and any tool that adapts cache sizes to RAM.
  - [x] SYS_CPU_COUNT (kernel #55) + posix wiring: replaces hardcoded 1-CPU answers with the real online CPU count from `smp::cpu_count()`. New kernel handler `sys_cpu_count` returns the AtomicU64 reported by the SMP bring-up path (always ≥ 1). posix `sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN | _SC_NPROCESSORS_CONF)` consults the syscall on bare metal and falls back to 1 in `cargo test` builds (host syscall ABI differs). `sched_getaffinity` now populates bits 0..N of the CpuSetT mask instead of always returning bit 0 only (with `min(CPU_SETSIZE=1024, ncpus)` capping). `sched_setaffinity` previously accepted any mask unconditionally; now validates non-NULL, sufficient cpusetsize, and at least one bit set in range 0..ncpus (EINVAL otherwise). Used by glibc `get_nprocs`, Java/Go/Rust runtime worker-pool sizing, OpenMP `omp_get_num_procs`, and any program that inspects affinity before launching its thread pool. Test coverage: 5 new tests (`test_sysconf_nprocessors_positive`, `test_sysconf_nprocessors_conf_ge_onln`, `test_sched_setaffinity_{null,too_small,empty_mask,unreachable_cpu}_einval`, `test_sched_getaffinity_roundtrip`).
  - [x] kill(pid, 0): canonical POSIX existence check — `kill` previously stubbed all `(pid, sig)` combinations as ENOSYS, but `kill(pid, 0)` doesn't actually send a signal (it's the canonical idiom for "does this process still exist?" used by bash, lock-file cleanup, daemon shutdown logic). Routed through the existing kernel `SYS_PROCESS_IS_READY` syscall, which returns a non-negative value if the PID is live and a negative error otherwise; collapses those into POSIX `0` (exists) or `-1`+`ESRCH` (no such process). `pid <= 0` (process-group and "all processes" forms) stayed ENOSYS at the time — **no longer true as of 2026-08-12**: `kill(0, sig)` and `kill(-pgid, sig)` now reach the kernel's shared group fanout over real process-group membership, and only `kill(-1, sig)` (the broadcast form) is still ESRCH-not-modelled. `kill(getpid(), SIGABRT)` now also routes to `abort()`, matching the existing `raise(SIGABRT)` behavior for the common `kill(getpid(), SIGABRT)` abort idiom. Out-of-range sig values now produce EINVAL instead of ENOSYS, matching Linux. All other `(pid, sig)` combinations remain ENOSYS per the design rule "no Unix signals for process control." Side bug fix: errno was a single global AtomicI32 in test builds, so cargo's parallel test runner could let one test's `set_errno` clobber another test's `get_errno` mid-assertion — flaky `test_translate_*` failures had been occurring intermittently. Switched the test-build errno backing to a `thread_local!(Cell<i32>)` (production build keeps the AtomicI32 since `__errno_location()` needs a stable address); removed a now-redundant CRYPT-style serialising mutex from the errno tests. Also exposed a latent bug in `linux_aio_abi::execute_iocb`'s unknown-opcode arm: it returned `-EINVAL` directly but relied on the wrapper to read errno; previously the polluted global happened to contain EINVAL, but with TLS each thread starts at 0 and the wrapper substituted EIO. Fixed by having the unknown-opcode arm explicitly `set_errno(EINVAL)` and return -1, taking the same wrapper path as `pread`/`pwrite` failures.
  - [x] adjtimex / ntp_adjtime / clock_adjtime: `<sys/timex.h>` kernel clock-discipline interface — replaces ENOSYS stub with a real process-local NTP state holder. Maintains a TimexState (offset, freq, maxerror, esterror, status, constant, tick, tai) behind a spinlock; reads return the current state plus sensible static fields (tolerance = 32_768_000 scaled ppm matching NTP MAXFREQ, precision = 1). Mode bits applied selectively: ADJ_OFFSET / ADJ_FREQUENCY / ADJ_MAXERROR / ADJ_ESTERROR / ADJ_STATUS / ADJ_TIMECONST / ADJ_TAI / ADJ_TICK update the corresponding state fields; ADJ_NANO sets STA_NANO; ADJ_MICRO clears it. Return code follows Linux semantics: TIME_ERROR when STA_UNSYNC is set, TIME_INS / TIME_DEL for pending leap seconds, TIME_OK otherwise. Boot state has STA_UNSYNC set (no NTP source yet). Rejects unknown mode bits with EINVAL and null pointer with EFAULT. clock_adjtime accepts CLOCK_REALTIME and CLOCK_MONOTONIC (both forward to the same shared state — we have only one underlying clock), rejects other clock ids with EINVAL. No privilege check yet (no user model); on a real multi-user system writes would require CAP_SYS_TIME. ntpd / chronyd / openntpd / Java's NTP probe / Go's `runtime.nanotime` calibration paths all link adjtimex; this implementation makes them succeed without lying about whether the system clock is actually disciplined (STA_UNSYNC stays set until a caller explicitly clears it).
  - [x] membarrier: Linux process-wide memory barrier syscall — replaces ENOSYS stub. `MEMBARRIER_CMD_QUERY` returns a real bitmask of supported commands instead of zero; CMD_GLOBAL / CMD_GLOBAL_EXPEDITED / CMD_PRIVATE_EXPEDITED / CMD_PRIVATE_EXPEDITED_SYNC_CORE and their REGISTER_* variants all succeed and issue a local x86_64 `mfence` (compiler SeqCst fence on non-x86 hosts). Each thread re-fences whenever it crosses a syscall boundary, so peer-CPU ordering is implicit pending a userspace-triggered IPI path through the kernel; this matches Linux behavior for everything except code that aggressively spins in userspace without ever syscalling. Rejects unknown commands and non-zero flag bits with EINVAL. RSEQ variants remain ENOSYS pending restartable-sequence infrastructure. Also fixes a pre-existing bug where `MEMBARRIER_CMD_REGISTER_GLOBAL_EXPEDITED` collided with `MEMBARRIER_CMD_REGISTER_PRIVATE_EXPEDITED` on bit 4 (Linux uses bit 2 for the global REGISTER); added a regression test. Used by Java's G1/ZGC, Go's runtime, Folly RCU, ConcurrencyKit, and any runtime that needs cheap asymmetric synchronization (one-shot expedited fences instead of acquiring a global mutex on every fast-path access).
  - [x] futex: Linux `<linux/futex.h>` fast userspace locking — replaces ENOSYS stub. Dispatches to the kernel's native futex syscalls (`SYS_FUTEX_WAIT` 210, `SYS_FUTEX_WAKE` 211, `SYS_FUTEX_LOCK_PI` 212, `SYS_FUTEX_UNLOCK_PI` 213, `SYS_FUTEX_WAIT_TIMEOUT` 214) after stripping `FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG` (our kernel is process-local — all futexes are effectively private) and `FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME` (we only have a monotonic clock). FUTEX_WAIT with a NULL timeout uses the indefinite kernel wait; with a non-NULL timeout it converts the `Timespec` to nanoseconds (overflow-safe, rejects negative seconds, nsec ≥ 1e9, or u64 overflow with EINVAL) and uses SYS_FUTEX_WAIT_TIMEOUT. Maps the kernel's `1 = woken / 0 = value mismatch` return into Linux's `0 = woken / -1 EAGAIN = mismatch / -1 ETIMEDOUT = timeout`. FUTEX_WAKE returns the woken count. FUTEX_LOCK_PI/UNLOCK_PI succeed with 0. The remaining ops (FUTEX_REQUEUE, CMP_REQUEUE, WAKE_OP, WAIT_BITSET, WAKE_BITSET, TRYLOCK_PI, WAIT_REQUEUE_PI, CMP_REQUEUE_PI) return ENOSYS pending kernel-side wiring. Used by glibc pthread_mutex/cond/barrier/rwlock, Rust std parking_lot, every Linux ELF binary that links libpthread.
  - [x] utime: legacy `<utime.h>` file-time setter — replaces ENOSYS stub. Forwards to `utimensat(AT_FDCWD, path, &ts[2], 0)`, converting the `Utimbuf` (actime/modtime as second-precision time_t) to two `Timespec`s with `tv_nsec = 0`. Null `times` is passed through, which utimensat treats as "set both timestamps to current time". The underlying utimensat is still a no-op stub (filesystem doesn't track per-file timestamps yet), so utime currently always succeeds without persisting any change — but the path is wired so that when utimensat gets a real implementation, utime gets it for free.
  - [x] sem_open/sem_close/sem_unlink: POSIX named semaphores — replaces ENOSYS stubs with a real in-memory implementation. Static pool of 16 named semaphores plus a single global spinlock; each slot carries an in-use flag, an unlinked flag, the name, a refcount, and the semaphore body (matching the existing unnamed `SemT` layout so `sem_wait`/`sem_post`/`sem_getvalue` work unchanged). sem_open's variadic `mode`/`value` args are folded into the extern "C" signature — 2-arg callers leave them undefined and we only consult them when `O_CREAT` is set. Supports `O_CREAT` (allocate a fresh slot), `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` (EEXIST if name exists), name validation matching POSIX (leading `/`, no embedded `/`, ≤64 bytes), and value capped at i32::MAX. sem_unlink marks a slot as unlinked; the slot stays alive as long as any open handle still holds a refcount, matching POSIX unlink-while-open semantics. Single-process only — cross-process named semaphores need kernel-side named objects (deferred along with cross-process mqueue).
  - [x] memfd_create: anonymous in-memory file descriptors (`<linux/memfd.h>`) — replaces ENOSYS stub. Routes through `/dev/shm/.memfd_<counter>_<name>` opened with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_RDWR` (plus `O_CLOEXEC` if `MFD_CLOEXEC`), then immediately `unlink()`s the path so only the returned fd keeps the file alive (true anonymous semantics). Process-wide AtomicU64 counter makes the temporary path unique. Validates the user name (≤200 bytes, no embedded `/`), rejects unknown flag bits with EINVAL, rejects `MFD_HUGETLB` (no hugepage backing in our PMM). Accepts `MFD_ALLOW_SEALING`/`MFD_NOEXEC_SEAL`/`MFD_EXEC` as no-ops pending fcntl seal infrastructure. Used by Wayland (wl_shm pools), Mesa GBM, Chromium IPC, systemd-journald and other modern Linux applications.
  - [x] dn_expand/dn_comp/dn_skipname: DNS name wire-format helpers in `<resolv.h>` — replaces ENOSYS-style stubs with real parsers. dn_expand walks a compressed name from a packet buffer, follows backward-only compression pointers (RFC 1035) with a 64-hop cap to catch malformed loops, rejects reserved label types 01/10, and returns the number of bytes consumed *at the original position* (so the caller can advance even when the name was compressed). dn_skipname walks the same encoding without expanding (pointer counts as 2 terminating bytes). dn_comp emits an uncompressed wire-format name from a dotted C-string, handling the root domain (".", or empty input) as a single zero byte, accepting a single trailing dot, and rejecting empty intermediate labels, leading dots followed by text, and oversize (>63-byte) labels. Compression-table args (`dnptrs`/`lastdnptr`) are accepted but ignored — uncompressed output is always wire-format-valid. Covers callers that parse DNS responses without pulling in a full resolver (e.g. `getaddrinfo` consumers, mdns_helper tools).

    - [x] **The three kernel-shaped gaps are closed (2026-08-16).** `waitid`
      used to return `ENOSYS` for a wait on process group 1, ignore `WNOWAIT`
      and reap anyway, and report `si_uid`/`si_utime`/`si_stime` as 0 — all
      three because it was built on a `waitpid`-shaped syscall whose single
      signed selector spends `-1` on "any child" and whose reap destroyed the
      facts before it could answer. Lane A added `WPGID`, `WNOWAIT` and a
      `WINFO`-gated 72-byte `WaitInfo` out-parameter to
      `SYS_PROCESS_WAIT_STATUS` (§206); libc consumes all three (§319).
      `waitpid`/`wait3`/`wait4`/`waitid` now funnel through one `wait_common`
      taking a `WaitTarget { Selector, Pgid }` rather than a signed integer,
      which is what stops a caller half-converting — under `WPGID`, `-g` is not
      group `g`, it is a huge unsigned pgid matching nothing. New ring-3
      coverage: `ctest-jobctl` checks 150-187, of which **157** (`arg4 = 128`,
      bytes 72..128 must come back zeroed) and **169** (`arg4 = 24`, bytes
      24..128 must be untouched) are the extensible-struct convention, which
      nothing else in the tree can test — libc always passes its own `sizeof`,
      and a kernel self-test task has no user address space to `copy_to_user`
      into.
