> ### ⛔ STOP — osh's bash-fidelity scope is FROZEN (design-decisions.md **§305**, operator, 2026-08-14)
>
> **Before doing any osh/bash-parity work, read §305.** The short version:
>
> - **GNU bash 5.2 already cross-compiles and runs on SlateOS** (`scripts/bash-spike/`,
>   `kernel/src/proc/spawn.rs::self_test_bash_on_slateos_libc`). This has been true
>   since 2026-07-22. §72's "no C/C++ cross-toolchain" premise — the reason osh was
>   reimplemented at all — has been false almost the whole time osh has existed.
> - The operator's call is the **hybrid**: osh stays the shell, bash ships beside it,
>   and **byte-for-byte parity with bash is no longer a goal.**
> - **Fix an osh divergence only if** something we actually ship or run hits it, *or*
>   it is a crash/hang/data-loss/security/wrong-exit-status bug, *or* it is a
>   regression against an already-green corpus case.
> - **Do not fix, and do not write a corpus case for:** diagnostic wording or the
>   exact substring a message echoes; artifacts of bash being 40-year-old C
>   (`OPTIND=4294967297` wrapping through an `int`); constructs reachable only by
>   adversarial input whose sole difference is the error text.
> - Out-of-scope divergences get `SCOPE: out of frozen scope (§305)` in their
>   `TD-OILS-*` entry and are **left unfixed**. If something truly needs exact bash,
>   run bash.
> - The **corpus does not grow for its own sake.** 662 cases green is a floor to
>   protect, not a number to raise.
>
> This is not a suggestion about tidiness — it is the resolution of a 25-day
> misdirection, and §305 records the history specifically so it is not repeated.

- [-] `[B]` Port **Oils (OSH)** — a bash-*superset* shell — for POSIX compatibility (replaces bash; this is the "A" initiative in the large-initiative ordering above, NOT bash itself). See roadmap-detailed.md §2.7. **In progress:** Rust reimplementation of the OSH language in-tree (`userspace/oils`, binary `osh`) — no C++→slateos cross-toolchain exists, so a faithful `oils-for-unix` cross-compile is blocked; see design-decisions.md §72 and open-questions.md Q26. MVP done: lexer + recursive-descent parser + tree-walking interpreter that forks/execs real externals via `std::process::Command`; pipelines, redirections, `&&`/`||`/`;`/`&`, if/while/until/for, functions, brace-groups/subshells, `$var`/`${…}`/`$(( ))`/`$( )`/backtick expansion, IFS field splitting, and ~20 builtins (`cd pwd echo printf export unset set shift getopts mapfile/readarray command builtin read test [ eval source . type exit return break continue : true false`). Grow phase since MVP: case statements, here-docs/here-strings, richer parameter expansion (`#`/`##`/`%`/`%%` trim, `:offset:len` substring, `/`/`//`/`/#`/`/%` replace), `[[ … ]]` conditional expressions (string/glob/numeric comparisons, file/string unary tests, `!`/`&&`/`||`/grouping, and `=~` POSIX-ERE regex match with `BASH_REMATCH` capture extraction — matched by an in-tree linear-time Pike-VM engine that is ReDoS-safe; RHS matching is quote-aware — quoted spans of the pattern match literally while unquoted spans are regex, per bash), `(( … ))` arithmetic commands, command-line pathname (glob) expansion (`*`/`?`/`[…]`, quoting-aware, leading-dot rule, unmatched-stays-literal), and indexed arrays (`a=(x y z)`, `a[i]=v`, `a+=(w)`/`a+=str`, `${a[i]}`/`${a[@]}`/`${a[*]}`, `${#a[@]}`/`${#a[i]}`, `unset a[i]`; `"${a[@]}"` preserves one field per element, unquoted `${a[@]}` field-splits), compound-command redirections (`while read …; done < file`, `for … done > out`, `{ …; } >> log`, pipeline-into-`while read`; body `read`s consume successive lines via a shared input cursor, captured stdout written to the target file, and compound *stderr* redirection — `{ …; } 2> err`/`2>>`, `for … done 2>&1`, `>&2` inside a group — honored via a per-shell `stderr_stack` that every fd-2 write (diagnostics, builtin `>&2`, external child stderr) consults; `2>&1` into a captured stdout folds stderr in after the body, see known-issues TD-OILS3), and associative arrays (`declare -A m`/`typeset`/`local`, `m[key]=v`, `m=([k]=v …)`, `${m[key]}`/`${m[@]}`/`${m[*]}`, `${!m[@]}` keys, `${#m[@]}`, `unset m[key]`; insertion-ordered, string subscripts; keyed/sparse indexed literals `a=([2]=x y)` and `${!a[@]}` indices too), and **concurrent, streaming pipelines** (all-external pipelines wire real OS pipes between child processes; any pipeline with a builtin/function/compound stage uses the *threaded* path — each stage runs in its own subshell on its own thread connected by real OS pipes, so data streams as produced and each stage is a subshell per bash semantics; downstream early-exit propagates upstream — an in-process producer stops via the `pipe_broken` SIGPIPE-analogue and an external producer on the OS broken-pipe signal, e.g. `yes | head`, on targets that deliver it), plus **pipefail + `${PIPESTATUS[@]}`** (both pipeline paths record every stage's exit code in `PIPESTATUS`, in order — including a one-element array for a bare command — and `set -o pipefail`/`set +o pipefail` folds `$?` to the rightmost non-zero stage), and the combined **`declare -A m=([k]=v)` one-liner** (array-literal operands to a declaration builtin are parsed as `decl_arrays` and applied with the declared kind; works for `declare -a a=(x y)`/flagless `declare a=(x y)` too). Negative array subscripts (`${a[-1]}` = last, scalar = one-element array), arithmetic subscripts inside `(( … ))`/`$(( … ))` (`(( a[i]+1 ))`, `a[-1]`), and subscripts combined with a parameter operator (`${a[i]:-def}`, `${a[i]#pat}`, `${a[i]:off:len}`, `${a[i]/pat/repl}`, `${a[i]:=v}` with element write-back; associative keys too — only `[@]`/`[*]`+operator bulk transforms are rejected) are also implemented. Indexed arrays are **sparse** (an ordered `index → value` map): `a=([5]=x)` stores one element, `${#a[@]}` counts only assigned elements, `${!a[@]}` lists only assigned indices, `unset a[i]` leaves a gap, and a negative subscript counts from `highest_index+1` — all bash-correct. Per-stage redirects compose with the inter-stage pipe (`a | b > f`, `a | b 2>err` route to the threaded path and merge the stage's `RedirPlan` with the pipe endpoints — verified by Windows tests). The `=~` regex engine (`ere.rs`) is an in-tree POSIX-ERE Pike-VM/Thompson-NFA implementation with capture groups (linear-time, ReDoS-safe); the lexer reads the `=~` RHS as one regex word so metacharacters (`(`, `)`, `|`, `<`, `>`) stay literal while parameter expansion still applies; the RHS is quote-aware (quoted spans matched literally via `regex_pattern_from_rhs`, unquoted spans are regex). Associative subscripts inside `(( … ))`/`$(( … ))` (`m[foo]`, `m[$k]`) are read by string key (not arith-evaluated), while indexed subscripts stay arithmetic — via `VarLookup::is_assoc`/`get_assoc`. The arithmetic evaluator also supports the ternary `?:` (right-associative) and comma operators (`$(( cond ? a : b ))`, `$(( e1, e2 ))`), plus the full **mutation set**: assignment `= += -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= |= ^=` (right-associative, chained `a = b = c`), pre/post increment/decrement (`++x`/`x++`/`--x`/`x--`), and exponentiation `**` — including on array/associative elements (`(( a[i] += 1 ))`, `(( m[key]++ ))`). Numeric literals accept the full bash syntax: `0x`/`0X` hex, leading-zero octal (`017` = 15), and `base#num` arbitrary bases 2–64 (`2#1010`, `16#ff`, `64#_` = 63; digits above 9 are lowercase then uppercase letters then `@`/`_`, with letter cases interchangeable for bases ≤ 36). `arith.rs` is a two-phase AST evaluator (parse with immutable `&dyn VarLookup`, evaluate with mutable `&mut dyn VarLookup` via `set`/`set_index`/`set_assoc`), so `&&`/`||` short-circuit and `?:` is branch-lazy (side effects fire only on the taken path). The **C-style `for (( init; cond; update )); do …; done`** loop is implemented (`ForArithClause`; empty condition ⇒ always-true; `update` runs after each iteration including after `continue`; `break`/`continue` levels propagate). **Case-modification parameter expansion** `${v^}`/`${v^^}` (upper), `${v,}`/`${v,,}` (lower), and `${v~}`/`${v~~}` (toggle) is implemented (doubled = every character, single = first character only; an optional glob pattern like `${v^^[aeiou]}` selects which characters convert; works on array elements). **Indirect expansion `${!ref}`** (reads the variable named by `ref`, including array-element referents `ref=a[0]`/`ref=m[k]`) and **prefix name-matching `${!prefix*}`/`${!prefix@}`** (sorted names of all set variables — scalars, indexed and associative arrays — beginning with `prefix`; quoted `@` form yields one field per name) are implemented. **ANSI-C quoting `$'…'`** processes backslash escapes (`\n \t \r \a \b \e \f \v \\ \' \" \?`, octal `\nnn`, hex `\xHH`, unicode `\uHHHH`/`\UHHHHHHHH`, control `\cx`; unknown escapes keep the backslash) and yields a literal (no expansion/splitting); `$"…"` is treated as a plain double-quoted string (no message catalogs). The **`getopts optstring name [args]`** builtin is implemented: POSIX-style single-option-per-call parsing with `OPTIND`/`OPTARG`, bundled short flags (`-abc`), options-with-arguments (`-b val` or `-bval`), `--` end-of-options, silent error mode (leading `:` → unknown sets `name=?`+`OPTARG`, missing arg sets `name=:`+`OPTARG`) vs. verbose mode (diagnostics to stderr), and external-`OPTIND=1` reset detection (a per-shell `getopts_col` cursor tracks bundling). **`mapfile`/`readarray [-t] [-d delim] [-n count] [-s skip] [-O origin] [array]`** reads its whole input (here-doc/here-string, `< file`, pipeline stream, or stdin) into an indexed array (default `MAPFILE`): each element keeps its trailing delimiter unless `-t`, `-d` sets an alternate delimiter, `-n` caps the count, `-s` skips leading lines, `-O` sets the starting index. **`printf` now recycles its format string** until all arguments are consumed (`printf '%s\n' a b c` → three lines), matching bash, and emits the format exactly once when it has no argument-consuming conversion. `printf` also supports **`-v var`** (assign the formatted result to a shell variable instead of writing to stdout) and a full conversion/format-spec set: `%s %b` (interpret backslash escapes) `%q` (shell-quote) `%c` (first char) `%d %i %u %x %X %o` (integers, with `0x`/`'c` input forms) `%f %F %e %E %g %G` (floats), plus flags (`- + space # 0`), numeric field width, and precision (`%5d`, `%-5s`, `%05d`, `%.2f`, `%.2s`) — with **dynamic `*` width/precision** taken from an argument (`printf '%*d' 5 42`, `printf '%.*f' 2 3.14159`, `printf '%*.*f' 8 2 3.14159`; a negative `*` width left-justifies, a negative `.*` precision is ignored) — and the **`%(FORMAT)T` strftime time conversion** (consumes one epoch-seconds argument — missing/negative ⇒ now — and renders it in UTC via an in-tree `civil_from_days`/`format_strftime`, supporting `%Y %C %y %m %d %e %H %I %M %S %p %P %A %a %B %b %h %j %u %w %s %n %t %F %T %R %D %%`; local-timezone offset is not yet applied — see known-issues TD-OILS9). **Brace expansion** (`brace.rs`) runs first (textually, before parameter/other expansion) on command words and `for`-loop lists: comma lists (`a{b,c,d}e`), numeric sequences (`{1..5}`, `{5..1}`, `{1..9..2}`), zero-padded sequences (`{01..10}`), character sequences (`{a..e}`, `{Z..A}`), cross-products/nesting (`{a,b}{1,2}`, `{a,{b,c}}`), and empty alternatives (`{,x}`); invalid braces (`{}`, `{abc}`) and quoted braces stay literal, and alternatives may contain parameter refs (`{$v,b}`) which expand after the brace pass. **`${var@op}` parameter transformations**: `@Q` (quote the value for safe reuse — safe words unquoted, control chars via `$'…'`, else single-quoted), `@U`/`@u`/`@L` (upper-all/upper-first/lower-all), `@E` (expand ANSI-C backslash escapes), `@a` (attribute flags: `a` indexed / `A` associative), `@A` (a re-inputtable assignment/`declare` statement recreating the variable — a plain scalar renders as the short `name=value` form via `shell_quote`, while an attributed scalar, array, or associative array renders as a full `declare` command via `format_declare_def`), the key-aware **`@k`/`@K`** (`${a[@]@k}` interleaves each subscript and value as separate words `0 x 1 y`; `${a[@]@K}` yields one field with double-quoted values `0 "x" 1 "y"`; both work over indexed/associative arrays and the positional parameters, keyed from 1, via a `bulk_keyvalue` helper), and **`@P`** (expand the value as a prompt string, interpreting the bash prompt escapes `\u \h \H \w \W \s \j \l \d \D{fmt} \t \T \@ \A \a \e \n \r \v \V \! \# \$ \\ \nnn` and `\[`/`\]`; time escapes render in UTC, `\h`/`\H` read `$HOSTNAME`, `\u` reads `$USER`/`$LOGNAME`, `\w`/`\W` use the live cwd with `$HOME`→`~`; via a `prompt_expand` helper). **Dynamic special variables** `$RANDOM` (15-bit LCG, reseeded by `RANDOM=n`), `$SECONDS` (elapsed seconds since shell start, rebased by `SECONDS=n`), `$EPOCHSECONDS`, `$EPOCHREALTIME` (`secs.micros`), and `$BASHPID` are implemented (computed on read via `Cell`-backed state, so they bypass `vars`). The **`command [-v|-V] [-p] name`** builtin runs `name` bypassing shell functions (builtin if it is one, else external) or describes it (`-v` terse name/path, `-V` verbose) with a `$PATH` search, and **`builtin name`** forces builtin lookup even when a same-named function exists. **Shell options `set -e`/`-u`/`-x`** (and `+e`/`+u`/`+x` to disable, `set -o errexit|nounset|xtrace|pipefail` long forms, and clustered `set -eux`) are implemented: **errexit** (`-e`) exits the shell when a command fails, with the correct POSIX exemptions — conditions of `if`/`while`/`until`, non-final `&&`/`||` operands, and negated (`!`) commands are ignored (tracked by an `errexit_suppress` counter and per-and-or "final element executed" logic); **nounset** (`-u`) makes referencing an unset variable (bare `$x`/`${x}`/`${#x}`, but not `${x:-def}` or special params like `$@`/`$#`/`$?`) an error that aborts the shell; **xtrace** (`-x`) prints each expanded simple command (prefixed `+ `) to stderr before running it. (Along the way the `while`/`until`/`for` loops now yield the POSIX exit status — the last body execution, or 0 when the body never runs — instead of leaking the failed loop-condition's status, which errexit made observable.) **Function-local variables** (`local`) now have real dynamic scoping instead of aliasing `declare`: each function call pushes a local frame, `local name[=val]` snapshots the name's full prior state (scalar/indexed/associative/export flag) and shadows it, and the frame is restored on return (including for names that were unset before, and for `local a=(…)` array locals); `local` outside a function is an error. `declare`/`typeset` remain global. The **`read`** builtin now supports **`-r`** (raw — no backslash escaping), **`-a array`** (split the line into an indexed array), **`-p prompt`** (write a prompt to stderr), **`-s`** (silent, no-op for non-tty input), and proper **`$IFS`-aware field splitting**: IFS-whitespace runs collapse and are trimmed while non-whitespace IFS characters each delimit a field, the final named variable receives the raw remainder (internal spacing preserved), and — without `-r` — a backslash escapes the next character (also preventing a split on it), plus **`-d delim`** (read up to an alternate delimiter; `-d ''` ⇒ NUL), **`-n N`** (stop after N characters *or* the delimiter, whichever comes first), and **`-N N`** (read exactly N characters, ignoring the delimiter). `-d`/`-n`/`-N` use a byte-level, UTF-8-aware `read_record` helper dispatched over the same `StdinSrc`/`RedirPlan` sources as `read_line`, and set the exit status correctly (0 on delimiter/count reached, 1 on a short read at EOF). (`read -t`/`-u` are parsed/consumed but not yet honored — they need timer/fd-table support — see known-issues TD-OILS6.) **Case fallthrough terminators** `;&` (fall through and run the next arm's body unconditionally) and `;;&` (resume pattern testing at the following arms) are implemented alongside the normal `;;` break, so bash-style `case x in a) …;& b) …;; c) …;;& esac` control flow works. The **`select name [in words]; do body; done`** menu loop is implemented: it brace-expands the word list (or iterates `"$@"` when `in` is omitted), prints the numbered menu to stderr (again after a blank line), writes the `PS3` prompt (default `#? `), reads a line from stdin, stores the raw line in `REPLY`, sets `name` to the chosen word (empty on an out-of-range/non-numeric entry), runs the body until EOF or `break`, and yields the last body execution's status; `select` is now a reserved keyword. **`readonly name[=value] …`** (and **`declare -r`**) mark variables read-only: a subsequent assignment (`x=2`), `unset`, or value-bearing `declare` is rejected with status 1 and the diagnostic `osh: NAME: readonly variable`, leaving the value intact (enforced by a per-shell `readonly` set consulted in `apply_assignment`/`builtin_unset`/`builtin_declare`); `readonly -p` (or no operands) lists the readonly variables in re-inputtable form, and `-a`/`-A` select the array kind. Read-only enforcement now also covers the **`read` builtin** (a readonly scalar/array target — `read x`, field `read a b`, or `read -a arr` — is rejected with status 1 and no mutation; earlier fields in a multi-name read are still assigned before the readonly field aborts, matching bash) and **temporary `NAME=val cmd` env prefixes** (`readonly x; x=1 cmd` errors `osh: x: readonly variable`, does not run the command, and yields status 1 — guarded before dispatch so no function/builtin/external path mutates the variable). TD-OILS7 fully resolved. The **`let arg …`** builtin evaluates each argument as an arithmetic expression (with assignment/increment side effects, reusing the `(( … ))` evaluator) and sets the exit status from the last result (0 non-zero, 1 zero; no args → error). The **`-v` set-test** — `[ -v name ]`, `test -v name`, and `[[ -v name ]]` — reports whether a variable is set: a plain scalar/array/associative name, an explicit indexed/keyed element (`a[2]`, `m[key]`), or `a[@]`/`a[*]` (any element), plus special/positional parameters that resolve to a value; an empty-but-set variable counts as set. **`declare -p [names]`** prints variable definitions in re-inputtable form (`declare -- x="5"`, `declare -a a=([0]="x" [1]="y")`, `declare -A m=([k]="v")`), combining the readonly/exported/integer attribute flags (`-r`/`-x`/`-i`) and array-kind flags into one group, double-quoting/escaping the value (`"`, `\`, `$`, backtick); with no names it lists every set variable sorted by name, and an unset name is an error (status 1). The **`shopt [-s|-u|-q] [optname …]`** builtin toggles/queries shell options (`-s` set, `-u` unset, `-q` quiet-query, no flag ⇒ list/query rendering `on`/`off`); unknown option names are a status-1 error. `nullglob` (an unmatched glob produces no word at all rather than the literal pattern) and `dotglob` (pathname expansion includes dotfiles — but never `.`/`..`) are honored in glob expansion (`glob_or_literal`/`glob_expand_field` take the two flags, read from a per-shell `shopt` map inherited by subshell clones); **`nocasematch`** is honored in `case` and `[[ == ]]`/`[[ != ]]` matching (both the glob and the fully-quoted-literal comparison fold case via `glob_match_ci`, which lowercases pattern and text — including class ranges), and **`nocaseglob`** is honored in pathname expansion (`glob_expand_field` matches an ASCII-lowercased copy of the pattern against ASCII-lowercased filenames, still returning the original names); **`nocasematch`** is also honored in `[[ str =~ regex ]]` matching — the ERE engine (`ere.rs`) takes a case-insensitive flag (`Regex::new_flags(pattern, ci)`) that folds literal-char and character-class comparisons via `char_eq`/`ClassData::matches_ci` (the positive set is folded *before* negation, so `[^a-z]` under `nocasematch` correctly excludes `A`). **`extglob`** is honored everywhere glob patterns are matched — pathname expansion, `case`, `[[ == ]]`/`[[ != ]]`, and parameter-expansion pattern operators (`${v#pat}`/`${v%pat}`/`${v/pat/repl}`/`${v^pat}`) — supporting all five extended operators `?(list)` (zero/one), `*(list)` (zero+), `+(list)` (one+), `@(list)` (exactly one), and `!(list)` (negation), with `|`-separated and arbitrarily-nested alternatives. This unified a previously-duplicated pair of glob matchers into a single recursive `PatTok` engine (`compile_glob`/`match_glob_toks`), and the lexer now consumes an unquoted `X(…)` group into one word token (parens/pipes/whitespace literal inside, `$`/quotes still expanded) so extglob patterns parse — the extglob *decision* is deferred to match time (`compile_glob` only treats the group specially when the option is set; otherwise it matches literally). One superset caveat: because parsing is shopt-independent, `!(cmd)` written with no space is now a pattern word rather than a negated subshell — use `! (cmd)` for the latter (see known-issues TD-OILS8). The **`declare -i`/`+i` integer attribute** is implemented (a per-shell `integer_attr` set inherited by subshell clones): a name marked `-i` has its assignments evaluated as arithmetic before storing (`declare -i x; x=5+3` stores `8`, a non-numeric value stores `0`), `+=` performs numeric addition rather than string append (`z=10; z+=5` → `15`), the initializer on the declaration itself is evaluated (`declare -i y=2*3` → `6`), and integer indexed/associative array elements are evaluated too (`declare -ia a; a[0]=3+4` → `7`); `+i` removes the attribute so assignments become plain strings again. The **`declare -l`/`-u` case attributes** (with per-shell `lower_attr`/`upper_attr` sets, also inherited by subshell clones) fold assigned values to lower/upper case before storing (`declare -l x; x=HeLLo` → `hello`; `declare -u y=abc` → `ABC`; array elements folded too); they are mutually exclusive (the last flag seen wins, including within a cluster like `-ul`), `+l`/`+u` clear them, and `unset` drops all attributes. All three attributes (`-i`/`-l`/`-u`) appear in `declare -p` output. **`globstar`** is honored in pathname expansion: a `**` path component matches across directory levels — as an intermediate component (`a/**/b`) it stands for the base directory plus every descendant directory (zero-or-more levels), and as the final component (`a/**`) it stands for every descendant file *and* directory; dotfiles are skipped unless `dotglob`, and symlinked directories are not recursed into (matching bash ≥ 4.3, which also prevents symlink-loop infinite recursion). With `globstar` off, `**` degrades to an ordinary single-level `*`. Other known options (`failglob`, etc.) are stored and reported faithfully but not yet behavior-affecting. The **directory stack** builtins **`pushd`/`popd`/`dirs`** are implemented (a per-shell `dir_stack: Vec<String>` inherited by subshell clones, holding the saved directories *below* the current one — the current directory is the conceptual top and is the live process cwd, not stored): `pushd DIR` changes to `DIR` and pushes the old cwd, `pushd` (no arg) swaps the top two, `pushd +N`/`-N` rotates the stack so the N-th entry (from the left / right) becomes current; `popd` pops the saved top and changes to it, `popd +N`/`-N` deletes the N-th entry (deleting the current entry falls back to a plain pop); `dirs` prints the stack (tilde-contracting `$HOME` → `~`), with `-c` clear, `-l` long (un-contracted) paths, `-p` one-per-line, `-v` numbered one-per-line, and `+N`/`-N` to print a single entry. **`cd -`** changes to `$OLDPWD` (echoing the new directory), and every directory change (`cd`, `pushd`, `popd`) maintains `$PWD`/`$OLDPWD` via a shared `change_dir` helper. The **`time` reserved word** (`time [-p] pipeline`) is implemented: it is recognized only at pipeline start (so `time` stays a usable plain word elsewhere, e.g. in a `for … in` list, and a bare `time` with no following command is an ordinary command), precedes an optional `!` negation, and after the pipeline runs it prints a timing report to stderr — bash's default `\nreal\tNmS.SSSs\nuser…\nsys…` form, or the POSIX `-p` form (`real S.SS` three lines, no leading newline). Real (wall-clock) time is measured exactly via `Instant`; user/sys CPU are reported as zero pending per-child CPU accounting (see known-issues TD-OILS10). The pipeline's stdout and exit status are unaffected. The **`trap`** builtin (`trap [-lp] [[action] sigspec ...]`) records signal/pseudo-signal handlers in a per-shell `traps` map (not cloned into subshells except ignored `''` traps, matching bash's reset-to-default): `trap 'cmd' SIG …` sets, `trap - SIG` resets, `trap '' SIG` ignores, `trap`/`trap -p [SIG …]` prints the current traps in re-inputtable `trap -- 'action' SIG` form (signal-number sorted), and `trap -l` lists the known signal names. Signal specs normalize case-insensitively with/without a `SIG` prefix and accept numbers (`0` = `EXIT`); the pseudo-signals `EXIT`/`ERR`/`DEBUG`/`RETURN` are accepted. All **synchronous** traps are fired: **`EXIT`** (once, when the top-level shell exits via the `exit` builtin, end of script, or interactive EOF — preserving the pending exit status), **`ERR`** (on a failing command outside an exempt context — the same rule as `errexit`, but independent of `set -e`), **`DEBUG`** (before each simple command), and **`RETURN`** (on function return, in the function's scope); a reentrancy guard stops a handler's own commands from re-triggering the same trap. Only **async** signal handlers (`INT`/Ctrl-C, `TERM`, `HUP`, …) are stored/printed but not yet delivered — that needs kernel signal/exception support (see known-issues TD-OILS11). The **file-comparison test operators** `-nt` (newer-than), `-ot` (older-than), and `-ef` (same file) are implemented in both `test`/`[` and `[[ … ]]` (shared `file_cmp` helper): `-nt`/`-ot` compare modification times with bash's existence rule (`a -nt b` is also true when `a` exists and `b` does not), and `-ef` compares canonicalized paths as a portable stand-in for a device+inode match (distinct-name hard links are not detected — see known-issues TD-OILS12). The **`type [-t|-p|-P|-a|-f] name …`** builtin now classifies commands fully: it recognizes shell keywords (`if`/`while`/`case`/`select`/`{`/`[[`/… → "shell keyword"), functions, builtins, and external files found via a `$PATH` search (`find_all_in_path` returns every match). `-t` prints one type word (`keyword`/`function`/`builtin`/`file`, precedence in that order; status 1 if unknown), `-p` prints the path only when the name resolves to a file, `-P` forces a `$PATH` search and prints the path, `-a` lists every location in precedence order (function line, builtin line, then each file path), and `-f` skips function lookup; flags may be clustered (`-ap`). **Background-job tracking with `jobs`/`wait`** is implemented: a `&` command is recorded in a per-shell job table (job number = lowest unused, bash-style, so numbering restarts at 1 once the table drains; the spawned `Child` handle is retained and `$!` set to its pid). **`jobs [-l|-p]`** polls the table without blocking (`try_wait`) and prints each job as `[n]  Running/Done  cmdline` (`-l` adds the pid column, `-p` prints pids only), then drops any jobs it reported as Done. **`wait [pid|%job ...]`** blocks until the named jobs finish and yields the last waited job's exit status; with no operand it waits for every job. **`wait -n [ids…]`** returns as soon as the *next* job in the candidate set (the named ids, or all jobs when none are named) terminates — polling the live child handles — and returns 127 when there are no candidate jobs, and **`wait -p VAR`** stores the returned job's pid in `VAR`. The **`disown [-h] [-ar] [jobspec …]`** builtin removes jobs from the table (so `jobs`/`wait` no longer track them): `-h` keeps the job but marks it no-SIGHUP (advisory, pending signal delivery), `-a` selects all jobs, `-r` only running (not-yet-finished) jobs, and with no jobspec the current (last) job is used. Jobs are not inherited by subshell clones. The POSIX **`times`** builtin prints the shell's and its children's accumulated user/system CPU times (two `user sys` lines in bash's `%dm%d.%03ds` form); both are currently `0m0.000s` pending per-process CPU accounting (see known-issues TD-OILS10). The **`enable [-a] [-n] [name …]`** builtin enables/disables shell builtins: `enable -n NAME` disables a builtin so command resolution falls through to a same-named external (checked at every resolution site — plain dispatch, `command`, `&` background, and `type`/`command -v` classification — via a `builtin_enabled` helper backed by a per-shell `disabled_builtins` set inherited by subshell clones), `enable NAME` re-enables it, and the listing forms (`enable`, `enable -n`, `enable -a`) print builtins in re-inputtable `enable NAME` / `enable -n NAME` form; `builtin NAME` still force-runs a disabled builtin. The builtin name set is now a single `BUILTIN_NAMES` source of truth. **`declare -F`/`-f`** operate on functions: bare `declare -F` lists every function as `declare -f NAME` (sorted), `declare -F name` prints each name that is a function (status 1 if any is absent), and `declare -f name` reports the correct existence status (0 iff the name is a function) so `declare -f fn >/dev/null` works — function *body* printing awaits an AST source pretty-printer (see known-issues TD-OILS18/TD-OILS16). The **`exec [command [args]]`** builtin replaces the shell with `command` (run with the current environment/redirections, after which the shell exits with the command's status — a following command never runs; a missing command exits 127); `exec` with no command is a no-op that keeps running (redirection-only `exec > file` rebinding of the shell's own fds is not yet supported — see known-issues TD-OILS14). A true in-place `execve` that preserves the pid awaits kernel support. **`cd` now honors `CDPATH` and the `-L`/`-P` flags**: a bare relative target (not `/`-, `./`-, or `../`-anchored) is searched under each colon-separated `CDPATH` entry and, when found through a non-`.` entry, the destination path is echoed (bash); `-P` reports/stores the canonical (symlink-resolved) `$PWD`, `-L` (default) keeps the logical path. The **`umask [-S] [-p] [mode]`** builtin gets/sets the per-shell file-creation mask: no operand prints the mask (octal `0NNN`, or symbolic `u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx` with `-S`, or a re-inputtable `umask …` command with `-p`), and a `mode` operand sets it from an octal number or a symbolic clause list (`u=rwx,g=rx,o=`, `go-r`, `a=`, `+`/`-`/`=` operators). The mask is inherited by subshell clones; applying it to created-file permissions is gated on the target file-mode model (see known-issues TD-OILS15). The **`-o optname` shell-option test operator** — `[ -o NAME ]`, `test -o NAME`, and `[[ -o NAME ]]` — reports whether a `set -o` option (`errexit`/`nounset`/`xtrace`/`pipefail`) is currently enabled (unknown option names report disabled, matching bash). Bare **`set -o`** now lists the modelled options as `name  on/off` columns and **`set +o`** lists them as re-inputtable `set -o NAME`/`set +o NAME` lines (only the options the shell actually models — errexit/nounset/pipefail/xtrace — are listed, alphabetically, so reported state is always truthful). Bare **`set`** (no operands) now lists every shell variable in sorted, re-inputtable `name=value` / `name=([i]="v" …)` form (function definitions are not yet included — see known-issues TD-OILS16). Two further behavior-affecting options are modelled: **`set -f`/`-o noglob`** disables pathname (glob) expansion so patterns stay literal (wired into the glob-expansion entry point), and **`set -a`/`-o allexport`** auto-exports every subsequently-assigned variable (wired into `apply_assignment`); both appear in the `set -o` listing and are readable via `[ -o NAME ]`. A third such option, **`set -C`/`-o noclobber`**, is modelled with its **`>|` clobber-override redirection operator** (new lexer `Op::GreatPipe`, `RedirectOp::Clobber`): under noclobber a plain `>` refuses to truncate an existing regular file (status 1, `NAME: cannot overwrite existing file`, wired into `resolve_redirects`), while `>|` and `>>` always proceed; `set +C` clears it, and it appears in the `set -o` listing / `[ -o noclobber ]` test. The **`hash [-lr] [-p pathname] [-dt] [name …]`** builtin manages a remembered command-path table that is now *actually consulted during execution*: external command resolution routes through a `resolve_external` helper that reuses a cached full path (bumping its hit count) or runs a fresh `$PATH` search and remembers the result (falling back to the bare name so the OS can still locate it). `hash` prints the `hits`/`command` table, `-r` forgets all, `-d` forgets named entries, `-t` prints the remembered path(s), `-p pathname name` remembers without searching, `-l` lists re-inputtable `builtin hash -p …` lines, and bare `name`s force a fresh search; the table is inherited by subshell clones, and **`type`** now reports a remembered command as `NAME is hashed (path)` (and `type -p` prints the remembered path when a live PATH search comes up empty). **`unset`** now honors the **`-v`** (variables only) and **`-f`** (functions only) flags, and without a flag unsets a set variable in preference to a same-named function (bash precedence) instead of removing both. **Array/positional slicing** `${a[@]:off:len}` / `${a[*]:off:len}` / `${@:off:len}` / `${*:off:len}` is implemented: it selects a contiguous run of elements by position (0-based over the set values; for `@`/`*` the list is `$0` then the positional parameters, matching bash), a negative offset counts from the end, a negative length trims that many from the end, and an absent length runs to the end; the quoted `"${a[@]:o:l}"` form preserves one field per element (via a new `WordPart::ArraySlice` and `slice_elements` helper). **Bulk (element-wise) array transforms** `${a[@]#pat}`/`##`/`%`/`%%` (prefix/suffix trim), `${a[@]/pat/repl}`/`//`/`/#`/`/%` (substitution), `${a[@]^}`/`^^`/`,`/`,,` (case), and `${a[@]@Q}`/`@U`/`@u`/`@L`/`@E` (transform) now apply the scalar operator to *every* element of an array (or every positional parameter, `${@#pat}`/`${*/x/y}`/`${@^^}`); the `[*]`/`$*` form is accepted too, the quoted `"${a[@]#pat}"` form yields one field per transformed element, and only the *default* operators (`:-`/`:=`/…) remain rejected on `[@]`/`[*]`. Implemented via a new `WordPart::ArrayBulk`/`BulkOp` AST pair, a shared `parse_bulk_op`/`parse_replace_pieces` parser, and `bulk_elements`/`apply_bulk_op`/`transform_value` interp helpers. **Namerefs** (`declare -n ref=target` / `local -n`) are implemented: a nameref variable holds the *name* of another variable, and reads/writes of the nameref transparently redirect to the target — scalar `$ref`/`ref=v`, array elements `${ref[i]}`/`ref[i]=v`, whole-array `${ref[@]}`/`${#ref[@]}`, and the canonical pass-an-array-by-reference-to-a-function pattern (`declare -n out=$1; out=(…)`). A `resolve_ref_name` helper follows nameref chains with a cycle guard and is applied at the read/write chokepoints (`param_value`, `param_elem_value`, `assign_elem`, `array_elements`, `array_keys`, `expand_array_ref`, and `apply_assignment` — which rewrites the name and recurses); `declare -n`/`+n` set/clear the attribute (shown as `-n` in `declare -p`), `unset -n ref` drops the nameref while plain `unset ref` removes the target (bash semantics). `${!ref}` on a nameref yields the target *name* (bash special case), and namerefs to an array element (`declare -n ref=arr[0]`) resolve for both read (`$ref`) and write (`ref=v`) — TD-OILS17 fully resolved. **Local attribute scoping** is now correct: the per-call `VarSnapshot` captures and restores each name's `-i`/`-l`/`-u`/`-n`/readonly attributes alongside its value, and `declare_local` clears `-i`/`-l`/`-u`/`-n` when a bare `local x` shadows a global (matching bash, which does not inherit a global's attributes; readonly is left intact so a readonly global is not silently shadowed) — so a `local -n`/`local -i` inside a function no longer leaks its attribute out on return. The **`FUNCNAME` array** reflects the function call stack (bash: `FUNCNAME[0]` is the currently-executing function, then each caller, then `main` at the bottom; unset outside any function) — backed by an `fn_stack` pushed/popped in `call_function` and materialised into `arrays["FUNCNAME"]` by `refresh_funcname`, so `$FUNCNAME`, `${FUNCNAME[@]}`, and `${#FUNCNAME[@]}` all read through the normal array paths; a subshell inherits the enclosing function context. The unary file-test operators **`-L`/`-h`** (path is a symbolic link, via `symlink_metadata` so a broken link still tests true) and **`-t fd`** (descriptor 0/1/2 is a terminal, via `IsTerminal`) are implemented in both `test`/`[` and `[[ … ]]`. Fixed a latent `test`/`[` 3-argument bug where a leading `!` negation (`[ ! -f X ]`) was misparsed as a binary operator; the 3-arg path now follows POSIX order (binary primary first, then `!` negation, then `( expr )` grouping). The **`alias`/`unalias`** builtins are implemented with a real bash-style pre-parse alias-expansion pass (`lexer::expand_aliases`, run over the token stream by `parser::parse_with_aliases` before parsing): `alias name=value` defines, bare `alias`/`alias -p` lists every alias in re-inputtable `alias NAME='VALUE'` form (single-quoted value, sorted via a `BTreeMap`), `alias name` prints one alias (status 1 if undefined), and `unalias name …`/`unalias -a` removes. Expansion only fires on a single unquoted-literal word in **command position** (start of a simple command — after `;`/`&`/`|`/`&&`/`||`/`(`/newline or a command-introducing reserved word like `then`/`do`/`{`/`!`), the alias value's own first word is re-checked (guarded against self-recursion so `alias ls='ls -l'` terminates), and a value ending in a blank makes the *next* word alias-eligible too (bash's trailing-blank rule, enabling `alias sudo='sudo '`). Aliases are inherited by subshell clones. One fidelity gap: because a whole `run_source` input is parsed at once, an alias defined earlier in the *same* script/`-c` string is not seen by later commands in that input (interactive per-line REPL use is unaffected); command-substitution bodies are also not alias-expanded — see known-issues TD-OILS19. **`declare`/`typeset` now honor bash's function-scope rule**: inside a function they create *locals* by default (exactly like `local`, snapshotting/restoring the prior binding on return), and **`declare -g`** opts back out to global scope even inside a function (the array one-liner `declare -g -a a=(…)` honors it too); at global scope `-g` is a harmless no-op. The **`command_not_found_handle`** hook is honored: when a bare command name resolves nowhere on `$PATH` and a function of that name is defined, it is invoked with the command word as `$1` and its arguments as `$2`… (its exit status becomes `$?`) instead of reporting "command not found"; a slash-containing path bypasses the hook (bash semantics), and the cheap function-existence check is done before any extra `$PATH` scan so the common case is unaffected. The **`fg`/`bg`** job-control builtins are implemented for a shell without terminal job control: **`fg [jobspec]`** foregrounds a background job — it prints the job's command line to stdout (bash behavior) and blocks until the job finishes, returning its exit status; with no jobspec the current (most recently backgrounded) job is used, and an empty table or unknown spec is a status-1 error. **`bg [jobspec …]`** reports each targeted job in bash's `[id] cmd &` form and returns 0 (backgrounded jobs already run here — there is no SIGTSTP/SIGCONT, so `bg` is a spec-resolving reporting form); no jobspec targets the current job, and an empty table or unknown spec is a status-1 error. Resuming a *stopped* job and controlling-tty transfer await kernel signal/job-control support (see known-issues TD-OILS13). A faithful **AST source pretty-printer** (`unparse.rs`) reconstructs re-parseable shell source from a parsed `Program`/`FunctionDef` — covering every compound command, all `WordPart` expansion variants, assignments, redirections, and `[[ … ]]`/`(( … ))`, round-trip-stability tested — so **`declare -f NAME`** and bare `declare -f` now print each function's reconstructed body, **`type NAME`** prints the "is a function" line followed by the source, and **bare `set`** lists function definitions after the variables (closing TD-OILS16 and TD-OILS18; here-docs are re-emitted as equivalent here-strings). **`$LINENO`** reports the 1-based source line of the currently-executing item: the parser counts the top-level newline tokens it consumes and stamps the running line number onto each parsed `Item`, the interpreter sets `self.current_line` before running each item, and `param_value` returns it on read (blank/comment lines advance the counter; semicolon-joined commands share a line). Lines inside multi-line quotes/substitutions/here-doc bodies are undercounted because their interior newlines are absorbed by the lexer (see known-issues TD-OILS20). The **`BASH_SOURCE`/`BASH_LINENO` call-stack arrays** and the **`caller [expr]`** builtin are implemented on top of the call stack: a per-shell `call_line_stack` captures the source line at each function call site (kept in lockstep with `fn_stack`), so `refresh_funcname` now materialises all three parallel arrays — `FUNCNAME[i]` (function), `BASH_LINENO[i]` (line where `FUNCNAME[i]` was called, `0` for the bottom `main` frame), and `BASH_SOURCE[i]` (source file, `$0`) — and clears them outside any function. `caller` prints "LINE SOURCE" for the current call site; `caller N` prints "LINE FUNCNAME SOURCE" for frame N (0 = current function), returning 1 outside a function or when N is out of range/non-numeric. Per-function definition source isn't tracked, so `BASH_SOURCE`/`caller` always report `$0` even for functions loaded via `source` (see known-issues TD-OILS21). The **`$_` special variable** tracks the last argument of the most recent simple command (set after each command's argv is expanded, read by the following command; a single-word command leaves `$_` as that word); the startup form where `$_` is the shell/script pathname is not modelled. The **`$BASH_COMMAND` special variable** holds the command currently executing — the *unexpanded* reconstructed source text of the running simple command (via `unparse::simple_src`, so `echo $BASH_COMMAND` prints `echo $BASH_COMMAND` and `x=1 echo hi` records the prefix/redirections too), stored in `vars` (visible to `set`/`declare -p`) and updated at the top of every simple command *except* while a trap handler runs — so a `DEBUG`/`ERR` trap still sees the command that triggered it (bash). Granularity is simple-command-level (compound commands are not separately recorded). The **`$-` special variable** reports the currently-enabled single-letter option flags: the modelled toggles `a` (allexport), `e` (errexit), `f` (noglob), `u` (nounset), `x` (xtrace), `C` (noclobber), plus `h` (hashall) and `B` (brace expansion) which are always on here — emitted in bash's fixed flag-table order regardless of the order they were set (`set -xu` ⇒ `huxB`); `-o`-only options without a letter (e.g. `pipefail`) are excluded, matching bash. The **`help [-dms] [pattern …]`** builtin displays information about shell builtins from an in-tree synopsis table (name, usage line, one-line description) kept in sync with `BUILTIN_NAMES`: with no pattern it lists every builtin's usage synopsis sorted; each pattern is matched against builtin names as a shell glob (a bare name is an exact topic); `-s` prints only the usage synopsis, `-d` only the short description, `-m` renders the default long form, and the default prints the usage line followed by an indented description; a pattern matching nothing writes `no help topics match` to stderr and returns 1. The **combined-output redirections `&>file`/`&>>file`** (and the equivalent `>&file` form with a non-numeric target) send both stdout and stderr to the file (truncate / append), equivalent to `>file 2>&1`: new lexer ops `AmpGreat`/`AmpDGreat`, `RedirectOp::WriteBoth`/`AppendBoth`, and a parser rule that keeps a numeric `>&N`/`>&-` as an fd duplication while treating `>&filename` as a both-streams redirect. When stdout and stderr target the same file the compound path now appends the buffered stdout after the stderr already written (fixing a latent truncation where flushing the stdout capture would clobber stderr) — both streams survive, in stderr-then-stdout order (interleaving is not preserved by the capture model). **Tilde expansion** now covers `~+` (→ `$PWD`), `~-` (→ `$OLDPWD`), and the directory-stack forms `~N`/`~+N` (Nth entry from the left, 0 = current dir) and `~-N` (Nth from the right), each keeping any trailing `/path` remainder; a `~` alone still expands to `$HOME`, `~/path` keeps the remainder, and an unresolvable `~user` prefix (no user database on this target) is left literal, matching bash's "no expansion if lookup fails" rule. In an **assignment RHS**, a tilde-prefix that follows an unquoted `:` (or begins the value) is also expanded (`PATH=~/a:~/b`, `x=$PATH:~/bin`), while a quoted tilde stays literal. This now extends to **declaration-builtin operands** (`export X=~/foo`, `declare Y=~/a:~/b`, `typeset`, `local L=~/lib`, `readonly R=~/r`): the command word is recognised syntactically as a declaration builtin and each `NAME=value`/`NAME+=value`/`NAME[idx]=value` operand is expanded in assignment context — tilde-expanded, and neither word-split nor glob-expanded (so `export S=$v` keeps embedded spaces). Along the way the **`NAME+=value` append form** on the declaration builtins `declare`/`typeset`/`local`, `export`, and `readonly` (previously mis-parsed as a variable literally named `NAME+`, silently dropping the append) now correctly appends to the current value (numeric add under `-i`). The **redirection-only `exec` form** now persistently rebinds the shell's ambient fd 1 / fd 2: `exec > file`/`>> file`/`2> file`/`2>> file`/`> file 2>&1`/`1>&2` store a per-shell `exec_stdout`/`exec_stderr` target (truncated once for `>`, then append), which every ambient-fd write consults — builtins via `write_bytes`, `>&2` diagnostics via `emit_stderr`, and external children via `run_external` — so all subsequent commands (and inherited subshells) route to the file. The **input** form `exec < file` (and `exec << EOF`) likewise rebinds the ambient fd 0: the source is read once into a per-shell `exec_stdin` cursor that every base fd-0 read consults (the `read` builtins, `read_all_bytes`/`mapfile`, and an external inheriting fd 0), so successive `read`s consume successive lines; a subshell inherits a snapshot of the remaining bytes. **Named input descriptors** are also modelled: `exec 3< file` (or `exec 3<< EOF` / `3<<< str`) opens a user-space fd ≥ 3 in a per-shell `open_fds` table (the file slurped once into a position-tracking cursor, errors surfaced at redirection time), `exec 3<&-` closes it, and **`read -u N`** consumes successive records from that descriptor independently of fd 0 (a bad/unopened fd is a status-1 `read: N: bad file descriptor`); a subshell inherits an independent-offset snapshot of each open fd. **Named write descriptors** complete the story: `exec 3> file`/`3>> file` opens a user-space write fd ≥ 3 in a per-shell `open_write_fds` table (a shared `Arc<File>`, truncate-once for `>`), `echo … >&3` routes a builtin's stdout there (via a `write_to_fd` helper) and `cmd >&3`/`cmd 2>&3` routes an external child's fd 1/fd 2 there (via `RedirPlan.stdout_to_fd`/`stderr_to_fd`), successive writes accumulate on the shared handle, `exec 3>&-` closes it, and a subshell shares the same handle (bash fd inheritance); an unopened write fd is a status-1 `N: Bad file descriptor`. This also fixed a latent bug where a per-command `N> file` (N ≥ 3) fell into the stdout arm and wrongly redirected fd 1 (now fd ≥ 3 output redirects route to `extra_fds`, a documented no-op on non-`exec` commands). **Scoped per-command extra-fd redirects** also work: a compound command carrying a fd ≥ 3 redirect (`while read -u 3 line; do …; done 3< file`, `{ …; } 4> log`, `… 3<&-`) installs the descriptor into the shell's fd table for the body's duration only — `exec_redirected` saves each touched fd's prior binding (by ownership) and restores it (removing the scoped fd) when the body finishes — so `read -u 3` inside the loop reads the file while fd 0 stays free, and fd 3 is gone afterward. **Builtin stderr redirects** also work now: a simple-command builtin honors its own fd-2 redirect — `read … 2> file`/`2>> file` (a builtin diagnostic lands in the file), `echo … 2>&3`/`read … 2>&3` (routes builtin stderr to a user-space write descriptor via a scoped `StderrTarget::WriteFd`), and `… 2>&1` (folds builtin stderr into fd 1's live sink — captured stdout, pipeline stage, or terminal) — installed as a scoped `StderrTarget` for the builtin's duration in `run_builtin` (the `exec` builtin is exempt, since it sets the persistent `exec_stderr` itself). **Function-invocation redirects** also work: a function call carrying its own redirects (`myfunc > file`, `myfunc 2> err`, `myfunc < in`, and compound-scoped fd ≥ 3 forms) runs the whole function body inside a redirect scope — `exec_simple` routes the call through a shared `exec_with_redirects` helper (extracted from `exec_redirected`) when the plan `needs_scope`, so the body's stdout/stderr/stdin and any diagnostics honor the redirect; without redirects the call dispatches directly to avoid scope-setup overhead. Still deferred: duplicating a write-fd *onto* a standard fd (`exec 3>&1`) — see known-issues TD-OILS14. Only a true pid-preserving `execve` remains (gated on kernel support — see known-issues TD-OILS14). **Process substitution** `<(cmd)`/`>(cmd)` is implemented via a temp-file model (the host has no `/dev/fd` or named pipes): the lexer reads an unquoted `<(`/`>(` as a `Seg::ProcSub` word (concatenation-friendly), the parser lowers it to `WordPart::ProcSub`, and at expansion `<(cmd)` runs the body *now* capturing its stdout into a temp file whose path is substituted (`diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`, `read x < <(cmd)`, `. <(cmd)`), while `>(cmd)` creates an empty temp file, substitutes its path, and defers the body until after the enclosing command — running it with the file's contents as stdin (`echo … > >(cmd)`); both temp files are cleaned up by an `exec_simple` wrapper (drained from a per-command mark on `procsub_in_temps`/`procsub_out_jobs`), and a subshell manages its own. Not streaming — an infinite producer like `<(tail -f)` would block at expansion — a documented limitation (known-issues TD-OILS22). **Colon vs. colon-less parameter expansion** is now distinguished: the parser records whether a `${var-word}`/`${var=word}`/`${var+word}`/`${var?word}` operator carried a leading `:` (new `colon: bool` on `WordPart::ParamOp`), and `expand_param_op` selects the "active" predicate accordingly — the colon forms (`:-`/`:=`/`:+`/`:?`) treat an empty-but-set value the same as unset (active only when set *and* non-empty), while the colon-less forms treat an empty-but-set value as set (active whenever the variable is set), so `x=; echo ${x-D}` now prints empty and `x=; echo ${x+A}` prints `A`, both matching bash (previously both were wrongly treated as the colon form). **Indirect expansion to a whole-array referent** now works: `${!ref}` where `ref` resolves to `name[@]`/`name[*]` expands like `${name[@]}`/`${name[*]}` (previously it fed `@`/`*` into the arithmetic subscript evaluator and errored) — the unquoted form space-joins/field-splits the elements and the quoted `"${!ref}"` form preserves one field per element (via `indirect_array_elems` in the annotated per-element path). **`printf -v` now targets array elements**: `printf -v 'arr[2]' …` / `printf -v 'm[key]' …` assign the formatted result to an indexed/associative array element (routed through `assign_elem` with a parsed subscript) rather than a scalar literally named `arr[2]`, and a readonly target is rejected (status 1) — the scalar form also now resolves namerefs. The **`read` builtin option parser is now cluster/attached-argument aware** (bash forms): short flags may be bundled (`-rs`) and an option-argument may be glued to its letter (`-d:`, `-n5`, `-u3`) as well as supplied as the next token (`-d :`) — previously only the exact separated form was recognised, so `read -d:` silently ignored the delimiter and read the whole line; `--` also ends option parsing. The **`${var@a}` attribute transform now reports scalar attributes** (`i` integer, `l`/`u` lower/upper, `r` readonly, `x` exported, `n` nameref) alongside the array kind (`a`/`A`) — previously only the array-kind flag was emitted, so `declare -i n; echo ${n@a}` wrongly printed empty; combined flags render in `declare -p` order (kind, n, i, l, u, r, x) via a shared `attr_flag_letters` helper. **Positional-parameter `"$@"`/`"$*"` semantics fixed**: quoted `"$@"` now expands to one field per positional parameter (preserving embedded whitespace, e.g. `set -- "a b" c; for x in "$@"` yields two fields) via a `[WordPart::Param("@")]` arm in the annotated per-element path — previously it collapsed into a single joined field; quoted `"$*"` now joins with the first character of `$IFS` (unset ⇒ space, empty ⇒ no separator) via a `star_sep` helper rather than always a space; and `${#@}`/`${#*}` now return the *count* of positional parameters instead of the character-length of their joined string. **Unquoted word splitting now honors a custom `$IFS`** (TD-OILS23): the whitespace-only `split_ifs` was replaced by `split_field_ifs(s, ifs)` implementing full POSIX field splitting — IFS-whitespace runs collapse and trim, each non-whitespace IFS character is a single delimiter (with adjacent whitespace absorbed), adjacent non-whitespace delimiters yield empty fields, a trailing delimiter yields no trailing empty field, an empty IFS disables splitting, and empty input yields no fields — with the unquoted `other =>` expansion arm reading `$IFS` from `self.vars` (default `" \t\n"`), so `IFS=:; x="a:b:c"; for w in $x` now yields three fields, `a::c` yields `a`/``/`c`, and leading/trailing custom delimiters behave per bash. The **`$(< file)` command-substitution fast path** is implemented: a command substitution whose body is solely a null command with an fd-0 input redirection reads and substitutes the file's contents directly (equivalent to `$(cat file)`, per bash), stripping trailing newlines like any command substitution — detected by `comsub_read_file` (single simple command, no assignments/words/decl-arrays, last fd-0 `Read` redirect wins). **Scalar assignment (and `read`) into an existing indexed array now updates element 0** (bash: `a=(1 2 3); a=x` leaves `${a[@]}` == `x 2 3` and `$a` == `x`; `read a <<< q` likewise) — a `set_scalar_store` helper routes a plain scalar write to `arrays[name][0]` when the name is an indexed array, used by the scalar-assign path and `set_scalar_checked` (the `read`/temp-env chokepoint). **Array-declaration value attributes fixed**: `declare -ia`/`-ai`/`-ua`/`-ra` (and friends) now apply the integer/case/readonly/export/nameref attributes to the *array* name — previously `exec_declare_with_arrays` parsed only the `-a`/`-A`/`-g` kind flags, so `declare -ia a=(…)` left `a` without the integer attribute; now the full flag set is parsed there and applied, and array-literal elements are transformed by those attributes at store time (a new `apply_elem_attrs` helper evaluates each element arithmetically under `-i` or folds its case under `-l`/`-u`, for both indexed and associative literals), so `declare -ua u=(ab cd)` stores `AB CD` and `declare -ia b=(1 2); b[1]=6+6` stores `12`. **`printf %q` now matches bash's backslash-escaping style** (a new `printf_quote` helper backslash-escapes each shell-special character — `a b` → `a\ b`, `it's` → `it\'s`, `a$b\`c` → `a\$b\`c` — with `''` for the empty string and the ANSI-C `$'…'` form for control characters), distinct from `${v@Q}`/`shell_quote` which stays single-quote style (bash uses different quoting for the two, verified against bash). **Command substitutions and nested arithmetic inside a `$(( ))` expression are now expanded before evaluation** (major fix): `expand_arith_params` previously handled only `$name`/`${name}`/`$1`, so `$(( $(f) + 1 ))` mis-tokenized `$(` as an empty-variable `0` followed by trailing `(f)` and aborted with "unexpected trailing input" — breaking *all* arithmetic containing a command substitution, including the canonical recursive-fibonacci `echo $(( $(fib $((n-1))) + $(fib $((n-2))) ))`. The pass now recognizes `$(cmd)` / `` `cmd` `` (parsed and run via `command_sub` through a `run_command_sub_text` helper, with balanced-paren scanning by `scan_paren_group`) and nested `$((expr))` (evaluated via `arith_sub`, `))`-matched by `scan_arith_sub`), substituting each result before the arithmetic evaluator runs; bare identifiers are still left for the evaluator's `VarLookup`. **`echo -e`/`-E` and clustered echo flags** are now implemented: the builtin previously honored only `-n`, so `echo -e '\n'` printed the flag and escape literally; it now parses any leading option word made solely of the letters `neE` (clustered, e.g. `-ne`), and under `-e` interprets backslash escapes via a new `echo_expand_escapes` helper (`\a \b \e \E \f \n \r \t \v \\`, `\0nnn` octal, `\xHH` hex, and `\c` which stops output and suppresses the trailing newline), matching bash exactly (`-E`/default leave escapes literal). **Command substitution now runs in an isolated subshell** (bash semantics): `command_sub` executes the body on a `clone_for_subshell()` copy rather than on the live shell, so variable/cwd/function mutations inside `$(...)`/backticks no longer leak into the parent — `count=0; r=$(count=5; echo $count); echo "$r $count"` now prints `5 0` (was `5 5`) — while the substitution still reads inherited parent variables and only the captured stdout and exit status ($?) propagate back. Alongside it, **a pure assignment's exit status now follows bash's command-substitution rule**: the status of `x=…` is that of the last `$(...)` performed while expanding its value (`x=$(false); echo $?` → 1), or 0 when the value contained no command substitution (`false; x=1; echo $?` → 0), while `$?` read *inside* the value still sees the prior status (expansion happens before the reset) — tracked by a monotonic per-shell `comsub_count`. **Arithmetic evaluation errors in a `$(( … ))` substitution now abort the command** (bash): a division-by-zero or bad expression in a command word (`echo $((1/0))`), an assignment value (`x=$((1/0))`), or a prefix assignment (`x=$((1/0)) cmd`) prints the diagnostic and discards the command with status 1 rather than running it with a fabricated `0` — tracked by a per-shell `arith_error` flag set in `arith_sub` and consumed by the simple-command driver after each expansion, while `(( … ))`/`let`/arithmetic-subscript contexts save-and-restore the flag so they report their own status without leaking the abort (bash's further top-of-line longjmp — discarding *all* commands sharing the input line — is not modelled; osh aborts just the offending command, see known-issues TD-OILS24). **`${var:?word}` on an unset/null parameter now aborts the (sub)shell** (bash): the message is written to stderr and the simple-command driver terminates via the same `Flow::Exit(1)` path as `set -u`, so `(echo "${zz:?msg}")` exits the subshell before `echo` runs (previously it printed the diagnostic but continued, echoing an empty line) — the diagnostic now routes through `emit_stderr` so a `2>` redirect captures it. **`${var/pat/repl}` now preserves literal whitespace in the pattern and replacement** (bash): both were parsed via the word-splitting lexer (`word_from_source`), which trimmed leading/trailing whitespace and collapsed internal runs — so `${s/#/hello }` dropped the trailing space (`helloworld` instead of `hello world`) and `${s/ /_}` mis-parsed the space pattern; a new `lexer::lex_word_verbatim` (and parser `word_verbatim_from_source`) lexes each piece as a single word keeping whitespace and operator characters literal while still processing quotes and `$…`/backtick expansions, matching bash's "expansion + quote removal, no word-splitting" rule for substitution operands. **The same literal-whitespace fix now also covers the sibling parameter operators** whose pattern/argument was likewise routed through the word-splitting lexer: the `#`/`##`/`%`/`%%` trim patterns (`${s%% *}` no longer collapses ` *` → `*`, so `${f%% *}` on `my dog runs` correctly yields `my`), the `^`/`^^`/`,`/`,,` case patterns, and the `:-`/`:=`/`:+`/`:?` default/alternate/error arguments (`"${x:-a  b}"` preserves the double space, `"${x:+hi }"` keeps the trailing space) — plus the array-wide `${a[@]#pat}`/`${a[@]^pat}` bulk forms — all now parse their operand via `word_verbatim_from_source`; unquoted default-value results are still IFS-split by the outer expansion context, so `echo ${x:-a b}` still yields two fields. The **legacy `$[ … ]` arithmetic expansion** (bash's deprecated pre-`$(( ))` syntax) is now supported as an alias for `$(( … ))`: the lexer reads `$[expr]` (balanced-bracket body, so array subscripts like `$[a[1]+5]` nest) into the same `Seg::Arith` token, so it flows through the existing arithmetic evaluator (`echo $[1+2]` → `3`, `echo "$[10/3]"` → `3`). **A `$` immediately before the closing `"` of a double-quoted string is now a literal `$`** (bash): `read_dollar` gained an `in_dquote` flag so that inside double quotes a `$` followed by `'`/`"` no longer starts an ANSI-C-quote/locale span (both are literal there, `"a$'x'"` → `a$'x'`) and a trailing `$"` is a literal `$` then the closing quote — previously the scanner consumed the closing `"` and reported "unterminated double quote", which broke any double-quoted string ending in `$` such as a regex anchor `"^[0-9]+$"`. The here-doc scanner uses the same literal-`$'`/`$"` rule. **The shell now imports the real process environment into its variable namespace at startup** (`Shell::import_environment`, called by the binary): inherited environment variables become ordinary exported shell variables, so they are visible to prefix name-matching (`${!PATH*}` now lists `PATH`), `set`/`export -p` listings, and — crucially — **`unset` on an inherited env variable actually hides it** (previously `unset PATH` was a no-op because reads fell back to `std::env::var`, which also meant a shell-local PATH edit and prefix matching ignored the inherited value). A per-shell `env_imported` flag makes `vars` authoritative once imported: variable reads no longer fall back to `std::env` (so `unset` wins and `${x-gone}` sees the removal), `$PATH`-based command lookup uses the shell's PATH (an unset PATH means no search, bash), and child processes are spawned from a **cleared base environment** populated only from the exported set (so a non-exported/unset variable cannot leak into a child via inheritance). Tests construct the shell via `new()` *without* importing, so they keep the on-demand `std::env` fallback and inherited child environment — remaining deterministic and host-independent (the real process env is never mutated, avoiding unsafe thread-racy `set_var`/`remove_var`). **Quoted `"${arr[*]}"` now joins with the first character of `$IFS`** (like `"$*"`) instead of always a space: `expand_array_ref` distinguishes the `[*]` star form (join with `star_sep()` — space when IFS is unset, empty when IFS is empty) from the `[@]` all form (space-joined, then word-split), so `a=(1 2 3); IFS=,; echo "${a[*]}"` yields `1,2,3` and an assigned `s="${a[*]}"` preserves the IFS separator. **`$SHLVL` is now incremented on shell startup** (in `import_environment`): bash bumps `SHLVL` for each nested shell invocation, so `import_environment` sets it to the inherited level + 1 (an unset or non-numeric value becomes 1) and exports it — a nested `osh -c 'osh -c …'` reports `2`, `3`, … while a `(...)` subshell keeps the same level (it copies `vars` rather than re-importing). **`printf` now honours the `+`, space, and `#` flags:** `+`/space add an explicit sign column to non-negative signed integers and floats (`%+d` on 5 -> `+5`, `% d` -> ` 5`), `#` prefixes nonzero hex with `0x`/`0X` and forces a leading `0` on octal, and the sign/base prefix is rendered separately from the digit body so zero-padding inserts the fill zeros *after* it (`%+05d` on 5 -> `+0005`, `%#06x` on 255 -> `0x00ff`). **An empty arithmetic expression now evaluates to 0** (bash): `$(( ))` and, after expansion, `x=; echo $((x))` / `$(( $unset ))` yield 0 instead of a syntax error. **The `${var@l}` transform now works** (lowercase only the first character, the mirror of `@u`); it was previously a silent no-op. **`printf` numeric conversions now validate their arguments like bash:** a non-numeric arg to `%d`/`%i`/`%u`/`%x`/`%o`/`%f`/etc. writes `osh: printf: ARG: invalid number` (or `invalid octal number`/`invalid hex number`) to stderr and makes `printf` return 1, while still emitting the best-effort value — the leading numeric prefix (`12x`->12, `3.5x`->3.5) or 0. Parsing now follows strtoimax base rules (leading `0`=octal so `010`=8, `0x`=hex), with trailing junk (incl. trailing whitespace) flagged. Non-interactive assignment fatality now matches bash: an arithmetic-expansion error (`$((1/0))`, `$[…]`) in a command word, a bare assignment value, or a temp-prefix value, and a readonly-variable reassignment (bare `x=2` or array element `r[0]=9`), all abort the shell with status 1 (while `(( )) `/`let`/`for ((` arithmetic *commands* stay non-fatal). Indirect expansion `${!ptr}` now validates its pointer like bash: an unset pointer (`${!nope}`) is a fatal "invalid indirect expansion" and a malformed target name (`ptr="a b"`) a fatal "invalid variable name", in the command-word, bare-assignment, and temp-prefix contexts (a valid-but-unset target still yields empty). Arithmetic now performs bash-style recursive variable evaluation: a scalar/array/assoc value is itself evaluated as an arithmetic expression (`b=a; a=5; $((b))` -> 5; `x="2+3"; $((x))` -> 5; octal/hex value literals honoured), with a depth guard that reports "expression recursion level exceeded" on cycles (`x=x`). The `@Q`/`@A` parameter transforms now match bash exactly: every set value is single-quoted (a plain word like `hi` becomes `'hi'`, not bare), a set-but-empty value becomes `''`, and an unset variable yields the empty string (not `''`). Arithmetic now deletes double quotes from an expression before evaluating, matching bash: `$(( "3" + "4" ))` -> 7, `$(( 1"2"3 ))` -> 123 (quotes fuse adjacent digits rather than acting as whitespace), while single quotes stay literal. `shopt -s failglob` is now enforced: a command-word, array-literal, prefix-assignment, or `for`-list glob that matches nothing reports `no match: PATTERN` and aborts the command list with status 1 (taking precedence over `nullglob`), matching non-interactive bash. `$BASH_VERSION` and the `$BASH_VERSINFO` array are now seeded at startup (5.2 compatibility level), and `declare -p`/`${v@A}` now match bash exactly for empty arrays (bare `declare -a name`, no `=()`) and non-empty associative arrays (trailing space before `)`). POSIX character classes (`[[:space:]]`, `[[:digit:]]`, the negated `[![:space:]]`, etc.) are now recognized inside `[...]` bracket expressions in glob/pattern matching, so parameter-expansion trim idioms like `${v#"${v%%[![:space:]]*}"}` (left-trim leading whitespace) and case/substitution over character classes work as in bash. Redirection ordering for the `>&2 2>file` dup-first idiom is now honored (bash applies redirects left to right, so `echo x >&2 2>/dev/null` sends stdout to the *original* stderr, not the /dev/null file) — fixed for both the builtin write path and the compound/function `exec_with_redirects` finaliser via `emit_stderr_depth`. $- now reports the `c` flag for `osh -c COMMAND` invocations (bash appends it last, e.g. `hBc`/`ehBCc`). `read -p PROMPT` now writes the prompt only when the input is a real terminal, matching bash (a piped/here-string/redirected read is silent). An unquoted-space array subscript in assignment position (`h[a b]=v`, `h[key with space]=v`) is now kept as one assignment word by the lexer, matching bash (argument-position subscripts still split). `declare -f`/`type` deparse output is now byte-identical to bash for the common constructs (opening `{ `, every statement `;`-terminated except the last before `}`, `do` on its own line for `for`/`select`, `case WORD in ` trailing space); four bash deparser quirks (elif-as-nested-if, subshell/background inline layout, `function` keyword on nested defs) remain, all still valid re-parsable bash (TD-OILS-DECLAREF-QUIRKS). Whole-array use/alternate/error operators now work (`${a[@]:-word}`/`${a[*]:+word}`/`${a[@]:?msg}`, treating `[@]`/`[*]` like `$@` — the elements when active, the operand word when null, with bash-exact null/unset tests and the `:=` bad-array-subscript error). Redirection-only `exec` now applies its redirects in strict left-to-right source order against the persistent fd table, so the standard fd-juggling idioms work: save (`exec 3>&1`), restore (`exec 1>&3`), and the classic stdout/stderr swap (`exec 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&-`); `exec_stdout`/`exec_stderr` were widened to `Option<Arc<File>>` handles so a restored fd can alias an arbitrary sink. `!`-style **history expansion** is implemented end to end (`set -H`/`set -o histexpand`): event designators `!!`/`!n`/`!-n`/`!string`/`!?str?`/`^old^new^`, word designators and the `:h :t :r :e :s :gs :& :p :q :x` modifiers, expanded per *physical line* before lexing via new `IncrementalParser::peek_raw_line`/`commit_raw_line`/`drop_raw_line` hooks, with bash's exact quoting rules (single quotes suppress, double quotes do not), stderr echo of the rewritten line, expanded-form history recording, and bash's three failure wordings. Pinned byte-for-byte by `tests/corpus/histexpand.sh`. The **history list itself** is implemented behind it (`set -o history`, `HISTCMD`/`HISTSIZE`/`HISTFILE`/`HISTFILESIZE` including assignment-time truncation), with bash's exact line-join rule for multi-line units and the full `history [-c] [-d offset] [-anrw [file]] [-s|-p arg…] [n]` builtin — `history -p` expanding without recording, `history -s` recording without running — pinned by `tests/corpus/history.sh` and `history-file.sh`. `set -v`/`set -o verbose` echoes each line as it is read, from the same reader hook. The two remaining history-facing builtins bash provides are done as well: **`fc`** (`-l`/`-n`/`-r` listing, `-s pat=rep` re-run, `FCEDIT`/`EDITOR`/`-e ename` editor invocation, with the range arithmetic taken structurally from bash's own `builtins/fc.def` rather than inferred from probes), and **`logout`**, which required a real `login_shell` state — set only at invocation by `-l`/`--login` or an `argv[0]` beginning with `-`, read-only to scripts, and surfaced through `shopt -p login_shell` and `$BASHOPTS`. Implementing `logout` exposed and fixed a latent bug shared by `exit` and `return`: a *second* status operand is bash's `no_args` unwind (report, discard the rest of the top-level unit, keep going — escaping an enclosing `eval`), not an exit, so all three now share one operand reader. **Startup files** are now read, keyed on the two independent facts that describe how the shell was *started*: a login shell reads `/etc/profile` then the first of `~/.bash_profile`/`~/.bash_login`/`~/.profile` that exists (never `~/.bashrc`), an interactive non-login shell reads `~/.bashrc` or `--rcfile`'s argument, and any non-interactive shell additionally reads `$BASH_ENV` after the profile — expanded as if double-quoted, then tilde-expanded, so substitutions apply but splitting and globbing do not. `~/.bash_logout` is deliberately *not* part of that table: bash reads it from inside the `exit`/`logout` builtin, so osh arms it there too, which is what confines it to a login shell leaving through that builtin and explains its two oddities (it runs *before* the EXIT trap, and `$?` in it is the status from before the `exit`). A startup file's `return` stops the file but its operand is discarded, while its `exit` pre-empts the command entirely; the files see `$0`/`$#`/`$*` already set and run before the script file is even opened. With them come the flags whose whole job is to control them (`--noprofile`, `--norc`, `--rcfile`/`--init-file`, plus `--verbose` and `--noediting`) and bash's **two-pass command line**: `parse_long_options` runs first, which is why long options must precede every single-letter one and why their diagnostics differ. Rewriting the letter pass exposed and fixed four pre-existing invocation bugs — `-o`/`-O` could not be bundled and did not take the *next word* (`-eo pipefail`, `-oc pipefail cmd`) nor list the options when no word followed; `-c`/`-s` wrongly *ended* the walk (`-c -x cmd` tried to run `-x`); `-cs` was last-wins instead of `-c` always winning; and a bare `-` was treated as `-s` rather than as pure end-of-options. **Interactivity** is now modelled the way bash models it, as *two* independent facts rather than one: `interactive_shell` (how the shell was **started** — `-i`, or a tty on fd 0 and 2 with no `-c` string and no script operand) governs `$-`'s `i`, the `expand_aliases`/`histexpand`/`history` defaults and whether a diagnostic carries bash's `line N:` token, while `repl_interactive` (is the shell **at a prompt** right now) keeps prompt printing and `ignoreeof`. Collapsing the two was why `osh -i -c` reported neither `i` nor `H`, expanded no aliases and over-reported `line N:`; the whole `$-` matrix now matches bash byte-for-byte (`-c`→`hBc`, `-i -c`→`hiBHc`, `-cs`→`hBcs`, `-i -cs`→`hiBHcs`, `-H -c`→`hBHc`, `-i +H -c`→`hiBc`, script→`hB`, `-i script`→`hiBH`, `-s`/`-`/bare stdin→`hBs`). Turning the history defaults on made the REPL run history expansion for the first time, which exposed three real histexpand bugs, all fixed against *measured* bash behaviour: the inhibition rules (bash's `bash_history_inhibit_expansion` — `$!`, `${!name}`, `[!…]` and, only with `extglob` on and only for a closed group at least two characters in, `!(pat)`), readline's missing `history_comment_char` (an unquoted `#` starting a word makes the rest of the line literal, so a `!` in a comment is never an event), and where an event's search string ends (`history_word_delimiters` plus `:^$*%-`, plus the closing `"` inside a double-quoted string — nothing else, so `!zz!b` quotes back all of `!zz!b`). 1072 host tests pass; the 200-case osh-vs-bash differential corpus matches with zero waivers; builds clean for x86_64-slateos; clippy-clean. Remaining gap: the `-r`/`-x` file-permission tests are approximated, gated on the slateos permission model (TD-OILS1). **YSH (the other Oils language) — blocked-on-C++-toolchain, NOT blocked-on-effort:** per design-decisions.md §73, YSH is not hand-ported/auto-translated (Oils source is typed Python → generated GC C++; no viable Python→Rust or C++→Rust automation). YSH is obtained later by cross-compiling genuine upstream Oils once a C++/slateos toolchain exists (a prerequisite Mesa/Chromium/WINE need anyway), which yields faithful OSH+YSH at once.

"SHA-256 auth" — what this line said until 2026-08-21 — meant a private `$sha256$<salt>$<digest>` scheme under a header claiming it "matches the passwd utility". It had not matched since `passwd` moved to `posix::crypt`, so **no password set the normal way could ever open a `doas` prompt**, and a user who existed only in `/etc/users.yaml` had no entry `doas` would even look for. It failed closed, so it was never an escalation hole — but a privilege gate nobody can pass gets repaired by being switched off. Now `authlib`, like `login`, `sshd` and `ftpd`; an account with *no* password is refused (doas.conf's `nopass` is the only consent that counts), which is the opposite of how `login` resolves the same answer and is deliberate. `known-issues.md` → `B-DOAS-COULD-NOT-VERIFY-ANY-PASSWORD-THE-SYSTEM-ACTUALLY-SETS`.
