  - [-] sshd: SSH server daemon (key exchange, user auth, channel multiplexing, debug logging; `exec` runs the command as the authenticated user with real stdout/stderr/`exit-status` — 2026-08-21). **User auth is real as of 2026-08-21** and was not before: publickey auth now verifies the client's Ed25519 signature over the RFC 4252 §7 signed blob (it previously accepted *possession of a public key*, which SSH transmits in the clear and `authorized_keys` stores world-readable — i.e. anyone who had ever watched the user log in); the host key is a genuine `posix::ed25519` key loaded from disk and signed with (it was an HMAC-SHA256 padded to 64 bytes and labelled `ssh-ed25519`, and a missing key file produced a pid-derived key that changed every restart); the DH private exponent comes from `posix::random` (it was `sha256(pid ‖ uptime_ms)` — a ~2^32 search space) and the client's `e` is range-checked per RFC 4253 §8; and `PASS`-equivalent password auth goes through `authlib`, which was the *fourth* disagreeing password hasher in this tree — it hashed `$5$`/`$6$` entries as `sha256(password ‖ salt)` in hex, which is neither SHA-crypt nor what `passwd` writes, then fell through to comparing the stored entry as plaintext. `known-issues.md` → `B-THE-SSH-STACK-AUTHENTICATED-NOBODY`. **Interactive sessions are real as of 2026-09-05**: `pty-req` allocates a pseudo-terminal sized to the client's window, `shell` runs the user's login shell on the slave under `login_tty` (with the hyphen-prefixed `argv[0]` that makes it a login shell), `window-change` resizes and raises `SIGWINCH`, client keystrokes go into the line discipline so editing/`^C`/job control are the kernel's job, and the shell's exit is reported as `exit-status` after its final output has been delivered. The connection loop became readiness-driven over the socket and the pty master with 0.5–20 ms backoff, keeping a blocking fast path for every connection with no session running (`design-decisions.md` §770). `known-issues.md` → `TD-B-SSHD-RUNS-A-COMMAND-BUT-CANNOT-HOST-A-SESSION` is FIXED. **Pipe-backed sessions landed later the same day**, closing `TD-B-SSHD-EXEC-DOES-NOT-STREAM-AND-SSH-DASH-T-IS-REFUSED`: a session's streams are now a `SessionIo` — a terminal *or* three pipes — and the pump carries both, so `exec` streams its output as the child produces it instead of collecting it with `wait_with_output()` (which also means `exec`'s stdin is a real pipe the client can feed), `shell` with no preceding `pty-req` runs a login shell on pipes rather than being refused (`ssh -T`), and `subsystem` spawns the configured binary the same way. Three rules make it correct: nothing is buffered daemon-side — the client's `remote_window` bounds each read, so back-pressure is the window's job; every descriptor is put in non-blocking mode at spawn or the session is refused, because `POLLOUT` promises only that *some* bytes can be written and a blocking pipe write would stall a single-threaded daemon; and a session ends at end-of-file on its output streams, not at the child's exit, so `ssh host 'sleep 60 &'` waits for the background job exactly as OpenSSH does. See `design-decisions.md` §771. This line previously read `[x] … PTY support, session management`, which was true only in the sense that the messages parsed. **Three more "answered without being honoured" bugs closed the same day.** (1) `env` requests were answered SUCCESS and thrown away; a client may now set variables from an `AcceptEnv` allowlist that is *empty by default* — a client's environment is attacker-controlled input to a process about to run as the authenticated user, and `LD_PRELOAD`/`PATH`/`IFS`/`BASH_ENV` turn "set a variable" into "choose the code that runs" — with `HOME`/`USER`/`LOGNAME`/`SHELL`/`TERM` refused outright as the server's facts rather than the client's preferences (stricter than OpenSSH; `design-decisions.md` §772). (2) That needed a glob matcher the daemon never had, and its absence meant `AllowUsers`/`DenyUsers`/`AllowGroups`/`DenyGroups` compared their documented *patterns* as literal strings: `AllowUsers admin*` locked everyone out, and `DenyUsers guest*` let the accounts it named straight in — one of the four failed **open**. The matcher backtracks only to the most recent `*`, because the pattern is the administrator's but the name is the client's and a naive recursive matcher hands a remote client unbounded CPU. (3) `SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST` was dropped entirely, so an OpenSSH client with `ServerAliveInterval` set — the option you turn on when a firewall drops idle flows — counted every `keepalive@openssh.com` probe as lost and tore down a healthy session after `ServerAliveCountMax` of them; global requests are now refused with `REQUEST_FAILURE`, which is exactly the proof-of-life the probe wants, unrecognised messages get the `SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED` (RFC 4253 §11.4) this daemon had never once sent, and `window-change` honours `want_reply`. The three matching `known-issues.md` entries are FIXED. **A fatal one closed the next**, and fatal in the plainest sense: the daemon could not complete a handshake with *any* client, ours or OpenSSH. The RFC 4253 §8 exchange hash — the value the server signs with its host key and the client independently recomputes to check that signature — was computed over a literal `"SSH-2.0-client"` in place of `V_C`, the client's real identification line, which the daemon read, logged and discarded. Two different `V_C` values give two different hashes, so every connection died at host-key verification, before authentication, reporting a bad signature: the symptom of an attack rather than of our own encoder. It shipped because *both* ends are unit-tested against themselves and nothing anywhere makes them agree. That diagnosis is now a structural fix — `userspace/sshwire` holds one definition of the encodings (`ssh_string`, `ssh_u32`, `encode_mpint`, `strip_leading_zeros`), the exchange hash and §7.2 key derivation; both binaries depend on it and neither keeps a private copy. It is the same argument that had already pulled `sha2`, `randrange` and `posix::ed25519` out of both crates, applied one layer up to the constructions built *on* them. The extraction then found the next bug by making it obvious where to look: a shared hash function says nothing about what each end *passes* to it, so the two ends' version-line parsing was read side by side, and the client turned out to build the server's line with `char::from(byte)` — the Latin-1 mapping — so any byte ≥ 0x80 was hashed as its two-byte UTF-8 re-encoding, one byte more than the server hashed. Unreachable from a conforming peer (§4.2 requires printable US-ASCII), invisible to every test on either side, and total when reached: the same shape as the `V_C` bug, found the same way, by reading rather than by testing. Fixed with a strict decode of the version line, plus escaping of the banner lines before it, which an unauthenticated server had until then been able to write to the user's terminal as raw control sequences. Fixing that in the client raised the obvious next question — *does the server do it the same way?* — and it did not: sshd dropped **every** carriage return in the line where the client dropped only the trailing one, and their length limits were 255 and 1024, so `SSH-2.0-a\rb\r\n` would have been hashed as `SSH-2.0-ab` at one end and `SSH-2.0-a\rb` at the other. Third bug of that exact shape; second found by reading the two files at once rather than by a test. The fix was not to patch sshd's loop — that makes the two agree today and leaves them free to diverge tomorrow — but to move the derivation into `sshwire` beside the hash that consumes it (`strip_line_terminator`, `is_identification_line`, `decode_identification`, `MAX_IDENTIFICATION_LINE`), on the grounds that the identification line does not merely feed the hash, it *is* two of the hash's eight inputs, so deriving it is as much a contract between the two programs as hashing it. §4.2's 255-byte limit now counts the CRLF the RFC counts it with, which sshd's did not. What stays per-crate is only what is genuinely that end's own: the client accepts banner lines ahead of the identification line, escapes them and bounds them for memory; the server accepts none, because §4.2 permits them only from a server. **The interoperability test now exists** (`userspace/ssh-interop`), which was the check that would have caught any of the three hash bugs without someone happening to read the right two functions on the same day: it runs this tree's real client against this tree's real daemon over an in-memory `Transport`, so the socket that `cargo test` could not open is no longer needed, and it pins the handshake transcript rather than only checking the two ends agree — two ends can agree on a value neither computed the way the RFC says, which is exactly the state this stack was in (`design-decisions.md` §776). **Rekeying is implemented as of 2026-09-05**, in both directions and at both ends, closing `TD-B-SSHD-DOES-NOT-REKEY-SO-A-LONG-SESSION-HANGS`. The bug was not a missing feature but a hang: a peer that has sent `KEXINIT` sends nothing else until the exchange finishes (RFC 4253 §7.1), so the daemon's dispatch arm — which logged the message and returned `Ok` — froze every session whose client asked, silently, with no error at either end. The handshake was factored into a `run_key_exchange` that runs against an already-encrypted connection as happily as a fresh one; the session identifier is fixed at the first exchange hash (§7.2) and deliberately does not move, because it is the value a `publickey` login signed over; each direction's cipher and MAC swap independently at the packet after its own `NEWKEYS`, while the sequence numbers deliberately do not reset. Both ends grew a `recv_during_kex`, because §11.2 lets `SSH_MSG_IGNORE` arrive at any point — OpenSSH sends it under `ObscureKeystrokeTiming` — and a key exchange that assumed the next packet was its own would have failed against the commonest client while blaming that client. The daemon also **initiates** on §9's thresholds (a gibibyte under the current keys, or an hour since they were installed) rather than leaving its own key lifetime to whoever connected; `start_rekey` buffers the client's in-flight channel data for the one round trip §7.1 still permits it, bounded at 64 packets, disconnecting rather than silently truncating a transfer. Shipping that half alone would have *introduced* the same hang against our own client, which had no arm for an unsolicited `KEXINIT` either, so `ssh` grew one in the same change (it needs no buffer: anything the server sent before its `KEXINIT` is earlier in the byte stream and already dispatched). Both directions run end-to-end in `ssh-interop`, two rekeys each, so the second travels under the first's keys and a disagreement cannot pass quietly. See `design-decisions.md` §1001 for the two judgement calls inside it: an unreadable clock disables the age threshold but not the byte one — the *opposite* of §775's fail-closed login-grace call, and for the opposite reason, since this bounds an already-authenticated session doing the user's work — and why the deferral buffer is bounded. Still open in sshd: `TD-B-THE-SSH-WIRE-LAYER-IS-WRITTEN-TWICE-AND-NOTHING-MAKES-THE-TWO-COPIES-AGREE` still lists the readers, framing and cipher written twice, and why they need a shared error type first; and no sftp *server* exists — the configured `/usr/lib/sftp-server` is absent from this tree, and `userspace/sftp` is a client speaking its own protocol over raw TCP, not SFTP over an SSH channel.

FTP still sends the password in the clear, which is the protocol's own doing and is why `sftp` is the real answer.

## Phase 3: Graphics and GUI

_Depends on: Phase 2 (drivers, filesystem, basic userspace). Goal: boot to a graphical desktop._

### 3.1 GPU drivers
- [-] `[A]` Port AMDGPU driver (open source, well-documented — first priority)
  - **Modern GCN/RDNA is untestable by any available route** — QEMU emulates no
    modern AMD part and the dev machine has an NVIDIA GPU. Blocked on an
    operator decision: `open-questions.md` Q49. Rationale: `design-decisions.md` §217.
  - [x] ATI/AMD legacy display block (R100 / Rage 128) — QEMU `ati-vga` emulates
        this faithfully, so it is the one AMD-family engine that can be run.
    - [x] `drm/ati/regs.rs` — register map; CRTC timing packing (8-pixel character
          units, bias-by-one totals, split sync-start, character-denominated sync
          width); `PixWidth` format mapping; pitch encoding. Pure, no MMIO.
    - [x] `drm/ati/timing.rs` — `ModeTiming` (full sync edges + polarity, which
          `DrmMode` does not carry); 5-entry VESA DMT table; exact-match lookup.
    - [x] `drm/ati/tests.rs` — boot-time self-test: hand-computed register values
          for all 5 DMT modes, each encoding quirk isolated, every rejection path.
    - [x] `drm/ati/mmio.rs` — BAR2 aperture mapping (NO_CACHE), bounds- and
          alignment-checked 32-bit register I/O, `MM_INDEX`/`MM_DATA` indirect
          path, PCI probe. `-device ati-vga,model=rv100` is now on the boot
          test's QEMU command line, so `drm::init()` proves on every boot that
          the offsets in `regs.rs` name the registers they claim to: VRAM size
          reads as a whole number of MiB, and the direct and indirect paths
          agree. Reads only — it does not reprogram a CRTC it does not own.
    - [x] `drm/ati/modeset.rs` — CRTC mode-set, split plan/apply. `ModeSetPlan`
          computes and validates every register value with no MMIO (VRAM fit,
          scanout alignment, pitch encoding, pixel format), so a rejected mode
          leaves the display untouched rather than half-retimed; `apply` writes
          it with the CRTC disabled for the duration, per Linux
          `radeon_legacy_crtc.c`. The boot test now programs 640x480@60
          XRGB8888 onto the emulated RV100 and reads all four timing registers
          back bit-exact — the write path and the whole encoding, confirmed by
          hardware rather than by assertion. Gated on
          `AtiDevice::owns_console()`, an address comparison against the
          bootloader framebuffer, so the driver never retimes the one screen
          the operator is looking at.
    - [x] `drm/ati/vram.rs` — first-fit suballocator over the card's video
          memory, with a coalesced free list. VRAM cannot come from the buddy
          allocator (it is not RAM and cannot hold kernel structures), and a
          bump allocator would leak a whole scanout buffer per mode change —
          about seven changes before 16 MiB is exhausted, reported as an
          out-of-memory error on a resolution the card can obviously display.
          Rejects double and overlapping frees rather than corrupting the list.
          Pure, so the self-test checks the list invariants after every
          mutation, not just the return values.
    - [x] `drm/ati/aperture.rs` — the BAR0 window: up to 16 MiB of the card's
          video memory mapped `NO_CACHE` so the CPU can put pixels in it.
          Consults the page tables afterwards rather than assuming the request
          was honoured, and keeps a `flush` for the case where it was not.
          Uncacheable rather than write-combining because nothing programs the
          PAT MSR yet — see `TD-NO-WRITE-COMBINING` in `known-issues.md`, and
          note that this is why the boot exercise draws at 640x480.
    - [x] `DrmBackend::Ati` — the card registered as a DRM device. GEM objects
          live in VRAM, so `page_flip` is a single `CRTC_OFFSET` write with no
          copy at any resolution, which is the whole reason a real GPU driver
          beats a framebuffer shim. `enumerate` advertises exactly the DMT modes
          that fit the mapped aperture, filtered by `ModeSetPlan::new` — the
          same predicate `page_flip` applies later, so the menu cannot drift
          from what is actually settable. Registered but deliberately *not*
          promoted to primary: on the machine this boots, virtio-gpu drives the
          screen and this card is an unused second head, so the whole path is
          exercised every boot without being load-bearing for the only display.
    - [x] `GemObject` backing became an enum (`GemBacking::SystemRam` /
          `::Vram`) as part of the above, and this is the load-bearing part.
          `free_backing` returns frames to the buddy allocator; a VRAM object
          carrying BAR addresses in a `Vec<PhysFrame>` would hand the system
          allocator memory that was never RAM — silent corruption surfacing
          arbitrarily far from the driver that caused it, not a leak. The enum
          makes it a compile error to reach the frame list without saying which
          case you handle, `free_backing` now returns `NotSupported` for VRAM,
          and the self-test asserts the refusal rather than trusting it.
- [~] `[A]` Port Intel i915/xe driver (integrated graphics — covers most laptops)
      — **blocked by `open-questions.md` Q50** (operator decision), not by effort.
      There is no device to write it against: `qemu-system-x86_64 -device help`
      lists sixteen display devices (`ati-vga`, `bochs-display`, `cirrus-vga`,
      `isa-cirrus-vga`, `isa-vga`, `qxl`, `qxl-vga`, `secondary-vga`, `VGA`,
      `virtio-gpu-device`, `virtio-gpu-gl-device`, `virtio-gpu-gl-pci`,
      `virtio-gpu-pci`, `virtio-vga`, `virtio-vga-gl`, `vmware-svga`) and not one
      of them is an Intel iGPU — re-measured 2026-08-18. That is the difference
      between this item and the ATI one above, which the boot test exercises
      every run via `-device ati-vga,model=rv100`. `design-decisions.md` §217
      already rejected "target Intel instead" for exactly this reason. Writing
      it anyway is Q50's option B and would tick a box for a driver nobody has
      ever seen initialise; the unblocking work is Q50's option C or D (bare
      metal, or a Linux host with GVT-g/VFIO passthrough), both of which are
      operator calls about hardware and setup, not code.
- [~] `[A]` NVIDIA: defer until open-source driver matures, or use Linux compat layer later
      — blocked for the same reason and more so: QEMU emulates no NVIDIA display
      device either, and the item's own text defers it by design. Nothing to do

### 3.2 Graphics stack

The default device is unchanged.
  - [x] `/dev/dri/card0` + `renderD128` bound to the primary GPU device (`drm::primary_device`), so a libdrm/Mesa client's render node targets the GPU rather than the fallback dumb framebuffer.
  - [~] **Acceleration payoff gated on Q18** (open-questions.md): real 3D/virgl needs a virgl-capable test env (`virtio-gpu-gl` + host GL/display + virglrenderer — ~~the headless CI is 2D-only~~ **no longer true as of 2026-08-19: `SLATE_GPU=virtio-gpu-gl-pci` boots the GL device green under `egl-headless`, see the entry two lines above**) **and** the Mesa port (§4583, a large external C port needing operator go-ahead). So only the Mesa half of this gate is still standing. Next kernel-side step (render-ioctl dispatch with honest no-3D reporting) is option B in Q18, available on request. Note the driver still issues no `CTX_CREATE`/`SUBMIT_3D` — it uses one 3D command to allocate a scannable framebuffer and nothing else, so "the GL device boots" is not "3D renders".
  - [-] **`gui/vulkan/` — crate `vkloader`, the loader's userspace half.** Started 2026-09-02. The two Loader–Driver Interface rules whose failure mode is memory corruption rather than an error, written against the Khronos spec text and `vk_icd.h` rather than from memory (which had `vk_icdGetPhysicalDeviceProcAddr` at version 3; it is 4). `icd`: `InterfaceVersion` — a newtype with seven capability predicates and no public integer — plus the pure `settle()` that resolves a driver's handshake reply, clamping a driver that over-claims down to the loader's offer and distinguishing `VK_ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_DRIVER` ("skip this driver") from a real failure. `dispatch`: the dispatchable-handle layout, `ICD_LOADER_MAGIC` with the mandatory 32-bit mask, and `adopt()` — the only way to write a handle's dispatch word, and it checks the magic first; there is deliberately no unchecked counterpart. 70 tests. design-decisions.md §577, §578. Instance-level Vulkan is exported as of the same day (see the fan-out child below). **The three `vkEnumerateInstance*` commands went from deliberately absent to exported on the same day** (see the global-commands child): the omission's argument was "a loader that exports one before it can answer it honestly reports success for work it never did", which expired the moment an honest answer existed for each — and nothing in the tree was watching for that moment, which is the habit worth taking from it. Device-level Vulkan is exported as of the same day (see the device child below), and building it corrected the guess recorded here previously — the device record is **per device**, not per driver, because `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` returns device-specific pointers. The nine physical-device commands landed the same day (see the last child) and were what made the device half actually reachable — until then an application could not learn a queue family index, so it could not call `vkCreateDevice` at all. Extension commands the loader has never heard of are forwarded as of the same day (see the unknown-commands child), by three instructions of assembly rather than by a signature — which is what makes the union-of-extensions promise above deliverable for physical-device commands, though not yet for instance-level ones. Drivers are registered statically because `posix/src/dlfcn.rs`'s `dlopen` returns null; manifest/JSON discovery is deferred to when dynamic linking exists, and its parser belongs in `textfmt`.
    - [x] **ICD registry** (`registry`, `vk`): `handshake()` — the loader's whole FFI surface for negotiation, which decides nothing and returns a `DriverReply` — plus `Registry::admit`, which decides everything and needs no driver, so the interesting cases (over-claims, refuses, fails with an unrecognised code, succeeds *without writing* the in/out word) are all testable. **The version gate is enforced by construction**: `Driver` never exposes the entry points it was given, only `instance_proc_addr()` and `physical_device_proc_addr()`, which apply the settled version first — a driver that offers `vk_icdGetInstanceProcAddr` but settles at 0 does not get called through it, and the version-4 gate is tested at 3 *and* 4. Rejections are kept rather than discarded, because "no devices found" from a driver that refused, from one that failed with a code only the loader saw, and from nothing being registered are three different problems with the same symptom. `vk` declares only the six Vulkan C types the loader's own signatures cannot avoid; `VkResult` is a plain `i32`, not an enum, because a driver may return an extension code this loader has never heard of.
    - [x] **`vkCreateInstance` fan-out across the registry, and physical-device aggregation** (`entry`, `instance`) — done 2026-09-02, verified against stub ICDs written to the spec rather than to this loader (one refusing, one with no `vkCreateInstance`, one reporting success while writing nothing, one returning an unstamped instance, one that creates instances but cannot list devices). `entry` is the composition root: the only module naming a `static`, holding the process-wide `Registry` behind a private spin lock (the crate has no dependencies, and no reusable lock exists in the tree). **Exported:** `vkGetInstanceProcAddr`, `vkCreateInstance`, `vkDestroyInstance`, `vkEnumeratePhysicalDevices`, plus SlateOS's own `vk_slateosRegisterDriver`. **Deliberately absent symbols at the time** — not empty-list stubs — were `vkEnumerateInstanceExtensionProperties` (its honest answer is the de-duplicated union of every driver's list), `vkEnumerateInstanceLayerProperties` (loading a layer needs `dlopen`) and `vkEnumerateInstanceVersion` (depends on both): an application that called one failed to *link*, naming it, rather than being told there was nothing available and filing a bug against the driver. **All three were exported later the same day** once each had an honest answer — see the global-commands child; the argument recorded here was right and expired. Three policy positions, each argued in-code because the LDI is silent on all three (its only normative fan-out rule is `LDP_LOADER_1`): a driver returning `>= VK_SUCCESS` with a null handle is disbelieved and recorded as `VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`; one driver returning an instance without `ICD_LOADER_MAGIC` sinks the whole call after every created instance is destroyed, rather than being skipped; and physical devices are *wrapped* in a loader-owned object carrying the driver index — because a bare `VkPhysicalDevice` arriving at an entry point is un-attributable across several drivers — while instances are *adopted*, which is what the LDI describes and is the loader's only chance to catch a driver that never stamped. The `create_across`/`destroy_across`/`enumerate_across` helpers take a `&Registry`, so every one of those cases is reachable from a registry a test builds, with no global state and no real driver. design-decisions.md §578.
    - [x] **Device-level Vulkan** (`device`, and the device half of `entry`) — done 2026-09-02. **Exported:** `vkCreateDevice`, `vkGetDeviceProcAddr`, `vkDestroyDevice`. **Not exported, and not a gap:** every other device command. A `VkDevice` this loader returns *is* the driver's own — the loader **adopts** it, replacing the dispatch word, rather than wrapping it as it must wrap a `VkPhysicalDevice` — so `vkCmdDraw` and its several hundred siblings are found through the driver's `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` and called with the loader nowhere in the path, which is what device-level dispatch exists to permit. Wrapping would have put the loader in a path that runs thousands of times per frame *and* required a trampoline for the entire device API, including commands invented after this loader. Three further positions, each argued in-code: the record is **per device, not per driver** (`vkGetDeviceProcAddr` returns device-specific pointers, so a shared record would cache under the wrong key — this corrects what `lib.rs` and this file previously guessed, and the wrong version is left named as wrong rather than deleted); there is **no accept-list** of device commands, because a list is the commands known when it was written and would answer null for a driver's extension, so `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` forwards by default with exactly two exceptions (itself, or every later lookup skips the loader; and `vkDestroyDevice`, or the driver frees its object and leaks the loader's record behind a handle still pointing at it); and the record holds **only the two fields that are read**, not the conventional few-hundred-slot table that nothing would look at. Creation resolves the driver's `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` *before* calling `vkCreateDevice`, so a driver that cannot supply one is refused while there is nothing to unwind; destruction reads the dispatch word before the driver's call and frees the record after it. 12 new tests, incl. an end-to-end run through the real exported symbols and the global registry (register two stub drivers → `vkCreateInstance` → `vkEnumeratePhysicalDevices` → `vkCreateDevice` → forward an invented extension command → `vkDestroyDevice` → `vkDestroyInstance`, with live-object counters proving nothing leaked and that the driver *was* told), and the device-incapable driver refused without creating anything. 82 tests total. design-decisions.md §800.
    - [x] **Physical-device commands** (`physical`, and the physical-device half of `entry`) — done 2026-09-02. **Exported:** the nine core Vulkan 1.0 commands taking a `VkPhysicalDevice` — `vkGetPhysicalDevice{Properties,Features,MemoryProperties,QueueFamilyProperties,FormatProperties,ImageFormatProperties,SparseImageFormatProperties}` and `vkEnumerateDevice{Extension,Layer}Properties`. **This was not a rounding-out exercise: it is the fix for a bug that made the device child above unreachable.** The loader answered null for every one of them, and `vkGetPhysicalDeviceQueueFamilyProperties` is the *only* command that reports which queue families a GPU has, while `vkCreateDevice` cannot be called without a queue family index — so the device layer was complete, tested, green and unreachable by any conforming application, and no test that stayed inside it said so. This is the invoice for wrapping a `VkPhysicalDevice`: because the handle is a loader object the driver has never seen, every command taking one must be hand-written, which is precisely the cost the device child avoids by adopting. It is bounded — ten commands (these nine plus `vkCreateDevice`), startup-only, none per-frame, and the set is closed because Vulkan 1.0 is finished — against the open-ended per-frame set adopting devices avoids. Three positions, each argued in-code: a driver is asked through `vk_icdGetPhysicalDeviceProcAddr` **first** where it has one (only that entry point distinguishes a physical-device command from a device command of the same name, which need opposite handling) and through `vkGetInstanceProcAddr` **after** a null (required by the LDI — a driver may route only its *extension* physical-device commands through the version-4 one), which finally gives `Driver::physical_device_proc_addr` a caller; all nine go in `entry`'s instance dispatch table, because the table's stated membership rule is what the handle dispatches through, and unlike a device table every one of its thirteen entries is read; and `vkCreateDevice` is deliberately *not* a `physical::Command`, because that table is the commands with no body. A driver missing one is not a Vulkan 1.0 driver, but is still handled: `VkResult` commands return `VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED`, count out-parameters are set to **zero** (leaving the count untouched hands the application a garbage count and then has it read that many structures), and the residual case with neither is left untouched and recorded as noticed. `vk.rs` still declares **no** Vulkan structure layout — every one is `*const c_void` — which is now stated as the invariant rather than justified by a count. 9 new tests, incl. one that iterates `physical::ALL` through the real `vkGetInstanceProcAddr` (the check whose absence *was* the bug), plus the end-to-end test extended to prove forwarding actually happens: the driver is called with its own handle rather than the loader's wrapper, a version-4 driver is reached through its version-4 entry point, a driver whose version-4 lookup declines is still reached through the instance one, a below-version-4 driver is asked once, and a driver answering nothing zeroes the caller's count. 91 tests total. design-decisions.md §801.
    - [x] **Global commands** (`global`, and the global half of `entry`) — done 2026-09-02. **Exported:** `vkEnumerateInstanceVersion`, `vkEnumerateInstanceLayerProperties`, `vkEnumerateInstanceExtensionProperties`. These are the three commands asked with a **null instance**, before any driver has been chosen — an application uses them to decide what to put in the `vkCreateInstance` it has not made yet — so the loader must *answer* rather than forward, and each answer is a decision: Vulkan 1.0, because that is what this loader implements (reporting 1.1 would be the generous lie — an app seeing it may call `vkGetPhysicalDeviceProperties2` and get null); an empty layer list, because loading a layer needs `dlopen`, which returns null on SlateOS; and the de-duplicated **union** of every registered driver's extension list. They live in `get_instance_proc_addr`'s null-instance branch alongside `vkCreateInstance`, **not** in `TABLE` — the table is what a *handle* dispatches through, and these have no handle. Two policy positions the Loader–Driver Interface is silent on, both argued in-code: **union, not intersection** (intersecting would let a driver the application was never going to use veto a capability its actual GPU has — a discrete card plus a software rasteriser would report whatever the rasteriser lacks as unavailable, which is the same failure §578's "a partial success is a success" rule exists to avoid), and the **lowest** `specVersion` among the drivers offering an extension, not the highest — under-promising costs a missed optimisation, over-promising costs a crash in an application that asked first and was told yes. Ordering is first-seen, so the list can be read against the registry. A driver that lacks the command, fails the query, or writes fewer records than it first promised contributes nothing rather than sinking the call; `extensions_across` takes a `&Registry`, so all of that is driven from stub ICDs a test builds. **This is where the crate's "no Vulkan structure is declared" invariant broke, on purpose and exactly once:** the union must be de-duplicated, de-duplication compares extension *names*, so the loader has to know where the name is. `VkExtensionProperties` is two fields, one a fixed-size byte array whose length is itself part of the ABI, with no `pNext` and no version-dependent tail — and `const _: () = assert!(size_of == 260)` plus the matching alignment assertion make a layout mistake a build failure rather than a driver reading the wrong field at runtime, which is the check the original argument said a structure declaration could not have. The name is `[u8; 256]`, not `[c_char; 256]`: layout-identical, and it drops a signedness question the loader has no use for since it compares these bytes rather than interpreting them. The rule is now "declare one only when the loader must read a field, and argue it at the point of use". 120 tests total. design-decisions.md §802.
    - [x] **Unknown physical-device commands** (`unknown`, and the fallback tail of `get_instance_proc_addr`) — done 2026-09-02. Closes the physical-device half of the conformance defect the global-commands child above created and filed: the loader now reports the union of every driver's extensions, so an application that enables `VK_KHR_surface` asks for `vkGetPhysicalDeviceSurfaceSupportKHR` — a command with no entry in `physical::Command`, previously answered null. §801's nine trampolines cannot be extended to it because there is no signature to write; the whole point is that the loader does not know the extension exists. **The escape is that a signature is not needed.** Both calling conventions the loader targets pass the first pointer argument in one register (`rdi` System V, `rcx` Win64) and leave every other argument where the caller put it, so three instructions — read the driver's table out of the wrapper, overwrite argument 0 with the driver's own handle, `jmp` — forward *every* signature at once: the stack, the float registers and the return path are untouched, and `rax` is the only clobber (caller-saved in both, an argument register in neither). That needs a guaranteed tail call, which Rust has not, so it is `#[unsafe(naked)]` + `naked_asm!` — the technique the Khronos loader uses (`unknown_ext_chain_*.asm`), and the reason `vk_icdGetPhysicalDeviceProcAddr` exists at interface version 4 at all. A forwarder must be a distinct *address* per command name (the address is all the application keeps), so there is a fixed compile-time `POOL` of 128 `tramp::<N>`, and **a slot is never reassigned** — Vulkan lets an application resolve a command once and call it forever, so recycling would silently turn one command into another in a program that did nothing wrong; exhaustion returns the null the C API already means by "no such entry point". The driver's function pointer lives in a per-driver `Table` boxed on `Driver` (its *address* is copied into every physical-device wrapper, and `Driver` lives in a `Vec` that moves), and an entry no driver answered holds an aborting stub rather than null. **The safety rule, and it is a memory-safety rule rather than a preference:** only a name answered through `vk_icdGetPhysicalDeviceProcAddr` may be given a slot. `physical::Ask`'s legitimate fallback to `vkGetInstanceProcAddr` would be corruption here — that entry point answers for device-level commands too and does not say which it gave, and a device command reached through a trampoline would have a `VkDevice` read as a loader wrapper. So a sub-version-4 driver contributes nothing even when it exports the symbol, with a dedicated test, because the failure it prevents is silent. Resolution is redone on every lookup (a driver registered later would otherwise be reachable through a slot nobody filled) and a slot is spent only after some driver says yes (a name nobody has must cost nothing permanent, since the pool is never reclaimed). 135 tests total. design-decisions.md §803. **Instance-level half, partly closed 2026-09-22.** A command taking a `VkInstance` needs a per-command fan-out policy, which is a decision rather than a forwarding rule, so it is made one command at a time. The first is done: `VK_EXT_debug_utils`' messenger pair (`gui/vulkan/src/messenger.rs`, design-decisions.md §867) fans out to every driver that offers the command, treats a driver without the extension as contributing nothing, unwinds the whole call if a driver that offers it then fails, and answers **null** when no driver implements it rather than handing back a pointer that could only fail. 141 tests. **Still open:** the surface family (`vkDestroySurfaceKHR`, the platform `vkCreate*SurfaceKHR`), and it is blocked on a *prerequisite* rather than a decision — there is no registered driver anywhere in the tree and no surface concept on SlateOS to decide about, since the display belongs to the compositor rather than to X11 or Win32. That makes it downstream of the Mesa port, not of a policy table; see known-issues.md `C-VKLOADER-ADVERTISES-EXTENSIONS-WHOSE-ENTRY-POINTS-IT-ANSWERS-NULL-FOR`.

The seam is deliberately at the *primitive* level, not per-pixel (no GPU can implement `blend_pixel` and remain a GPU) and not per-scene (that would force every backend to re-derive decoration geometry — the exact drift the compositor's comments already guard against). Everything above it is backend-agnostic and stays written once: window management, damage tracking, the occlusion cull, decoration geometry, the clip and translate stacks, and text *shaping* — a GPU backend uploads the same `GlyphMask`es to an atlas. Below it is only putting colour on the surface. `RenderEngine::{execute, execute_command, fill_rect, stroke_rect, draw_text, draw_line}` and `blit_run` are generic over `T: RenderTarget + ?Sized` (monomorphised, no `dyn`); `Framebuffer` now *implements* `RenderTarget`, absorbing the rasterization that used to live in `RenderEngine` (row fills, clipped Bresenham, glyph-mask blending) and in `Compositor` (`blit_buffer`), with every fast path intact — parallel row-band clears, `clear_except` span merging, the `blit_opaque` memcpy path. `Compositor.framebuffer: Framebuffer` became `Compositor.backend: RenderBackend`, so nothing in the compositor may assume the pixels live in local memory. Output is byte-identical: the pixel-exact regression tests (occlusion-cull equivalence, parallel-vs-serial blit, unclipped-Bresenham equivalence, the ellipsis comparisons) all still pass unchanged. 8 new tests in `render.rs` drive the real `RenderEngine` through a *second* `RenderTarget` implementation that owns no pixels at all, proving the pipeline names no `Framebuffer`, that a fully-clipped quad never reaches a backend, that a stroke crosses as four quads rather than an outline to interpret, that a line crosses whole (a client asking for `x2 = 2e9` cannot make the compositor walk per-pixel), and that text crosses as one placed coverage quad per drawn glyph. 194 compositor tests green, clippy-clean, see design-decisions.md §488. **Remaining:** the GPU backend variant itself, which needs a render node that accepts commands — see `requests/c-a-virtgpu-render-ioctl-dispatch-blocks-compositor-gpu.md` (nothing under `kernel/` issues `CTX_CREATE`/`SUBMIT_3D`; `virtgpu_uapi.rs` is pure ABI), and beyond that the Mesa port the operator has not yet green-lit (Q18).

SharedBuffer::import validates client geometry against a hostile trust boundary — caps dimensions to the framebuffer pixel limit, requires stride >= width*bpp, rejects strides/sizes that overflow or mappings shorter than the declared rows, all with checked arithmetic and bounds-checked reads (no panic/index) — and normalizes the source (stride padding + format) into densely-packed ARGB8888. IPC note: real SlateOS shm handles not yet wired into the still-stubbed compositor IPC — import currently takes the mapped bytes directly; when channel IPC lands only the byte source changes (a mapping of the pages named by handle), validation/blit/release stay identical.)

Each window is now created in a band it can never leave, and raising is confined to the band; `Normal` is the default and the wire byte is trailing, so every pre-existing caller is unchanged and the 194 existing compositor tests passed untouched. Automatic refocus on close also became band-aware, since "focus the topmost remaining window" would otherwise hand the keyboard to the taskbar every time an application quit. Deliberately *not* `SCEN`: that is a remote viewer's frame (geometry + draw commands, to reproduce pixels), this is a shell's (title, focus, minimized, layer, pid) — same window set, different question, and collapsing them would give each consumer most of a frame to skip past. Push not poll (a poller lags a frame or asks every frame for an answer that never changes); snapshot not delta (a shell that missed one delta would be wrong forever with nothing to tell it so); unfiltered (a taskbar wants minimized windows and not overlays, Alt-Tab wants neither — a pre-filtering compositor picks one and leaves the other unable to recover what was dropped). Subscription is *link* state, so it is intercepted in `ClientLink::answer_requests` and `to_compositor_request` treats reaching it as a dispatch bug. **Staleness is derived, not counted:** `route_window_list` compares the encoded list against the exact bytes last sent that link, rather than an epoch counter bumped at the eight window-mutating sites — a forgotten bump does not fail loudly, it silently leaves a taskbar showing a stale title, which is §494's counting-vs-searching trap again; byte comparison has no site to forget and covers a new mutator the moment it exists. Fixed at the documented chokepoint: `Window::frame_insets` is "the single place the geometry derives from … hit testing, damage and drag detection included", so scaling there carried the whole system, and `Window::scale_factor` scales *only* what the compositor draws — never `width`/`height`, which are the client's own pixels and resizing them behind the owner's back would be a worse bug than the one being fixed. Which display a window is on is decided by largest intersection rather than by which display holds the top-left corner (the corner is the *last* part to cross a seam, so the corner rule keeps the first monitor's decorations on a window nine-tenths onto the second), and the scale is re-derived by `refresh_window_scales` at the top of `compose_frame` and `handle_input` rather than bumped at each of the six placement sites — the §494/§495 argument that a value recomputed before use has no site to forget. Producers were everywhere and all correct — `guitk`'s widget borders, the SVG renderer's `rx`/`ry`, the tab strip, the launcher's search field, the power menu, the resource monitor, and the shell's `corner_radii()` fed from the user's `WindowCorners` setting — and `gui/remote`'s `write_radii`/`read_radii` serialised them faithfully across the wire. The outline is literally "outer shape minus inner shape" sharing the fill's arc code, because an outline with its own curve parts company with its fill by a pixel somewhere and floats free of the window at the corners. Radii under half a pixel fall through to the flat path untouched, so `CornerRadii::ZERO` — nearly every command in the tree — is bit-identical to before. The compositor — the process that actually draws window frames — was outside that arrangement entirely, drawing every frame from a hardcoded twelve-colour `DecorationTheme` with no dependency on `appearance` at all, so `window_corners` produced one square window for all four choices and `drop_shadows` left every shadow exactly where it was. This is §498's fault one layer up and hidden the same way: a square window looks perfectly plausible, and nothing about the picture said a setting was being ignored. Fixed by depending on `appearance` (no cycle — it depends only on `guitk` and `yamldoc`) and holding the **whole** `AppearanceSettings`, not the two fields usable today: a compositor-local `corner_radius: f32` + `shadows: bool` is a third independent appearance model in miniature, which is the exact thing `TD-THREE-INDEPENDENT-APPEARANCE-MODELS` was filed about, and `DecorationTheme`'s twelve hand-copied Catppuccin colours are the next thing that should be a field read rather than four more parameters. `decoration_radius` scales by the display factor and feeds the title-bar fill, the border stroke, the buttons and every ring of the shadow — but deliberately does *not* inherit `scale_dimension`'s non-zero floor, because that floor exists so a 1px border never rounds to 0 (hit-testing derives from the same number, and a 0px border is a window that cannot be grabbed to resize), whereas a radius of 0 is the user having chosen `Square` and must survive scaling as a square corner rather than being promoted to a 1px curve. **A maximized window now casts no shadow, and the reason is not the shell's** — worth recording because a reader who assumes the two cases are the same will draw the wrong conclusion about one of them: the shell suppresses a fill-based `BoxShadow` that "would bleed over the screen border", true of a fill and false of the compositor's concentric rings, which cannot bleed because `maximize_window` fits the frame to the display exactly, so every ring is either clipped off-display or drawn *underneath the window's own frame* — invisible overdraw on an opaque window (eight stroked rounded rectangles per frame for nothing, on the common case) and a dark smear along the top and left on a translucent one. Fullscreen needs no such test: `has_title_bar` is `decorations && !fullscreen`, so it never reaches the decoration path. `set_appearance` forces a full recomposite, because an appearance change generates no damage — no window moved — yet changes pixels *outside* every window's extent (the quarter-disc a squared corner reclaims, the strip a removed shadow vacates), and without it the user drags the corner control and the screen does not change, which reads as a broken control rather than a stale frame. `main` reads the file, not `Compositor::new`, so no test in the crate depends on the machine's `$HOME` — the same split `AppearanceFile::new` vs `::load` already draws. Ten tests, 10/10 caught by reintroduction on the first pass; **two were wrong before they were right** and §499 records both, because neither error would have announced itself: one asserted an absolute pixel count that is simply false (a square 20×20 corner block paints 339 of 400, the rest being the border stroke and the first letters of the title — a sound *relative* measure and an unsound absolute one), and one was reading `compose_frame`'s vsync gate instead of its damage state, since three calls in a row at 60 Hz all fall inside one 16 ms interval, so its middle assertion was passing for entirely the wrong reason and its last failed for that reason. One property is honestly disclaimed as unguarded: the shadow rings grow their radius by their own distance out, and no test here distinguishes that from a stack of same-shaped outlines. 243 compositor tests green, clippy `--all-targets` clean, slateos target builds. design-decisions.md §499. This closes prerequisite 2 of `TD-C-THE-DESKTOP-AND-THE-COMPOSITOR-BOTH-DRAW-WINDOW-TITLE-BARS` except for live reload — the channel is startup-only, and the fix is a `ReloadAppearance` request carrying *no data* so the compositor re-reads the user's own file rather than being told what to draw (a setter would let any connected client restyle the whole desktop). Then the shell's duplicate renderer can be deleted.

Closed with `RequestBody::ReloadAppearance` (tag `0x0F`, `gui/remote/src/control.rs`), the one request in the protocol that **carries no data at all** — and that is the design, not an omission. `SetAppearance(AppearanceSettings)` would have saved a file read and was rejected twice over: anything that can open the display socket can send any request on it, so a setter lets any program restyle the whole desktop, and a hostile *style* is not an abstraction (title-bar text the colour of the title bar, a close button the colour of the bar behind it) — none of it crashes, which is what makes it good as an attack; and a wire encoding for the settings would be a fourth copy of a model whose whole point (`TD-THREE-INDEPENDENT-APPEARANCE-MODELS`, §499) is having one owner, in the one place where it would also need versioning. A *notification* inverts the trust: the compositor re-reads the user's own file, which the sender may have no permission to write, so the worst a hostile client achieves is a redundant read and a repaint of a screen that already looks the way it looks. A test asserts the **encoded length** — header, seq, tag byte, nothing else — so that "just a corner radius, to save a file read" fails where it is added rather than in review. `to_compositor_request` maps it with no `link.resolve`, deliberately: it names no window, so a client that has never opened one may still send it, which is not a nicety — Settings is exactly such a client. The comparison against the current settings lives in `set_appearance` rather than the handler, because `reload_appearance` is not its only caller (startup calls it, and a future file watch would), and because an unlimited-rate notification that forced a full recomposite each time would be a way to hold the compositor at a full-screen redraw for nothing. Instead `save_appearance` sets a private `appearance_dirty` flag and the loop drains it with `take_appearance_change()`, which is not a workaround but the correct shape: it makes the notification track **the file changing** rather than **an event being consumed**, and those are not the same thing in either direction. Notifying on `Consumed` turns a drag across a slider into hundreds of compositor file reads; notifying *only* on `Consumed` loses the notification of any future control that writes the file and returns `Ignored`. The drain therefore happens before the redraw check and independently of the result, and both directions are pinned by their own tests. The flag obeys §522's resting-state rule transplanted from animations to settings: **the change is saved and in force before the flag is read**, so a caller that never drains it still gets a correct file and a correct window and loses only the liveness of the update elsewhere — including the case that looks wrong for a second and is not, that `save_appearance` sets the flag *even when the write failed*, because the compositor answers the notification by re-reading the file and "look again" is the honest thing to say after a partial write. A track wider than the setter's clamp has a dead zone at each end (the handle slides, the number stops) and neither side's tests can see it, because each side is individually correct. `MIN_/MAX_/DEFAULT_DOUBLE_CLICK_MS` are now `pub` in `inputsettings` and the compositor's private copies are deleted; the ordering invariant is a `const _: () = assert!(…)` rather than a test, because there is no run in which it could hold in one place and fail in another. **`ReloadInput` is a second verb rather than a payload or a shared one, and both halves of that matter:** no payload, because a verb that *set* the values would let anything that can open the display socket swap the user's mouse buttons or make a double click a two-second affair, whereas a *notification* only makes the compositor re-read a file it already trusts (asserted on the encoded bytes, not the enum's shape); and not shared with `ReloadAppearance`, because an appearance reload sets `full_recomposite` and repaints every window, so one verb would mean dragging the double-click slider repaints the desktop on every motion event and picking an accent colour re-reads the pointer configuration. The rule that generalises: *ink is chosen for the background the shape's outline is read against, and containment decides which background that is.* `slider.rs` asserts the containment premise directly rather than trusting the prose, so a future shape whose thumb fitted inside its track fails a test instead of inheriting reasoning that stopped applying to it. **The scope in the entry was wrong twice and only measuring found it:** it said "`network_settings.rs` alone has four sites", but a grep for `toggle_bg`/`p.accent` missed every panel that uses `p.green` for *on* (accessibility, notifications, user accounts — where *on* means safe rather than selected), and `p.text` on `green` is no better than `p.text` on `blue`. It also proposed a shared test asserting the knob equals `readable_on(pill)` "in both modes and under every accent", which **cannot be written as a floor over every role**: `readable_on` picks between exactly two inks, so on a mid-grey (`overlay0`, `#6C7086`) the better of the two is 4.32:1 and 4.5 is unreachable without a third ink. Split into a 4.5:1 floor over the colours a track can actually be, plus the weaker universal claim — that the choice between the two inks is the right way round — over all 42 role-mode pairs. That second test earns its keep: `readable_on` decides with a fast weighted-luma threshold while legibility is governed by gamma-corrected WCAG relative luminance, and nothing before now had checked that the approximation never crosses over. None was relaxed; each was rewritten to state the claim the fix makes, with the superseded reasoning kept in the doc comment rather than overwritten. Answers lane A's `requests/a-c-evdev-input-devices-exist-and-they-need-a-capability.md` (kernel commits `46e69a1c1`, `f37616f4c`); replied in `requests/c-a-the-compositor-now-reads-your-evdev-nodes-and-is-waiting-only-on-the-capability.md`. `gui/compositor/src/present/evdev.rs` opens `/dev/input/event*`, decodes the 24-byte `input_event` records and turns them into the compositor's own `InputEvent`s; `present::Paired` marries it to `DrmScanout` so `Server::run_with` sees one display that both draws and listens. **The kernel hands over a stream of *changes* and a desktop needs *state*, and that gap is the whole of this task:** key repeat (the kernel returns `ENOSYS` for `EVIOCGREP` and never emits value 2, so it is synthesised from key-down/up timing — capped at 4 repeats per tick, or a frame delayed by a slow composite pays out the backlog as a screenful of one letter, and modifiers excluded by name, or a repeating Caps Lock toggles itself thirty times a second); absolute pointer position (integration, the user's speed and acceleration, clamping, and the sub-pixel remainder without which a 0.25× speed setting rounds every packet to zero and the pointer cannot move at all); and `SYN_DROPPED` resynchronisation via `EVIOCGKEY`, **reconciled in both directions** — down-in-our-books-and-not-in-the-bitmap is the obvious stuck-Shift case, but up-in-our-books-and-down-in-the-bitmap is just as real, since a Ctrl held across a drop would otherwise be missing from every shortcut until the user let go. **Three sub-decisions worth the space** (design-decisions.md §544): the raw `MSC_SCAN` scan code the kernel helpfully attaches to every key event is our *fallback*, not our primary route, because it is only a set-1 code on a PS/2 device — Linux puts the HID usage there for a USB keyboard, so the same bytes read the same way name a different key the day a USB stack exists, and `uapi::set1_for_keycode` inverts lane A's table instead, with `the_table_is_the_kernels_table_backwards` transcribing their table and asserting the round trip so a row added on one side and not the other fails a test rather than silently delivering the wrong key; a device that cannot answer `EVIOCGKEY` has **everything it holds released**, asymmetric on purpose, because a key wrongly reported up recovers the instant it is pressed again and one wrongly reported down never recovers at all; and buttons are skipped in the *press* direction of a resync, since synthesising one from the bitmap delivers a click nobody made. Devices are found by trying indices `0..32` and keeping whatever opens, rather than listing `/dev/input/` — devfs is flat and the directory reads empty — and every record is routed by *its own type*, so a keyboard with a trackpoint or nodes numbered differently need no change; the cruder mechanism is also the more robust one, and lane A's devfs fix does not block us. **`Paired` is a separate adapter rather than an input half welded onto `DrmScanout`**, so that headless, recording and the host window do not all grow the same seam; it takes the desktop size at *construction* because `Server::run_with` calls `input()` before the first `show()`, and a pointer that learned its bounds from the first frame would spend that frame clamped to nothing. **The four syscalls sit behind a trait and everything above them is driven by a fake device scripting a real byte stream**, so the whole module is proved on the Windows development machine — which matters because `open` still returns `EACCES`: the compositor needs an `InputDevice` capability granted at spawn, that grant is lane B's (`requests/a-b-the-compositor-needs-an-inputdevice-capability-to-inherit.md`) and is not landed, so the missing capability blocks the hardware run and not the suite. `EvdevError::Denied` is its own variant so the failure reports itself in words rather than as a missing file, and the compositor prints the capability tuple and the request filename and then **carries on without local input** — a desktop that draws and can be connected to is worth having even when nobody can type at it, and refusing to start would make an unlanded cross-lane dependency look like a broken compositor. **`scripts/reintro-evdev.py` puts 54 plausible one-line bugs back one at a time**; 46 were named immediately, and the other eight are what the harness is for. **Five were tests passing *vacuously***: `Pointer::set_bounds`'s clamp was untested because every test observed the pointer only after an `EV_REL` and `nudge` clamps on its own (the real bug it allowed: unplug a monitor, then click without moving, and the click lands at a coordinate the desktop no longer has); the divide-by-zero guard in `accelerate` was untested because an infinite factor is clamped back to `MAX_ACCELERATION` further along, so the finiteness assertion held with the guard deleted; "an idle device produces nothing" never went on to show the device was still being *read*, so treating idleness as a fault was invisible; and both device-scan tests put their devices at indices 0 and 1 — where the search starts — so neither could tell "scans every index" from "looks at the first two", nor "skips a refusal" from "stops at the first one". None is visible by reading, and each now has a test observing what the guard promises rather than a symptom something downstream also prevents. **The remaining three were not test gaps at all, and the difference matters**: one invariant was *self-referential* (the only thing asserting the per-frame read budget was bounded was a test comparing the constant to itself — it moved into a `const _: () = assert!(...)`, and the harness learned that a build break counts as a catch); one was a bug in the *defect* (it inserted a resync before the drain while leaving the after-drain pass, which changes nothing, since on entry there is nothing to resync); and one is a genuine *no-op* — deleting the resync loop's skip-buttons guard is unobservable, because no button code has a set-1 scan code, so it is recorded as a no-op and the checkable half (that the table never grows one) is pinned by a test sweeping every code from `BTN_MISC` up. A harness that called all eight "weak tests" would be a harness whose output gets skimmed. `known-issues.md` gains `TD-C-A-POINTER-SPEED-CHANGE-DOES-NOT-REACH-THE-POINTER`: `Compositor::reload_input` still adopts only `double_click_ms` and `EvdevInput::set_settings` has no caller, because the missing piece is not a line but a direction — `Compositor` is deliberately display-agnostic, and the fix is a `Present::reload_input` with an empty default body, the pattern `Present::monitors` already uses.

The decoder existed and nothing called it: `WallpaperManager` allocated an image id, emitted a `RenderCommand::Image` naming it, and the compositor drew *nothing, silently*, because no pixels had ever been stored under that id — a wallpaper that failed to appear and produced no error anywhere. **The whole difficulty was deciding where the read goes and what a failed one costs.** `WallpaperManager` performs no I/O by design and says so in three doc comments — `populate_slideshow_paths` exists precisely so the *caller* scans the directory — and its ~2000 lines of tests all run with no filesystem, so giving it a loader would have made every one of them take a stub or stop covering the load path. The read went into `ShellSession::refresh_wallpaper_image` instead, which adds no dependency edge at all: that layer already owns the connection, and uploading is a method on a window handle. Four decisions with a defensible other side, all in §557: an unshowable wallpaper (missing, corrupt, *or refused by the compositor* under §556's per-link image budget) records `wallpaper_error()` and lets the repaint finish, because the only thing a shell's main loop can do with "your wallpaper is corrupt" is carry on painting — and a taskbar that did not draw because of a `.png` is strictly worse than the plain background `render_image`'s colour underlay already provides, commented *"visible ... if image fails to load"* since before there was anything to load; every *other* connection error still propagates, the line being that a refusal is a fact about the picture while a closed socket is a fact about the link, and the `submit` two statements later would fail on it anyway. The `(image id, path)` pair is remembered **including when the attempt failed**, so a corrupt wallpaper is read once rather than on every repaint — `paint_background` runs on every repaint and a repaint happens on every click that changes anything, so the alternative is re-inflating a 4K file per click; the accepted cost is that repairing a file in place needs one extra settings touch. Both halves of the pair are load-bearing: the id alone misses an edit in place, the path alone misses the fresh id `set_image` and every slideshow step allocate. And a slideshow step **drops the old id before uploading the new one**, because uploading first charges the link's budget for two full-screen pictures at once and a budget sized to one wallpaper would then refuse every slide after the first. `WindowHandle::upload_image`/`drop_image` added to `oswindow` to carry it. 8 tests against the offline `oswindow::testing` compositor, reading the sibling crate's real libpng fixtures rather than a copy — a copy inherits the bytes without inheriting the property that makes them worth using. Still unwired and now the next step: `apps/explorer` thumbnails and `apps/imageviewer` (which still synthesises a grey checkerboard in `Image::load`), both of which need an `oswindow` dependency first, and nothing yet *shows* `wallpaper_error()` to the user. design-decisions.md §557.
  - [x] `[C]` **Applications can hand the compositor pixels, and the image viewer shows the photograph you opened** — the third part of `TD-C-NOTHING-DECODES-A-PICTURE-SO-EVERY-IMAGE-ID-NAMES-NOTHING`, and the part that unblocks the other ~140 apps rather than just this one. `apps/imageviewer` opened *every* file as the same 16-pixel grey checkerboard, under a comment in `display_image` reading "in a real implementation, this would decode the image", and the entire test suite passed over it because the tests asserted on a placeholder the code was honest about producing. **The blocker was structural and applied to every application in the tree, not to this one:** `oswindow::app::App` — the strap ~140 crates share — has exactly one drawing method, `render(width, height) -> RenderTree`, and a `RenderTree`'s `RenderCommand::Image` carries an image *id* and never the pixels behind it. Uploading is `WindowHandle::upload_image`, and an app implementing `App` never sees a `WindowHandle`. So there was no route from an application to the compositor's image store at any price, and the wallpaper only had one because `ShellSession` bypasses `App` entirely. `App::take_images() -> Vec<ImageChange>` is that route, drained by `drive` **after `render` and before the frame is submitted** so a picture queued while drawing is up before the frame that names it. **Four decisions with a defensible other side, all in §558.** (1) *A drained queue rather than giving `render` the window handle*: the alternative makes `render` a method that performs I/O and can fail, which propagates a `Result` and a transport type parameter into 140 implementations and makes every render test need a connection — today they are pure `(w, h) -> RenderTree` functions runnable on a build machine with no compositor, which is the property that makes the app suites in this tree runnable at all. (2) *One ordered `Vec<ImageChange>` rather than `take_uploads()` + `take_drops()`*, because §557 established that a slideshow must drop before it uploads or §556's per-link budget is charged for two full-screen pictures at once and refuses every slide after the first — two methods cannot express "this drop precedes that upload", the caller has to pick an order, and whichever it picks is wrong for someone. The guarding test is order-sensitive rather than a presence check. (3) *Drained per **frame**, not per event* — deliberately unlike the neighbouring `take_reloads`, and the asymmetry is the interesting half: a settings file rewritten by the last click before a window closes must be announced even though no frame follows, so reloads drain per event; a picture with no frame behind it has nothing to be early for, and an upload still queued at exit is freed with the window, so draining images per event would only upload pictures for frames that never get drawn. (4) *The viewer reuses **one** image id for every file*, replacing an id hashed from the path. Nothing evicts — §556 has the compositor refuse rather than evict — so per-path ids mean a session paging through a directory of 400 photographs holds all 400 and is refused somewhere in the middle, and a cache to prevent that needs its own eviction policy, its own budget accounting, and a way to know the compositor agrees with it. Reading the compositor's actual arithmetic settled it: `image_budget_refusal` computes `after = held - freed + incoming` where `freed` is what that same `(window, id)` already holds, so **re-registering an id is a replacement**, and one fixed id gives §557's never-hold-two property for free with no explicit drop at all — the wallpaper had to arrange it by hand only because it genuinely uses two ids. The accepted cost is that Left-then-Right decodes the same file twice, which is milliseconds. Also settled: the pending queue is *cleared* before each push, since a held arrow key crosses a directory faster than the loop draws and an appending queue would upload every file passed over into the same slot; `main` no longer `process::exit(1)`s on an unreadable file, because that argument was made when there was no window at all and now `render_image` has a purpose-built "Cannot display this image" state and `open_file` builds the directory listing either way, so the user gets a window naming the broken file and an arrow key that carries them off it instead of a flash and a stderr line nobody reads; and `decode_failure` separates "these bytes are not a picture" from "this is a JPEG and no decoder claims it yet", using the viewer's own signature sniffing, because telling a user their photograph "is not a picture format this system reads" sends them looking for a corrupt disk. `parse_png_dimensions` also stopped reading two integers out of raw offsets 16 and 20 — unchecked, so a truncated download reported whatever sat there — and delegates to `imagecodec::dimensions`, which validates the IHDR as a chunk. **The test fixture was upgraded rather than the tests weakened:** `png_bytes` emitted a bare 13-byte header, which was sufficient *precisely because* nothing decoded, so rather than let four already-written scratch-directory tests take a stub it became a real encoder — stored deflate blocks, CRC-32 per chunk, Adler-32 over the stream — and every one of those tests kept its exact signature while now running against a genuine picture. That is what lets `the_pixels_are_the_files_own_and_not_a_pattern` assert a specific pixel's four bytes. **Ordering is proved offline by arming a refusal**, not by the round-trip-versus-fire-and-forget trick the wallpaper used: `drive` runs to completion, so instead the harness is told to refuse, the upload fails, `drive` returns `Err` at exactly the point under test, and `submitted.is_empty()` shows the frame had not gone first — `absorb()` records frames regardless of refusal, so the assertion is not vacuous. 5 tests in `gui/window/src/app.rs`, 8 in the viewer, 110 imageviewer tests green, clippy `--all-targets` clean, rustfmt clean. **Still placeholder and logged:** the viewer's own filmstrip (`render_thumbnail_strip`) still draws a grey `FillRect` per entry, and `apps/explorer`'s thumbnails are unwired — the same problem, needing a bounded off-the-draw-path decode scheduler and a per-thumbnail eviction rule, and it should be solved once for both. The video path is frameless for a different reason: no video decoder exists. design-decisions.md §558.
  - [x] `[C]` **The file manager shows the picture in each file, and is a window you can click** — the fourth part of `TD-C-NOTHING-DECODES-A-PICTURE-SO-EVERY-IMAGE-ID-NAMES-NOTHING`, leaving only the image viewer's filmstrip. `apps/explorer` thumbnailed a `.png` as a flat green rectangle of the right aspect ratio and nothing more, its own source saying so — *"we produce a placeholder ... since we lack a full decoder in this crate"* — with only uncompressed BMP getting a real preview, which is the one format nobody's photographs are in. It also had no `main` worth the name: a scripted print-only demo, no `oswindow` dependency, so it could lay out a frame but had nowhere to put it and no way to be clicked. Both halves are done. **The decode half** routes through `imagecodec` (`try_decoded_thumbnail`) and is bounded: `DEFAULT_MAX_SOURCE_PIXELS` (24M — a 6000×4000 full-frame photograph) refuses a picture too big to decode at full size rather than allocating for it, surfaced as `ThumbConfig::max_source_pixels` so a small machine can lower it, and the reason it must exist at all is logged as `TD-C-A-THUMBNAIL-COSTS-A-FULL-SIZE-DECODE` (the proper fix is a scaled decode that box-filters during scanline reconstruction, at which point the cap can go away entirely). **The upload half needed three things nothing else in the tree had needed, all of them tradeoffs.** (1) *An eviction rule* — §556 has the compositor never evict, it holds what it is given until told to stop, so a file manager walking a photograph library accumulates every preview it ever made and is eventually refused by the 256 MiB per-link budget; and a refusal is `?`-propagated by `apply_images`, so the failure mode is not "previews stop appearing" but "the file manager quits". The decision (§559) is that the bounded LRU `ThumbnailCache` *is* the policy: every route out of the map — LRU fall-off, `invalidate`, `clear` — records the id that left with it, and `take_evicted_image_ids()` drains that into `Drop`s. The rejected alternative, a separate residency tracker with its own limit, could hold more on the server than in local memory (drawing without re-decoding) but adds a second bounded structure that must agree with the first about what is held, and when they disagree the renderer names an id the server has forgotten, which draws *nothing, silently, by design*. Two details that are easy to get wrong and are asserted by tests: only **actual** removals are recorded, because `invalidate` takes a path and is called routinely for files never cached and a stale drop can forget pixels a later insert re-uploaded under the same derived id; and drops go out **before** uploads in one ordered list, since the budget is `after = held - freed + incoming` — §557's slideshow reason again. (2) *An id keyed on the same three facts as the cache entry* — it was hashed from (path, mtime) while `CacheKey` is (path, mtime, **length**), so a file rewritten twice inside one second (the clock does not move; the length does) produced two cache entries sharing one id, the second upload silently replacing the first and one entry drawing the other's picture. Not a rare race: a resumed download, a double save, a rebuilt asset. `thumbs::image_id(path, mtime, size)` now takes all three and `CacheKey::image_id()` calls it with its own fields so the two cannot drift; a counter was rejected because the id would then be state carried through every path producing a `Thumbnail`, and a re-generated file would get a *new* number and a new upload where a derived id gets a free replacement. `simple_hash` is deliberately **not** changed — it also names the on-disk cache *files*, where keying on two facts is merely conservative rather than incorrect, and changing it would invalidate every user's saved thumbnails for nothing (§560). (3) *A byte-order conversion, because "ARGB" names two opposite layouts here and both are spelled the same way*: `Canvas::to_argb` writes `A, R, G, B`, `BufferFormat::Argb8888` (`gui/remote/src/control.rs:186`) is `B, G, R, A` — a little-endian `u32` of `0xAARRGGBB`. Passing one where the other is wanted is neither a compile error nor a panic; red arrives as blue and alpha is read out of the blue channel. The first draft did exactly that and it was caught by reading the two definitions side by side, not by a test. Neither order can go: the wire order is the format's own definition, the other is already written to users' disks. So `Canvas` gained `from_argb8888`/`to_argb8888` **named after the wire enum rather than its byte order** — `to_bgra` describes the bytes better and is worse, because the caller would then pick between `to_argb` and `to_bgra` by guessing, whereas `to_argb8888` matches `BufferFormat::Argb8888` character for character at the call site — and the conversion lives in `Canvas` rather than as a `chunks_exact_mut(4).reverse()` in the thumbnailer, which would work, would be a *third* statement of the byte order free to drift from the two it sits between, and would silently accept a trailing partial pixel where `from_argb` returns `None` (§561). The relationship is asserted executably, not just documented. What that does *not* fix is that both orders are still `Vec<u8>` with identical signatures: `TD-C-TWO-BYTE-ORDERS-ARE-BOTH-CALLED-ARGB` logs the newtype that would make the mistake impossible, deferred only because it touches every upload site in `gui/**` and `apps/**` at once. **The window itself** is a full `impl App`: a title leading with the folder name, `tick_interval` returning a clock **only while thumbnails remain to be made** (with `completed_count` in the condition as well as `pending_count`, because a batch that has finished generating still has not been filed into the cache), mouse hit-testing that reads *exactly the rectangles the renderer registered* — `DropZoneRegistry` already recorded a row index and threw it away, and the alternative is a second copy of the layout arithmetic in the click handler, which when the two disagree means the user clicks one file and opens another — and a keyboard map of arrows/Home/End/Enter/Backspace/Ctrl+A/F5/Ctrl+H/Alt+Left/Right. The keys that *edit* are deliberately absent and logged as `TD-C-EXPLORER-HAS-NO-EDITING-KEYS`: `fileops.rs` has copy, move, rename and recycle ready, but Delete needs a confirmation and a visible undo, F2 needs an in-place rename field and Ctrl+V needs a clipboard that can hold a file reference — none of which this window has, and a Delete key that recycled the selection with no prompt and no way back is worse than one that does nothing. Scrolling is likewise logged rather than half-built (`TD-C-EXPLORER-DOES-NOT-SCROLL`): it is a viewport change — a first-visible-row offset threaded through three view layouts, a scroll-into-view rule so keyboard movement drags the viewport, wheel handling, and a scrollbar — and folding it into the commit that made the window clickable would have made both harder to review. Writing that entry turned up that `gui/toolkit` has already solved all three (`listview::ListViewport`, `scroll_window::visible_count`, `wheel::Accumulator`, each built for the settings panels that hit this first), so the fix is mostly adoption — and it should take explorer's hand-rolled `move_selection` with it, that being a second copy of `ListViewport::select_prev`/`select_next` written without knowing the first existed. +19 tests (258 → 277 in `explorer`), among them one that decodes an upload's bytes back through `Canvas::from_argb8888`, compares against `Canvas::from_argb` of the stored ones, and then asserts the two byte buffers are `assert_ne!` — a byte-order test that passes trivially if you forget the conversion is a test that does nothing. `guitk` 1129, `imagecodec` 56+6, `imageviewer` 110, `oswindow` 85 all green; clippy `--all-targets` adds no warning to the 33 pre-existing `arithmetic_side_effects` sites already filed as `TD-C-EXPLORER-DOES-ARITHMETIC-ON-UNCHECKED-VALUES`; rustfmt clean. design-decisions.md §559, §560, §561.

Popup TTLs and asking clients to enumerate their own surfaces are not built. design-decisions.md §1304.
